[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_the-customer-journey-has-been-split-down-activity-7459939717422166016-OSNs)

> The customer journey has been split down the middle. 
>
> But businesses are only optimising for one half...
>
> The go-to for your customers used to be to "Google it". 
> But that is rapidly being replaced by AI as the default. 
>
> Now they might Google something, but also read the AI Overview. 
> Or they will even interact with "AI Mode" instead, now.
>
> Or they will ask ChatGPT, Claude or Perplexity directly... 
>
> The point is, search is now both SEO and AEO. 
> And your business needs to be visible in both. 
>
> Start by finding out where your business appears now: 
> https://lnkd.in/gQTVD-CW
>
> That's a full AI Search Visibility Report.
>
> Then read on for a full breakdown of SEO vs. AEO: 
>
> 📣 Top of Funnel: Awareness
>
> SEO:
> → User types keywords into Google
> → Sees list of ranked results
> → Clicks multiple links to compare
>
> AEO:
> → User asks AI a question
> → Gets one synthesised answer
> → Sees 2-3 sources cited
>
> 🧠 Middle of Funnel: Consideration
>
> SEO:
> → User opens 5-10 tabs
> → Reads different sources
> → Compares information manually
> → Forms own conclusion
>
> AEO:
> → AI has already compared sources
> → Answer includes recommendations
> → User trusts AI's synthesis
> → No tab-switching required
>
> 💡 Bottom of Funnel: Decision
>
> SEO:
> → User returns to the best source
> → Bookmarks or remembers brand
> → Takes action on chosen site
>
> AEO:
> → User acts on AI's recommendation
> → Clicks cited source (if needed)
> → Or proceeds without clicking
>
> With traditional SEO, the user did most of the work. 
> They had to research, compare and make their decision. 
>
> Now with AEO, it's AI that does the legwork. 
> It researches, compares, and decides which brands to cite. 
>
> Your customers are searching in both Google and AI tools. 
> It's your job to understand the funnel mechanics and meet them halfway. 
>
> Find out where you stand across both right now with our Visibility Report: https://lnkd.in/gQTVD-CW
>
> If you have any SEO or AEO questions, feel free to drop them below.  
> I will try to get back to many as I can !
>
> ♻️ Save and repost to help others understand the new reality of search. 
> And follow Chris Donnelly for more on mastering both funnels.

> Two types of people need to read this:

> 1. The person is unsure whether to start a business. 
> 2. And the overfunded founder who's lost touch with product market fit. 
>

>
> In 4th place: 
>
> ⏰ The 4-Hour Workweek by Tim Ferriss
> Probably my favourite book ever. 
>
> Most people read it and want to work four hours a week. 
> What it actually teaches is leverage. 
>
> Read it at the start of your career. Then read it again.
>
> In 3rd place: 
>
> 🥉 Shoe Dog by Phil Knight
> The origin story of Nike. 
>
> The Swoosh cost $30. The name came later. 
> The whole thing grew out of momentum rather than strategy. 
>
> It's a reminder that great businesses rarely look like it at the start.
>
> The runner up...
>
> 🥈 Good to Great by Jim Collins
> A foundational book for thinking about what makes an exceptional business. 
>
> I read it heavily in the early years. Worth going back to.
>
> And the clear winner (no pun intended)...
>
> 🏆 Atomic Habits by James Clear
> The best-selling book of a generation for a reason. 
>
> You don't rise to your goals, you fall to your systems. 
>
> Read this if you read nothing else.

> Here are the 3 signals and how to make them work for you: 
>
> ☑️ Signal 1: Authority
> AI cross-references your content against all other info about your brand. 
>
> Focus on: 
> → Backlinks
> → Directory listings
> → Third-party mentions
> → Earned media
>
> If the broader web doesn't validate you, AI won't cite you. 
>
> ☑️ Signal 2: Relevance
> Your content needs to match the exact query intent, not just the general topic. 
>
> Focus on: 
> → Question-format headings
> → Specific answers
> → Current statistics
> → Strong topical coverage
>
> Provide the most accurate and up-to-date information in your niche. 
>
> ☑️ Signal 3: Extractability
> AI parses content in chunks using semantic structure. 
>
> Focus on: 
> → Proper heading hierarchy
> → FAQ schema
> → Short paragraphs
> → Crawable, machine-readable pages
>
> Poorly structured content gets skipped regardless of quality. 
>
> Most brands fall into one of 3 traps:  
>
> 🚫 Trusted, But Invisible Expert
> ↳ Strong authority and relevant content, but poorly structured.
> ↳ AI recognises the credibility but can't extract a clean answer.
>
> 🚫 Visible But Unverified
> ↳ Well-structured and on-topic, but no off-site authority signals.
> ↳ AI can read it, but doesn't trust it enough to cite it.
>
> 🚫 Credible But Off-Topic
> ↳ Strong technical setup and brand authority.
> ↳ Content doesn't match what AI is actually searching for. 
>
> Here are 5 rules to ensure that doesn't happen to you: 
>
> 1. Prioritise third-party validation. 
> AI trusts what others say about you more than what you say about yourself.
>
> 2. Be specific
> Precise answers get cited. General overviews get skipped.
>
> 3. Structure for machines. 
> Dense prose gets ignored regardless of quality.
>
> 4. Stay current. 
> 76.4% of ChatGPT's top-cited pages were updated in the last 30 days.
>
> 5. Track your citations. 
> You can't improve what you don't measure.
>

> 1️⃣ Focus on Your Best Customers
> ↳ Identify who stays longest and buys the most, then build around them.
>
> Why it matters: Become the only option in your category 
> Apply it: List your top 10 clients and shift your focus to them. 
> Common mistake: Treating every client as equal. 
>
> 2️⃣ Fix Your Product Economics
> ↳ Work out your margin per client and cut whatever is killing it.
>
> Why it matters: Thin margins mean revenue costs more to produce. 
> Apply it: Calculate your margin per client after acquisition costs. 
> Common mistake: Chasing revenue without watching margin. 
>
> 3️⃣ Grow Existing Accounts
> ↳ Add a second service to your best clients before you look for new ones.
>
> Why it matters: Turn one client into a long-term high-value account at no cost.
> Apply it: Map the next purchase and present a specific offer within 30 days. 
> Common mistake: Delivering the work, filing the invoice, and moving on. 
>
> 4️⃣ Re-engage Past Clients
> ↳ Go back to the clients who already trust you and make them a new offer.
>
> Why it matters: Reactivating past clients costs almost nothing. 
> Apply it: Send each a short personalised message to one-time clients.  
> Common mistake: Spending the entire marketing budget on new acquisition. 
>
> 5️⃣ Build a Referral Engine
> ↳ Get your content and your clients bringing new business to you.
>
> Why it matters: Referrals + inbound = a cost-effective acquisition channel.
> Apply it: Post your frameworks, case studies and knowledge on LinkedIn. 
> Common mistake: Spending on ads before building a content habit. 
>
> 6️⃣ Hire for Operations
> ↳ Get out of the day-to-day so you can focus on growth.
>
> Why it matters: Running operations takes away from activities that move revenue.
> Apply it: Hire an ops manager or EA and protect your time.

> Claude's writing on its own is pretty much slop.
>
> Here's how to make it sound like you (and not a robot):
>
> When people complain about Claude's tone, they say it's robotic and unnatural. 
>
> Fair enough.  
>
> And if left to its own devices, it will stay that way. 
>
> But Claude is perfectly capable of producing writing that sounds human. 
> Even writing that sounds exactly like you ! 
>
> You just have to put in a little elbow grease to configure it. 
> Do that, and Claude can mimic any tone you give it. 
>
> Here's the exact process I use to capture my tone in Claude: 
>
> Step 1: Create a new Project
> ↳ Open Claude and create a new Project. Name it "My Voice" or "Content Writing."
>
> This is where you'll store tone materials across every session.
>
> Step 2: Define your content goal
> ↳ Pick one content type to start: LinkedIn posts, newsletter sections, emails, or articles.
>
> Don't try to train everything at once. Just test one format first.
>
> Step 3: Write your voice brief
> ↳ Tell Claude exactly how you write. Include tone, sentence structure, banned words, and what you always do.
>
> Prompt template: "Here is how I write. Tone: [describe your tone]. I always [key habits]. I never use [words to avoid]. My sentences are [short/long/varied]. My audience is [who they are]. When I write, I want people to feel [outcome]."
>
> Step 4: Paste in your best examples
> ↳ Give Claude 3 to 5 real pieces of your actual writing. Include your top-performing posts, emails that got replies, writing you read back and thought "yes, that's me." 
>
> Examples teach Claude more than instructions alone.
>
> Step 5: Write the training prompt
> ↳ Tell Claude how to use the brief and examples together. This goes in your Project instructions.
>
> Prompt template: "You are writing in my voice. Use the brief to understand my tone. Use the examples to understand how I write in practice. Match the sentence length, structure, and energy of my examples. Never add words I wouldn't use."
>
> Step 6: Test and correct
> ↳ Give Claude a topic and read the output out loud. Ask: Does this sound like me or like a marketer? Are the sentences right? Would I post this as-is? 
>
> Correct it directly and update your brief with what you learn.
>
> Step 7: Save it as a Skill
> ↳ Go to Settings, open Skills, and save your voice brief and training prompt.
>
> It auto-loads every time you need it, across any device.
>
> Step 8: Use it
> ↳ Open a new chat inside your Project, give Claude a topic or a rough idea, and let it write.
>
> Claude will handle the first draft and you handle the last 20%. 
> The more honest your voice brief, the better the output. 
>
> Include as much detail as you would give to a human ghostwriter. 
>
> 99% of people are still writing content from scratch.
> If you want an edge in 2026, save the sheet below.

> Step 1: Map your root identity
> ↳ Define a 3 to 5-word phrase that captures what your brand does.
> ↳ Build out your topic tree: root identity, categories, and child topics.
>
> Step 2: Identify your competitors
> ↳ Start with known competitors, then go deeper using the Neighbour Theory.
> ↳ The businesses a few streets away are the ones you haven't found yet.
>
> Step 3: Build your prompt universe
> ↳ Add your brand and competitors to Searchable and load your prompt themes.
> ↳ Use the Mentions tab to see exactly where you appear versus where they do.
>
> Step 4: Find your gaps
> ↳ Apply the Missing filter to find prompts your competitors are answering.
> ↳ Segment by intent: Learn, Consider, and Purchase.
>
> Step 5: Find citation gaps
> ↳ Open the Sources tab to see which content is being cited.
> ↳ This reveals editorial and creator partnerships you need to build.
>
> Step 6: Close the gap
> ↳ On-page: learn specific formats for each layer of the sales funnel.
> ↳ Off-page: co-produce content with creators being cited in your space. 
>
> Step 7: Measure and track
> ↳ Add target prompts to Prompt Tracking and monitor daily movement.
> ↳ Track mentions, citations, and source improvements over time.
>
> Keyword research is still important to rank in search engines. 
> You need those to get cited by AI as well. 
>
> But prompt research is about showing up in AI recommendations.  
>

## Post 60 — 2026-03-22

**Likes:** 1186 | **Comments:** 269 | **Shares:** 121

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_no-founder-is-above-learning-the-fundamentals-activity-7441468044968882176-li5w)

> No founder is above learning the fundamentals. 
>
> Every billionaire CEO knows these 12 business terms:  
>
> And if you're building or scaling a business in 2026, you should too.  
>
> When I started Verb Brands at 22, I didn't know what half these terms meant.
>
> I was running a growing agency, hiring people, winning clients, 
> And making decisions that would shape the next five years of the business.
>
> But if someone had asked me about burn rate, CAC, or EBITDA, 
> I'd have nodded and quietly Googled it later.
>
> Not knowing the language of business means you:
>
> 🚫 Make slower decisions 
> 🚫 Miss warning signs earlier
> 🚫 Walk into rooms less prepared than you should be
>
> I had to learn it the hard way. But you don't have to.
>
> Here are the 12 terms every CEO should know by heart: 
>
> 1. CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost)
> ↳ The total cost to acquire one new customer.
> ↳ If your CAC is higher than what a customer is worth, the business doesn't work.
>
> 2. Unit Economics
> ↳ The profit or loss made on a single customer or transaction.
> ↳ Poor unit economics means you lose money faster as you scale.
>
> 3. Cash Flow
> ↳ The money moving in and out of your business over time.
> ↳ Revenue on paper means nothing if the cash isn't in the account.
>
> 4. Runway
> ↳ How long the business can operate before running out of cash.
> ↳ A founder with 6 months left makes very different decisions to one with 24.
>
> 5. Burn Rate
> ↳ The amount of cash the business spends each month.
> ↳ You can't manage runway without knowing this number cold.
>
> 6. Working Capital
> ↳ Current assets minus current liabilities.
> ↳ Negative working capital is a warning sign founders miss until it's too late.
>
> 7. PMF (Product Market Fit)
> ↳ When a product meets a real need and customers pay for it consistently.
> ↳ Don't scale spend until you have it.
>
> 8. Churn
> ↳ The percentage of customers who stop paying over time.
> ↳ Acquisition means nothing if they don't stay.
>
> 9. Operating Leverage
> ↳ The ability to grow revenue without a proportional increase in costs.
> ↳ This is what separates a scalable business from an expensive one. 
>
> 10. EBITDA
> ↳ Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation.
> ↳ Know yours before you walk into any deal room.
>
> 11. Gross Margin
> ↳ Revenue minus direct costs, as a percentage of revenue.
> ↳ High-margin businesses have options. Low-margin businesses are fragile. 
>
> 12. ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue)
> ↳ Total predictable revenue expected over a year from subscriptions or contracts.
> ↳ It tells you how much revenue is locked in before the year starts.
>
> If someone had handed me this list at 22, 
> I would have years of my life back. 
>
> Take it from someone who's spent 15+ years as an entrepreneur...
> You are never too good or too experienced to learn the basics. 
>
> Is there a fundamental business term I missed? 
> Drop it in the comments below. 
>

> Building a business on passion < Building a business on profit
>
> Let me explain: 
>
> That might sound ill-intentioned.
>
> However, you can be passionate about what you're building... 
> In fact, I'd argue that you need to be to a degree. 
>
> But leading with passion won't ensure your company makes a profit. 
>
> You need a model that puts profit as the primary goal and builds from there. 
>
> Here’s the framework I use when evaluating a business idea:
>
> Step 1: The First Decision 
> Is it a business idea or a passion project? 
>
> Ask three questions: 
> 1. Who can you help?
> 2. Who cares?
> 3. Who can buy?
>
> ✅ Profit is your north star
> You listen, iterate, and find what people pay for again and again.
>
> 🚫 Identity is your north star
> It's harder starting from zero, and you risk wasting years. 
>
> Step 2: Product Criteria 
> 4 things your product must have: 
>
> 1. High Margin: No margin = no room to grow
> 2. Proven Demand: Red oceans beat blue oceans
> 3. Specific Niche: Focused beats broad every time
> 4. Content Runway: Can you tell stories about it forever?
>
> Step 3: Niche Down 
>
> Get it down to one customer, one product, and one platform.
> You can expand later. In the beginning, being niche is your advantage.
>
> Step 4: Idea Generation 
> 7 questions to find a really good idea: 
>
> 1. What are you really good at?
> 2. What do you wish someone had built for you?
> 3. What are your biggest daily frustrations?
> 4. What could you work on for the next 10 years?
> 5. What content does your audience already love?
> 6. What do people ask you for help with?
> 7. What do you find yourself doing in your spare time?
>
> Step 5: Find Your Angle 
> Complete your Ikigai: 
>
> Love: What excites you?
> Good at: Where's your edge?
> Paid for: What will people buy?
> World needs: What problem exists?
> Sweet spot: Where all four overlap
>
> Step 6: Choose Your Model 
> Pick a business model: 
>
> Agency: High margin, founder-dependent early on.
> Community: Scales without 1:1 time investment.
> Course: One-time build, long-tail revenue.
> SaaS: High margin at scale.
> Coaching: Hard to scale past your own hours.
>
> Step 7: Scale the Idea 
>
> Build a product ecosystem. 
> 8-figure businesses require a product ladder.
>
> See the cheat sheet for more details 👇

> If you've been struggling to get good results from Claude...
>
> Anthropic has released the perfect prompt: 
>
> As you may well know, Claude has overtaken ChatGPT. At least, it seems.
> (For now, who knows what Sam has up his sleeve).
>
> So, you may as well learn how to use Anthropic's tool.
>
> There's no excuse not to implement this, as it comes straight from their team. 
>
> If there was ever a prompt to steal, this would be this one ! 
>
> Here's the full structure:
>
> 🎯 1. Task context
> ↳ Vague context produces vague output.
> ↳ Set the scene properly before you ask for anything.
>
> 🗣️ 2. Tone context
> ↳ Tell it exactly how to communicate (direct, actionable, no filler)
> ↳ Every output should be specific enough to hand straight to a team member.
>
> 📎 3. Background data, documents, and images
> ↳ Feed it everything relevant (URLs, existing content, rankings)
> ↳ The more context it has, the sharper the output.
>
> 📋 4. Detailed task description and rules
> ↳ Be specific about what you want it to focus on and what the rules are.
> ↳ Tell it exactly what matters and what to ignore.
>
> 💡 5. Examples
> ↳ Paste in an example of the output format you want.
> ↳ Claude follows examples better than instructions alone.
>
> 🕐 6. Conversation history
> ↳ If there's previous work or feedback from earlier sessions, include it.
> ↳ Claude has no memory between conversations unless you give it one.
>
> ✅ 7. Immediate task description
> ↳ After all the context, tell it exactly what you need today.
> ↳ Specific, scoped, with one clear request.
>
> 🧠 8. Think step by step
> ↳ Ask it to reason before it responds. 
> ↳ This step alone dramatically improves output quality.
>
> 📐 9. Output formatting
> ↳ Tell it how to structure the response before it writes anything.
> ↳ Summary, top priority fixes, secondary recommendations, and quick wins.
>
> We actually use this prompt structure when using Claude whilst building Searchable.
>
> And you can use the same, in our free AI SEO Agent.

> For decades, marketing operated in a clear funnel. 
>
> Now, it's taken on a completely new shape: 
>
> And most marketers have yet to respond accordingly. 
> Some might call it a network, others a web. 
>
> But the point is that it's more complex, with far more touchpoints. 
> And most businesses are only showing up at one or two touchpoints.
>
> Therefore missing out on huge opportunities for visibility.
>
> (To find where you're missing out, we actually have a free tool for just that at Searchable. Grab your free visibility report here: https://lnkd.in/g6XApkfm) 
>
> This is what marketing actually involves in 2026... 
>
> ☑️ Google Search
>
> What to do:
>
> - Target conversational queries, rather than short-tail keywords.
> - Strengthen your E-E-A-T signals by adding and updating content regularly.
> - Answer questions directly in the first paragraph to capture featured snippet positions.
>
> ☑️ AI Search (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude)
>
> What to do:
>
> - Structure your content with clear definitions, FAQ sections, and schema markup.
> - Write in natural language that answers specific questions.
> - Get mentioned on third-party sites, forums, and trusted publications. 
>
> ☑️ Social Search (LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok, X)
>
> What to do:
>
> - Participate in genuine conversations in your niche. 
> - Share original educational content that get saved and reshared.
> - Publish consistently so the algorithm associates your profile with your topic.
>
> ☑️ Video Search (YouTube, TikTok)
>
> What to do:
>
> - Write video titles as questions people actually ask.
> - Add full transcripts to every video so AI crawlers can parse the content.
> - Create short summaries of longer content and publish them as Shorts or Reels.
>
> ☑️ Community & Trust Platforms (Reddit, Quora, G2, Trustpilot)
>
> What to do:
>
> - Seed value-driven answers on Reddit threads relevant to your category.
> - Encourage customers to leave detailed reviews that mention specific use cases.
> - Monitor and respond to mentions so AI platforms see active brand engagement.
>
> ☑️ Traditional Search (Bing)
>
> What to do:
>
> - Don't ignore Bing. ChatGPT pulls heavily from Bing's index.
> - Optimise for Bing with clean structure, fast load times, schema markup.
> - The brands that do are showing up in ChatGPT results their competitors aren't.
>
> ☑️ Voice Search (Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant)
>
> What to do:
>
> - Write in natural, conversational language that mirrors how people speak.
> - Answer "near me" and "best for" queries explicitly in your content.
> - Format key pages as direct question-and-answer pairs.
>
> Again, to spot where you are missing opportunities...
> Highly encourage you to grab a free visibility report here: https://lnkd.in/g6XApkfm
>

>

>
> If you want to rank in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, etc,

>
> (If you're looking for immediate AEO suggestions... 
> We built a free AI Agent at Searchable you can experiment with for that: https://lnkd.in/gVwCJJDX) 
>
> If you're not optimising for AI Search now, while it's still an advantage, 
> You could lose more revenue than you think.  
>
> Here's how to build a winning AEO strategy in 2026:
>
> 1. Understand How AI Engines Find You
>
> AI models like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Claude pull from three sources:
>
> - Training data 
> - Live web crawls 
> - Trusted sources 
>
> 2. Fix Your Technical Foundation
>
> Here's the technical checklist:
>
> ✓ Create/optimise llms.txt to guide AI crawlers
> ✓ Configure robots.txt to allow GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot
> ✓ Fix crawlability issues (no broken links)
> ✓ Optimise page load speed by compressing images
> ✓ Ensure mobile responsiveness by testing on mobile devices
> ✓ Implement structured data (schema markup)
> ✓ Set up XML sitemaps for all important pages
> ✓ Configure HTTP headers properly
>
> If AI can't crawl your site, it can't cite you.
>
> 3. Structure Your Content For Direct Answers
>
> AI engines favour content that directly answers questions.
>
> - Write in Q&A format. 
> - Use clear headings. 
> - Answer the question in the first paragraph.
> - Think like a search query: "What is [X]?" "How do I [Y]?" "Best [Z] for [A]?"
>
> 4. Implement Schema Markup
>
> Schema markup speaks directly to search engines and AI crawlers. 
>
> For e-commerce: Product schema 
> For blogs: Article schema 
> For local businesses: LocalBusiness schema 
>
> 5. Build Citation Authority
>
> AI models cite sources they've seen referenced repeatedly.
>
> That means:
>
> - Getting featured in industry roundups and "best of" guides
> - Earning mentions on high-authority sites. 
>
> The more credible citations, the more AI trusts you.
>
> 6. Track And Iterate
>
> Here's what to monitor:
>
> - Brand mentions across AI platforms
> - Which prompts surface your brand
> - Competitor citations 
> - Content freshness
>
> There is a window open now to get ahead of AI search. 
> But you have to be ready to accept and act on these changes. 
>

## Post 90 — 2026-03-01

**Likes:** 1519 | **Comments:** 316 | **Shares:** 180

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_if-you-want-to-start-a-business-you-need-activity-7433857898528563200-GkDD)

> If you want to start a business, you need to know the rules.
>
> These are 15 KPIs every Founder should know: 
>
> Follower growth can boost confidence and visibility. 
>
> But those types of metrics don't drive sustainable growth and profitability. 
> Without tracking the right KPIs, it's impossible to grow your business.  
>
> That's why I've combined the top 15 into one cheat sheet. 
>
> You should save it if you're serious about scaling this year 👇
>
> But I'll give you a quick rundown here as well: 
>
> (See the cheat sheet for how to calculate each one) 
>
> 1. Net Revenue Retention (NRR)
>
> Measures revenue kept after churn, contractions, and expansions.
> This is the north-star for SaaS/AI businesses.
>
> 2. Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)
>
> Average revenue a customer generates over their relationship with you.
> Always paired with CAC to prove ROI of growth.
>
> 3. Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
>
> Average spend required to win a new customer.
> Set budgets and check efficiency of growth.
>
> 4. LTV to CAC Ratio
>
> Compares lifetime value of a customer to acquisition cost.
> Validate sustainable growth. Rule of thumb: >3 is strong.
>
> 5. Monthly Active Users (MAU)
>
> Number of unique active users in a month.
> Measure adoption and stickiness.
>
> 6. Churn Rate 
>
> Number of customers or revenue lost in a period. 
> Track retention. Rising churn = weak product-market fit.
>
> 7. Burn Multiple 
>
> Cash burned for every $1 in new ARR. 
> Use it during fundraising and growth phases. 
>
> 8. EBITDA 
>
> Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, amortisation. 
> Measure profitability at scale.
>
> 9. Operating Cash Flow 
>
> Net cash from operating activities. 
> Confirm the business can fund itself.
>
> 10. Customer Retention Rate 
>
> Percentage of customers who continue to buy from you over a set period. 
> Measure loyalty and product-market fit.
>
> 11. Revenue Growth Rate 
>
> Percentage increase in revenue over a given period. 
> Show business momentum and scalability.
>
> 12. AI Search Visibility 
>
> Share of prompts where your brand/product is surfaced in AI answers. 
> Measure discoverability in AI-led search.
>
> 13. Runway (Cash Runway) 
>
> How many months your business can operate before running out of cash. 
> Balance growth vs. cash preservation.
>
> 14. Experiment Velocity 
>
> Number of product, content, or GTM experiments shipped. 
> Track speed of iteration and learning.
>
> 15. Gross Margin 
>
> Profitability after direct costs, including AI infra. 
> Prove scalability and efficiency to investors.
>
> Social media is useful for many things. 
>
> But it tells you very little about the long-term health of your business. 
>
> These are the metrics that matter if you want to scale. 
>
> What are the primary KPIs you're tracking in your business? 
> Leave a comment below. 
>

>
> GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation)
> Get cited in AI-generated responses on ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Claude.
>

>
> We've created this free visibility report to analyse your current gaps:

>
> Here's what you need to know right now: 
>
> ➡️ SEO = Appearing in traditional search engines (Google, Bing)
>
> Focus: Rankings and click-through traffic
> Outcome: Your page appears in search results
>
> ➡️ AEO = Content extracted into Google Snippets and short AI answers
>
> Focus: Featured snippets, answer boxes, "People Also Ask," quick AI responses

## Post 95 — 2026-02-25

**Likes:** 2046 | **Comments:** 451 | **Shares:** 259

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_the-number-one-most-ineffective-phrase-within-activity-7432408083873783809-i03z)

> The number one most ineffective phrase within business: 
>
> ”Let’s create a plan”. Here’s why: 
>
> An incorrect plan means poor execution and no growth.
>
> In order to approach your business with clarity... 
> Adopt these 3 types of planning 👇
>
> Strategic Planning 🗺️
>
> What is it:
> Sets the long-term vision and direction for the business.
>
> Timeline:
> 3-5 years out.
>
> Use case:
> Deciding to expand into a new market.
> Choosing to build a product vs acquire one.
> Planning a fundraise or an exit.
>
> Suited to:
> CEOs, Founders, Co-Founders, Board Members.
>
> Top tips:
> Keep it to 3 priorities max.
> Decide what you WON'T do.
> Revisit it annually.
>
> Common errors:
> Setting goals so vague they could mean anything.
> Avoiding the hard trade-offs.
> Trying to go after 5 markets at once and winning none.
>
> Tactical Planning 🔀
>
> What is it:
> Turns the strategy into specific initiatives and projects.
>
> Timeline:
> 1-3 years ahead.
>
> Use case:
> Launching a European sales team to support expansion.
> Hiring 10 engineers over 6 months to ship a new product.
> Running a paid beta programme for a new features.
>
> Suited to:
> Head of Departments, VPs, Senior Managers, COOs.
>
> Top tips:
> Assign one owner per project.
> Set quarterly checkpoints.
> Kill projects that aren't working.
>
> Common errors:
> Taking on too many initiatives at once.
> Building plans that sound good but have no clear owner.
> Spending 3 months planning and 1 month executing.
>
> Operational Planning ⚙️
>
> What is it:
> Daily and weekly execution of tasks and processes.
>
> Timeline:
> Days to 12 months.
>
> Use case:
> Weekly content publishing schedule.
> Daily sales outreach targets and pipeline reviews.
> Monthly reporting cadence.
>
> Suited to:
> Team Leads, Managers, Project Managers, Individual Contributors.
>
> Top tips:
> Build SOPs for anything done more than twice.
> Track the 2-3 KPIs that actually matter.
> Keep plans realistic.
>
> Common errors:
> Confusing being busy with making progress.
> Losing sight of why you're doing the work.
> Overloading teams with tasks.
>
> I see many teams blending all three and lack clarity to progress.
>
> When you separate it into these three approaches, it's a bit of a progress unlock to be honest.
>
> Give your team the clarity they need to grow !
>
> Anyway I'm curious to hear your experience with planning in your business...
>
> Is it something you or your team typically struggle with?
> Let me know and I'll see if I can provide guidance.

## Post 96 — 2026-02-24

**Likes:** 1689 | **Comments:** 500 | **Shares:** 181

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_42-of-startups-fail-because-no-one-wants-activity-7432045764610076672-lDsl)

> 42% of startups fail because no one wants what they built.  
>
> Here’s how to fix that: 
>
> It blows my mind how many businesses still get this wrong. 
>
> The purpose of your minimum viable product (MVP) is in the name. 
>
> It’s the simplest version of your product with the most viable parts...
>
> And the best way to tell if people actually want what you’re selling. 
>
> It shouldn't: 
>
> 🚫 Have loads of features
> 🚫 Solve numerous problems instead of one
> 🚫 Basically be a full product, instead of a test
>
> That's just a waste of time and resources.
>
> When in doubt, subtract, don't add.
>
> I recently built an MVP myself and documented the entire process. 
>
> It's the same playbook I used to kickstart multiple 7 and 8-figure businesses, 
> Including The Creator Accelerator and Searchable... 
>
> Save and steal it for your own business 👇
>
> 1. Who is my MVP for?
>
> 👥 Who is your target audience?
> ❓ What problem are you solving?
> 💸 How does your MVP provide value?
>
> 2. The Problem Validation Phase
>
> Go through the checklist of validation steps (below) 👇
>
> 💬 Would you actually pay for this?
> 🔸 If no one is eager for a solution, rethink your MVP.
>
> 3. The Core MVP Features
>
> 🏆 The golden rule: Solve ONE specific problem in the simplest way possible.
>
> What your MVP should do:
> ✅ Focus on the absolute essential feature(s).
> ✅ Be usable without extensive training.
> ✅ Provide immediate value.
> ✅ Be built in 4–8 weeks max.
>
> Common MVP mistakes:
> ❌ Trying to build the full product vision from day one.
> ❌ Packing too many features into v1.
>
> 4. The MVP Launch Strategy
>
> Get early adopters through:
>  
> 🔗 Social Media
> 🎟️ Early Access
> 📧 Email Outreach
>
> First users = your best testers.
>
> 5. Feedback & Iteration Process
>
> Measure everything, improve constantly.
>
> 🌀 Key Feedback Loop:
> Launch → Get Feedback → Iterate → Relaunch
>
> 6. Monetisation & Scaling Strategy
>
> Ways to monetise:
> 💵 One-time purchase
> 💳 Subscription
> 🛒 Upsells
>
> Key signs your MVP is ready to scale:
> ✅ Strong retention & repeat users
> ✅ Demand for more features
> ✅ Customers willing to pay
> 	
> The keys to a successful MVP are repetition and consistency. 
>
> To ensure the best outcomes, make sure to: 
>
> - Build fast, validate often, and iterate quickly. 
> - Launch it early and use incoming feedback to improve. 
> - Remove any features that aren't working before adding more. 
>
> When it comes to an MVP, think simplicity over complexity. 
>
> What's your biggest obstacle to building your MVP? 
> Let me know in the comments. 👇
>

> SEO was never "easy"... but it was simpler.  
>
> Then the behavioural shift happened that you cannot ignore.
>
> And now SEO is not just about Google anymore. 
>
> It's expanded to LLMs and AI Overviews on Google. 
>
> You might not even know if you're visible in these AI responses or not...
>
> (Btw, Searchable has a free tool that checks your visibility and gives you a full report: https://lnkd.in/g6XApkfm)
>
> ChatGPT processes 2.5 billion searches daily.
>
> And a good chunk of those are going to determine purchases...
>
> Businesses are still in denial about it, but I suggest you don't be. 
>
> Here's what you need to know 👇
>
> 1️⃣ There are 3 types of search visibility: 
>
> SEO (Search Engine Optimisation)
> Outcome: You rank higher on Google, so more people find your website.
>
> AEO (Answer Engine Optimisation)
> Outcome: You become the direct answer Google gives.
>
> GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation)
> Outcome: AI tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini cite your brand.
>
> 2️⃣ Old SEO is not the same as New SEO. 
>
> Old SEO focused on:
>
> - Keyword density and exact match phrases
> - Backlinks at volume (quality was secondary)
> - Page rank and domain authority
> - Getting clicks to your website
>
> New SEO focuses on:
>
> - Natural language and question-based content
> - Authoritative citations from trusted sources
> - Entity recognition and schema markup
> - Being cited before the click happens
>
> 3️⃣ You need to be found inside LLMs. 
>
> There are 4 levels to this.
>
> Level 1: Crawlable
> AI can access your website.
>
> - AI crawlers are not blocked in robots.txt
> - Site loads fast, clean HTML, updated sitemaps
> - But being crawlable doesn't mean being visible
>
> Level 2: Understandable
> AI can make sense of your content.
>
> - Schema markup implemented 
> - Clear headings, Q&A formatting, short paragraphs
> - Answer-first structure so AI can extract what it needs
>
> Level 3: Trustworthy
> AI recognises you as a credible source.
>
> - Backlinks and citations from high-authority domains
> - Real author bios with visible credentials on every page
> - Wikipedia, Wikidata, and Google Knowledge Panel claimed
>
> Level 4: Citation-Worthy
> AI actively recommends and cites your brand.
>
> - Original research and proprietary data
> - Content that answers specific questions 
> - Recently updated and fact-checked regularly
>
> When we built Searchable, we implemented all this knowledge into the product to help businesses rank inside LLMs 
> (Without working harder)...
>
> And I'm thrilled with the results so far: 
>
> £1 million turnover in 60 days
> 700+ paying customers
> Winning clients daily from legacy SEO competitors.
>
> It's completely automated to find gaps and fix them autonomously.
>
> Which you can find with our free AI Visibility Report: https://lnkd.in/g6XApkfm

> These are the 8 prompt frameworks I use to power my businesses:
>
> 1️⃣ R-T-F
> Role: Specify the role you want the AI to assume.
> Task: Define the task you want the AI to perform.
> Format: Indicate the format in which you want the output.
>
> 2️⃣ S-O-L-V-E
> Situation: Define the context or situation.
> Objective: Specify the goals.
> Limits: Define any limitations or constraints.
> Vision: Outline the vision or goal.
> Execution: Plan the steps for execution.
>
> 3️⃣ T-A-G
> Task: Define the task at hand.
> Action: State the action needed.
> Goal: Clarify the goal to be achieved.
>
> 4️⃣ R-A-C-E
> Role: Specify the character you want the AI to play.
> Action: State the basic instruction or the job you need to be done.
> Context: Provide the background information the AI will need.
> Expectation: Describe the outcome you need.
>
> 5️⃣ D-R-E-A-M
> Define: Define the problem or context.
> Research: State the research needed.
> Execute: How to execute the plan.
> Analyse: How to analyse the results.
> Measure: Define how to measure the outcomes.
>
> 6️⃣ P-A-C-T
> Problem: Define the problem.
> Approach: Describe the approach.
> Checks: Write about potential compromises.
> Test: Define the test or measurement.
>
> 7️⃣ C-A-R-E
> Context: Give the context.
> Action: Describe the action needed.
> Result: Clarify the expected result.
> Example: Provide an example for clarity.
>
> 8️⃣ R-I-S-E
> Role: Specify the role.
> Input: Describe the input needed.
> Steps: Could you ask for steps to follow?
> Expectation: Describe the expectation.
>
> AI is the single biggest source of leverage across all my businesses.
> But we couldn't have achieved any of it without learning how to prompt.
>
> If you spend 1-2 hours scrolling on Instagram per day...
> I know you have time to learn these prompting techniques.

## Post 108 — 2026-02-11

**Likes:** 1811 | **Comments:** 435 | **Shares:** 179

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_ai-agents-and-agentic-ai-are-not-the-same-activity-7427334638345400320-Xp_V)

> AI Agents and Agentic AI are not the same thing. 
>
> Your competitors already know the difference:  
>
> There are actually 3 major types of AI workflows you need to know.
>
> Each one fills a slightly different gap in your business.  
>
> But be warned: the window is narrowing. 
>
> Your competitors are already using them to automate their businesses.  
>
> Here's how they differ (and how to use them properly): 
>
> 🤖 Non-Agentic AI
> ↳ Basic prompt-response AI with no memory/reasoning. 
>
> ⚙️ How it works:
>
> - User types a single prompt, model processes 
> - Generates a direct response immediately 
> - Interaction ends with no context retention
>
> ✅ Pros:
> ↳ Fast, cheap, and universally accessible
> ↳ Requires no technical build or integration
> ↳ Great for clear, one-off tasks
>
> 🚫 Cons:
> ↳ No reasoning or context awareness
> ↳ Quality depends heavily on prompts
> ↳ Struggles with multi-step work
>
> 📈 How to build fast:
> ↳ Open ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini
> ↳ Write clear, specific prompts with context
> ↳ Copy output, edit as needed, and repeat
>
> 🧠 Agentic AI
> ↳ A self-managing AI system that can plan and execute. 
>
> ⚙️ How it works:
>
> - The system breaks your goal into sub-tasks
> - Connects to tools, APIs, data sources 
> - Evaluates results with feedback loops
>
> ✅ Pros:
> ↳ Handles complex, changing projects 
> ↳ Can integrate with tools and databases
> ↳ Produces more reliable outcomes 
>
> 🚫 Cons:
> ↳ Slower and more expensive than agents
> ↳ Requires human oversight and guardrails
> ↳ Risk of overbuilding for simple problems
>
> 📈 How to build fast:
> ↳ Start with a code-native LLM like Claude Code
> ↳ Give structured goals, constraints, & acceptance criteria
> ↳ Add an execution loop and persist memory
>
> ⚡ AI Agent
> ↳ Single-task AI worker designed to automate one task.
>
> ⚙️ How it works:
>
> - User defines one clear responsibility
> - Agent receives inputs, accesses connected tools
> - Executes and outputs without guidance
>
> ✅ Pros:
> ↳ Automates repetitive, time-consuming tasks
> ↳ Quick setup and cost-efficient
> ↳ Easy to test and refine within roles
>
> 🚫 Cons:
> ↳ It can't handle broader projects 
> ↳ Breaks if inputs are unclear or data is missing
> ↳ Needs orchestration to work alongside other agents
>
> 📈 How to build fast:
> ↳ Define one clear outcome with measurable success criteria
> ↳ Connect the agent to structured inputs (e.g. CRM)
> ↳ Use worfklow tools like Zapier, MNake, or n8n
>
> TL;DR: 
>
> AI Agents perform single-task automation. 
> Agentic AI is for multi-step problem solving.  
>
> Dominant businesses have graduated to building these AI systems.  
>
> Searchable is the perfect starting point for Agentic AI. 
>

>
> Letting you focus on your business.

> Demand generation ≠ lead generation.
>
> Not knowing the difference is killing your business:
>
> One is about visibility and interest in your business. 
> The other is about actual conversions that generate revenue. 
>
> You need both to feasibly grow a business. 
>
> Putting the mechanisms in place early will help a lot down the line. 
>
> Here's a clear breakdown of each: 
>
> 🫴 Demand Generation
> ↳ Build awareness and interest before buyers are ready to purchase.
>
> Role: Create trust and visibility across your entire market. 
>
> Where it sits: Top of funnel—before people are ready to buy.
>
> Who it targets: ~95% of your total addressable market, many of whom are unaware. 
>
> Tactics:
>
> - Ungated content
> - Thought leadership
> - Educational videos
> - Newsletters
> - Communities
>
> Mindset: Provide value up front so buyers trust and remember you. 
>
> Difficulty:
>
> - Hard to measure with traditional metrics
> - Requires consistent, value-led content
> - Takes time before it shows pipeline impact
> - Must work with sales alignment
> - Needs strategic distribution channels
>
> How success is defined:
>
> - Brand recall and recognition
> - Trust and expertise established
> - Increase in high-intent inbound over time
> - Higher conversion when buyers are ready
> - More efficient pipeline overall
>
> 🤝 Lead Generation
> ↳ Capture contact information and convert people showing buying intent.
>
> Role: Move ready buyers quickly through validation to a sale.
>
> Where it sits: Mid/bottom of funnel—when people are ready to talk to sales.
>
> Who it targets: ~5% of your market that is meaningfully ready. 
>
> Tactics:
>
> - Landing pages with forms
> - Gated eBooks
> - Demos
> - Free trials
> - Direct-response ads
>
> Mindset: Capture and move them through validation to a sale.
>
> Difficulty:
>
> - Easier to count leads and MQLs
> - Shorter feedback loops
> - Conversion optimisation is measurable
> - Risk of low-quality leads
> - Can feel productive without creating demand
>
> How success is defined:
>
> - Number of leads captured
> - MQL and SQL counts
> - Short-term conversion from form fills
> - Immediate pipeline contribution
> - Optimisation of capture mechanisms
>
> Lead gen might be more measurable and feel productive.
>
> But the pipeline will dry up if you never build demand.
>
> ✅ Demand generation fills the top of the funnel with buyers who trust you.
> ✅ Lead generation converts that trust into sales when buyers are ready.
>
> But be warned, AI is shifting demand generation as we speak.  
>
> You need to think beyond Google to the new places customers search...
>
> Namely ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and other AI platforms.

## Post 113 — 2026-02-07

**Likes:** 1029 | **Comments:** 387 | **Shares:** 123

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_the-market-doesnt-reward-overinflated-egos-activity-7425885356740280320-Ht35)

> The market doesn't reward overinflated egos. 
>
> Your "billion-dollar" idea is probably worth 1000s.
>
> A product that belongs in a $2M market will drown in a $200B one. 
>
> You only need to know three things to determine market size: 
>
> TAM → Everyone in the world who could buy your product. 
> SAM → The select people who can feasibly buy your product. 
> SOM → The number of places you'll actually deliver to. 
>
> Here's the full breakdown of each one: 
>
> 🌎 TAM → Total Addressable Market
> ↳ The full revenue opportunity if you captured 100% of the market.
>
> How It Works
> ↳ Calculate the broadest possible market
> ↳ Includes every potential customer 
>
> When To Use
> ↳ Validate if a market is big enough to pursue
> ↳ Attract investors who want to see scale potential
>
> How To Calculate
> ↳ Customer base × average annual spend
> ↳ Use industry reports or analyst research
>
> Pros
> ✅ Shows market ceiling — easy to communicate scale
> ✅ Useful in high‑level planning and fundraising
>
> Cons
> 🚫 Unrealistic — you’ll never capture it all
> 🚫 Can mislead founders into overestimating opportunity
>
> 👥 SAM → Serviceable Addressable Market
> ↳ The portion of the TAM your product can actually serve.
>
> How It Works
> ↳ Takes TAM and removes markets you cannot serve
> ↳ Factors in product features, language, or region limitations
>
> When To Use
> ↳ Planning go‑to‑market and expansion strategy
> ↳ Setting realistic growth goals
>
> How To Calculate
> ↳ Start with TAM → remove areas you can’t serve
> ↳ Focus on the audience matching your product scope
>
> Pros
> ✅ Grounds big market numbers in reality
> ✅ Useful for targeting and prioritisation
>
> Cons
> 🚫 Still assumes 100% share in reachable segment
> 🚫 Requires detailed market data (not always easy to get)
>
> 📦 SOM → Serviceable Obtainable Market
> ↳ The slice of SAM you can realistically win in 1–3 years.
>
> How It Works
> ↳ Starts with SAM and factors in execution capacity + competition
> ↳ Represents the share you could actually capture 
>
> When To Use
> ↳ Building 1–3 year revenue forecasts
> ↳ Setting sales targets and hiring plans
>
> How To Calculate
> ↳ Estimate achievable market share of SAM 
> ↳ Analyse competitor penetration and your growth rate
>
> Pros
> ✅ Forces realistic planning
> ✅ Anchors forecasts to achievable milestones
>
> Cons
> 🚫 Conservative — can underplay upside
> 🚫 Requires accurate competitive intel
>
> Most founders try to reach their TAM, neglect their SAM, and lose their SOM.  
>
> Start with the smallest denominator and work from there. 
>
> If you can capture your SOM, scaling at every level becomes easier. 
>
> Have you determined your TAM, SAM, and SOM? Or are these new to you? 
> Share your thoughts in the comments. 
>

> Agentic AI is not “ChatGPT with extra steps.” 
>
> Here's how to explain it to your leadership team: 
>
> ChatGPT can perform complex tasks. 
>
> But Agentic AI is an elevated experience. 
>
> Here are the 7 layers it uses to build real systems: 
>
> 1. Machine Learning 
>
> Identify data patterns and improve performance.
>
> → Supervised learning for labelled data predictions
> → Unsupervised learning for pattern discovery
> → Reinforcement learning for optimal decision-making
> → Feature extraction and pattern recognition
> → Model training, evaluation, and optimisation
>
> Tools: AWS SageMaker, Google Vertex AI, Azure ML
>
> 2. Large Language Models (LLMs)
>
> Comprehend natural language and process multiple inputs.
>
> → Natural language understanding and reasoning
> → Tokenisation and embeddings for text processing
> → Multimodal input handling (text, image, audio)
> → Pre-training on massive datasets
> → Fine-tuning, adapters, and prompt engineering
> → Extended context windows for long conversations
>
> Tools: OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini
>
> 3. Generative AI 
>
> Generate new content across multimedia. 
>
> → Text and code generation from prompts
> → Image and video synthesis
> → Speech recognition (ASR) and text-to-speech (TTS)
> → Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for accuracy
> → Structured output generation with validation
>
> Tools: ChatGPT, Midjourney, Runway, ElevenLabs
>
> 4. AI Agents 
>
> Plan tasks and execute autonomously.
>
> → Task planning and decomposition
> → Tool use and function calling
> → API execution and integration
> → Memory and context management
> → Autonomous execution with error handling
> → State persistence across sessions
>
> Tools: LangChain, AutoGPT, CrewAI
>
> 5. Agentic Systems 
>
> AI agents working together with specialised roles.
>
> → Multi-agent collaboration and specialisation
> → Inter-agent communication protocols
> → Workflow orchestration and task routing
> → Shared state coordination
> → Failure recovery and parallel execution
>
> Tools: Microsoft AutoGen, LangGraph, Semantic Kernel
>
> 6. Agentic AI 
>
> Sets goals and adapts behaviour.
>
> → Goal setting and decomposition
> → Goal chaining for complex outcomes
> → Long-term autonomous operation
> → Dynamic decision-making with feedback loops
> → Self-improvement and adaptive behaviour
>
> Tools: Custom implementations, research frameworks
>
> 7. Governance, Safety & Control
>
> Ensure AI safe, transparent operations. 
>
> → Human-in-the-loop oversight and approval
> → Guardrails and operational constraints
> → Observability, tracing, and audit logs
> → Risk management and compliance controls
> → Rollbacks, overrides, and cost controls
>
> Tools: LangSmith, Weights & Biases, custom monitoring
>
> For Searchable, we needed multi-agent workflows to build out our original product. 
>
> That's not possible with an LLM alone.
>
> Agentic AI is the future of building businesses faster and smarter.

> I run a £20K/month research process through Perplexity for free.
>
> Founders don't realise what they're sitting on:
>
> When I was building Searchable, I needed:
>
> - Deep market analysis on AI search adoption
> - Competitive intelligence on legacy SEO platforms
> - Regulatory landscape research on AI governance
>

> Instead, I built a prompting system that turned Perplexity into a Harvard research team.

> Here's the system I use to get the most out of Perplexity:

> ✅ Demand structure → Tables, headings, sections beat wall-of-text responses
> ✅ Force citations → "Cite all claims" makes output defensible
> ✅ Require both sides → Evidence for, against, and what's uncertain
> ✅ End with action → "So what?" or "What should someone do next?"
> ✅ Apply domain knowledge → Review sources, validate, add your expertise
>
> And the prompts to get started: 
>
> (Find the full prompts in the sheet 👇)
>
> 1. Market Landscape Snapshot
>
> Breaks down market size, growth rate, main players, and 3-5 trends that matter. 
> Ends with practical "So what?" No speculation allowed.
>
> 2. Competitive Comparison Breakdown
>
> Creates a positioning table comparing offerings, pricing, and distribution.  
> Flags contradictions in public information.
>
> 3. Trend Validation Check
>
> Determines if a trend is real or hype by gathering evidence on both sides. 
> Verdict: hype, early signal, or established shift.
>
> 4. Deep Dive on a Single Question
>
> Goes beyond surface summaries. 
> Shows where experts agree, disagree, and what nuance is missed. 
>
> 5. Buyer & User Insight Synthesis
>
> Analyses real customer language from reviews, forums, and discussions. 
> Surfaces pain points and desired outcomes.
>
> 6. Regulation & Risk Overview
>
> Maps the regulatory landscape by region. 
> Focuses on what affects real decisions, not theoretical compliance theatre.
>
> 7. Evidence-Based Opinion Builder
>
> Lays out the strongest arguments on both sides. 
> Highlights where evidence is strong versus mixed. 
>
> 8. Research-to-Decision Summary
>
> Structures output as: what's known, key risks and sensible next steps. 
> Practical decision framework, not predictions.
>
> Market validation that used to take days now takes minutes.
>

> A business idea without validation is a dream. 
>
> Here’s why 47% of businesses don’t make it past year 3: 
>
> I've spent 15 years building multiple 7- and 8-figure businesses.
>
> The reason they did well was insanely simple: 
>
> We knew people wanted and/or needed what we were selling. 
>
> I urge you to never start building before testing your ideas. 
>
> This CODE Framework will save you money, time, and energy.  
>
> Here's a brief summary:
> (More details in the sheet below)
>
> 1. C = Consumer Trends
>
> Find the rising tide first.
>
> Look for shifts in behaviour, tech and demand. 
>
> The test question: If this trend doubles, does my idea get easier to sell?
>
> 2. O = Opportunity
>
> Attach the trend to a pain point people pay to fix.
>
> Ask:
> → Who has the pain? (be specific)
> → What is it costing them? (time, money, stress, risk)
> → Why now? (what changed this year)
>
> Quick filters:
> → Is it tied to revenue or customer acquisition?
> → Can I deliver it asynchronously?
> → Can it become recurring revenue?
>
> 3. D = Demand Validation
>
> Prove the pain exists before you build anything.
>
> → Find people already complaining (Reddit, forums, LinkedIn)
> → Save exact phrases they use (these become your messaging)
> → Build a waitlist landing page
> → Offer a small "proof tool" or report (free, fast, specific)
> → Talk to 10 potential buyers and write down patterns
>
> Once you reach 100 paying customers, you have a business.
>
> 4. E = Economic Sizing
>
> Make sure the maths can reach $1 million.
>
> Revenue = Customers × Annual value per customer
>
> If the ceiling is low, your effort won't matter.
>
> There has never been a better time to build a business.
>
> But only if you validate it properly first.
>
> Do you have a business idea you're struggling to validate? 
> Share your process in the comments. 
>
> This is the exact framework we used when building Searchable. 
>
> And we hit $83k MRR in under a month after launching. 
>
> We did that by: 
>
> 1. Spotting the trend (AI search)
> 2. Identifying the pain (businesses not visible in ChatGPT)
> 3. Validating demand with a waitlist, and proving the economics work

> Success as a Founder doesn't come from experience.
>
> It comes from consistent curiosity to learn more.
>
> It's easy as an entrepreneur to fall into a common trap I see often:
>
> Thinking you've got all this sh*t figured out.
> Spoiler alert: you have not. Not by a long shot.
>
> You've got to sharpen your tools, consistently. 
>
> That's where these books come into play.
>
> I've read every single one, some of them several times.
>
> And I would recommend each one to a specific Founder at a specific time:
> (You can see one key lesson from each in the visual below)
>
> 1. Atomic Habits by James Clear 🔁
>
> Who?
> Founders who set goals but struggle to keep consistent.
>
> Why?
> Because progress is found in the everyday habits. 
>
> 2. The Hard Thing About Hard Things by Ben Horowitz 🪖
>
> Who?
> Founders dealing with pressure and uncertainty. 
>
> Why?
> It talks honestly about what to do when there are no 'good' options.
>
> 3. The Learn Startup by Eric Ries 📐
>
> Who?
> Early-stage founders building something they hope people want.
>
> Why?
> It helps you test reality early before money disappears. 
>
> 4. The 4-Hour Workweek by Tim Ferriss 🌴
>
> Who?
> Founders who feel busy all the time but stuck in the business.
>
> Why?
> It forces you to question whether the way you're working makes sense.
>
> 5. Deep Work by Cal Newport 🔦
>
> Who?
> Founders who are constantly interrupted.
>
> Why?
> Because clear thinking is hard to find once your calendar piles up.
>
> 6. Start With Why by Simon Sinek ❓
>
> Who?
> Founders trying to hire well and rally a team.
>
> Why?
> It explains why some companies inspire loyalty and others struggle.
>
> 7. Key Person Of Influence by Daniel Priestley 👤
>
> Who?
> Founders who want their reputation to open doors.
>
> Why?
> It shows how authority compounds when you're known for something specific.
>
> 8. Zero to One by Peter Thiel 1️⃣
>
> Who?
> Founders building in crowded or competitive markets.
>
> Why?
> It challenges you to think about whether you're actually doing anything different.
>
> 9. Blue Ocean Strategy by W. Chan Kim & Renée Mauborgne 🌊
>
> Who?
> Founders stuck competing on price or features.
>
> Why?
> It reframes growth around finding opportunity where others aren't looking.
>
> And so I think every founder would benefit from at least one book here.
>
> They won't give you all the answers you're looking for.

## Post 129 — 2026-01-24

**Likes:** 880 | **Comments:** 313 | **Shares:** 85

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_i-lost-several-clients-while-building-my-activity-7420812136970514432-CGR-)

> I lost several clients while building my first business. 
>
> Not because the work was bad. Because I couldn’t prioritise my time.
>
> When everything is “high priority,” your clients sense the lack of focus. 
>
> That was 14 years ago. 
>
> Since then, I’ve built and exited multiple 8-figure businesses.
>
> I still worked incredibly hard to make that happen… 
>
> But only on the things that actually needed my attention. 
>
> And these 7 frameworks were the key to making that happen. 
>
> Use them to shift your focus back to what truly matters for your business: 
>
> (Save the sheet and come back to it as needed 👇) 
>
> 1. The Eisenhower Matrix
> By Dwight D. Eisenhower
>
> A 2x2 matrix that sorts tasks by urgent vs important. 
>
> Use it for:
> When your day is run by messages, requests, and putting out fires.
>
> 2. Timeboxing
> By James Martin
>
> Give a task a fixed time limit so it can't swallow up your whole week.
>
> Use it for:
> Strategy, planning, writing, and decision-making.
>
> 3. Impact/Effort Matrix
> Popularised by Lean/Agile practices
>
> A 2x2 matrix that ranks tasks by impact vs effort.
>
> Use it for:
> Feature requests, growth ideas, and deciding what to build next.
>
> 4. Kanban Board
> By Taiichi Ohno
>
> A visual workflow that tracks tasks through stages.
>
> Use it for:
> Team execution, project delivery, and reducing context switching.
>
> 5. The Stop Doing List
> By Jim Collins
>
> A framework for prioritisation where you win by removing commitments.
>
> Use it for:
> Freeing time, eliminating legacy tasks, and stopping your calendar from owning you.
>
> 6. The One Metric That Matters (OMTM)
> By Alistair Croll & Ben Yoskovitz
>
> Force everything to answer one question: What matters most right now?
>
> Use it for:
> Weekly prioritisation, product focus, and stopping drag.
>
> 7. The 80/20 Principle (Pareto Principle)
> By Vilfredo Pareto
>
> A principle to help you focus on the few things producing the most results.
>
> Use it for:
> Finding your best customers, best channel, best offer, and cutting distractions.
>
> Prioritisation is still the no.1 thing I see founders struggling with. 
>
> If everything is of the highest priority...
>
> Nothing ever gets your full attention. 
>
> For the health of your business, and your own peace of mind, 
> Test one of these frameworks this week. 
>
> The more order you bring to building, the more you can look ahead. 
>
> How do you approach prioritisation for your business?

>

> Founders make 1000s of decisions daily. 
>
> But these 8 are the ones that matter most:
>
> The natural instinct for most founders is to be overly involved. 
> Controlling minor decisions feels like maintaining control.  
>
> I was guilty of this for years, and I lost so much time and momentum. 
>
> I thought all decisions were created equal...
> But only a select few actually drive your business forward. 
>
> Knowing that would have saved countless wasted hours I'll never get back. 
>
> Don't make the same mistake.  
>
> These are the 8 decisions that define great founders: 
>
> 1. What You Build First
>
> A great founder ships the smallest thing that proves demand.
> A landing page, waitlist or a manual MVP.
> Build to learn, not to impress.
>
> 2. Who You Take Advice From
>
> Everyone has an opinion. Very few have earned it.
> If someone hasn't done what you're trying to do, listen politely and move on.
> Advice from people who haven't done it is just theory.
>
> 3. What You Personally Own
>
> Delegation isn't abdication.
>
> Early on, there are things only the founder should own:
>
> - Vision  
> - Hiring standards  
> - Culture  
> - Distribution
>
> Don't outsource these too early. No one will care about them like you do.
>
> 4. What You Say No To
>
> Every yes creates drag.
> Great founders protect focus like their business depends on it (because it does).
> Strategy is mostly subtraction.
>
> 5. How You Spend Your Time
>
> Your calendar is your real business plan.
> If you're spending all your time reacting, you're not leading.
> Block time for what matters. Ruthlessly.
>
> 6. How Fast You Act On Feedback
>
> Founders fail because they ignore reality for too long.
> Great founders ship fast, listen hard, and iterate immediately.
> The market cares about what works.
>
> 7. What You Tolerate When It's Uncomfortable
>
> What you tolerate sets the ceiling for your business.
> Be cautious about what you allow to continue.
> Kindness doesn't mean lowering the bar.
>
> 8. How You Show Up Under Pressure
>
> Anyone can lead when things are going well.
> Founders are remembered for how they act when things go wrong.
> Pressure reveals character. Don't let it change you.
>
> These decisions are the ultimate litmus test for a founder. 
>
> They determine how quickly and how well you build and scale your business. 
>
> Take this list and study it.

> You could save yourself from countless mistakes your competitors are making now.

## Post 151 — 2026-01-09

**Likes:** 1761 | **Comments:** 569 | **Shares:** 184

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_bad-prompts-vs-good-prompts-vs-great-prompts-activity-7415376677381607424-080J)

> There's a good chance your prompts are rubbish.
>
> It's 2026. Let's fix that together:
>
> Lots of you have been using ChatGPT, and AI in general, for a few years now.
>
> For most, it's treated like a Google replacement or a simple problem-solver.
> And as a result, the outputs aren't as sophisticated as they could be.
>
> Take these examples to see what the difference between bad, good, and great is:
>
> ❌ Bad Prompt
>
> Write a viral LinkedIn post about entrepreneurship.
>
> Why it's bad: it's far too vague to produce anything of value.
>
> ✅ Good Prompt
>
> Write 5 LinkedIn posts aimed at founders building real businesses.
> I’ll pick the strongest one, explain why it worked, then you’ll rewrite 5 more using that feedback.
>
> Why it's better: it is more specific and allows for iteration and improvements.
>
> ✅ ✅ Great Prompt
>
> Role
> Act as a founder who has built and sold £10m+ businesses and writes for other founders.
>
> Task
> Here are 5 LinkedIn posts I’ve written that performed well: [PASTE POSTS].
>
> Analyse why they worked, then write 5 new posts for founders running £1m+ businesses.
>
> Format
> • Short pattern breakdown
> • 5 hook-first posts
>
> Constraints
> • Founder-first
> • No generic motivation
> • One clear point per post
>
> Stop when
> • Patterns are identified
> • 5 posts are written
>
> Context: [INSERT DUMP]
>
> Why it's great: it's clear, detailed, and importantly, uses negative prompting for what not to do.
>
> The last one follows a format my team and I swear by.
>
> 1. Role 👤
> 2. Task 📕
> 3. Format 📄
> 4. Warnings ⚠️
> 5. Reasoning 🧠
> 6. Stop Conditions 🛑
> 7. Context Dump 🗑️
>
> It saves us all so much time and brainspace (arguably more important).
>
> Like everything with AI... do not let it replace your thinking.
> With each output, be critical about the quality and reprompt as and when necessary.
>
> But not using AI for the sake of "authenticity" just isn't an option in 2026.
>
> How are you getting on with AI? Using it often?
> I'm curious to hear in the comments. ⬇️

> My new business Searchable helps businesses appear inside these LLMs that you prompt.

> If you're a business owner or marketer interested in gaining more visibility for your business...

>  
> So this year can be your best one yet on the platform.

> I'm still seeing the same old practices:  
>
> Bland hook structures, over-relying on motivational quotes, 
> And sticking to safe, but irrelevant topics...
>
> If you want to see real growth, you need to know the new rules. 
>
> LinkedIn users want more value and substance than ever before. 
>
> Here’s what will actually win in 2026: 
>
> 1. How to build a brand
> ❌ Go broad for maximum growth. 
> ✅ Become an authority in your niche. 
>
> 2. Text hooks
> ❌ Generic contrarian hooks.
> ✅ Proof of work, authority and personal story hooks perform best.
>
> 3. Comments that count
> ❌ “Get as many comments as possible.”
> ✅ Comments from authority figures have the most impact. 
>
> 4. How to go viral
> ❌ Top 1% posts would get 455x the reach of average posts.
> ✅ A Top 1% viral post gets ~80% less reach than 12 months ago 
>
> (But you can still grow your business and following...) 
>
> 5. Carousels are still king
> ❌ Purely educational carousels preferred. 
> ✅ Contrast and storytelling carousels are outperforming.
>
> 6. Emojis
> ❌ A tell-tale sign of AI.
> ✅ Improve readability.
>
> 7. Lead magnets
> ❌ Just playbooks and step-by-step guides.
> ✅ Top lead magnets are often GPTs.
>
> 8. Questions?
> ❌ Every post must end with a question. 
> ✅ Only include genuine questions.  
>
> 9. Video
> ❌ Videos get insane reach. 
> ✅ Videos are for product demos and building trust.
>
> 10. Single images
> ❌ Generic motivational billboards.
> ✅ Surprising pictures OR authority pictures.
>
> 11. Hashtags

>
> 3. AI won’t feel impressive anymore. People will see through it. What matters is how AI augments human workflows. Copycat, vibe-coded apps won’t last.
>
> 4. SaaS and agents will blur into one category. Every SaaS will add agentic features. Every agent will need SaaS fundamentals. Those that don’t adapt won’t survive.
>
> 5. Analog businesses will surge. In-person events, film cameras, magazines. These become status signals as people crave craftsmanship and real connection.
>
> 6. Specialised, vertical AI models will drive innovation. Real innovation will come from vertical models in regulated sectors like healthcare, finance, and public safety.
>
> 7. AI-powered education will disrupt traditional learning. Parents who adapt will use AI as a coach to build personalised learning around skills that actually matter.
>
> 8. Widened gap between "leaders" and "laggards". AI-mature companies will win through better decisions, better foundational data, and stronger customer experience.
>
> 9. The dead internet theory becomes visible in 2026. Bots already dominate traffic. Expect more gated spaces, stronger identity checks, and friction to prove you’re human.
>
> 10. Hybrid creator-media models will rise in popularity. Editorial standards, recurring formats, and diversified revenue like memberships, courses, and SaaS.
>
> 11. Long-form video will dominate socials in 2026. People are tired of short-form junk. Long-form builds trust and depth at scale.
>
> (Here's hoping.)
>
> 12. Platforms like Substack will keep growing. Especially for thinkers who layer written content with audio and video.
>
> 13. We’re entering a zero-trust era. Content supply is infinite. Knowing what’s real won’t be obvious. Verification and authentication will matter.
>
> 14. The quiet winners will focus on basics. Clean data, good tracking, and deep customer understanding, while others chase shiny AI tools.

## Post 167 — 2025-12-24

**Likes:** 1232 | **Comments:** 315 | **Shares:** 152

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_revenue-doesnt-mean-profit-you-could-activity-7409579321314590720-sk24)

> Revenue doesn't mean profit. 
>
> You could be bleeding cash without realising.
>
> Nothing kills momentum faster than reaching $1M revenue...
>  
> Only to realise you are haemorrhaging $1,000s every week.  
>
> That's why you need to know OpEx vs CapEx vs RevEx vs FinEx:
>
> OpEx → The recurring costs to keep your business running.
> CapEx → Long-term investments that create future value.
> RevEx → Costs that scale directly with revenue.
> FinEx → The cost of capital and your financial structure.
>
> Here's a clear breakdown of all four: 
>
> (See the cheat sheet to get the full picture of each ↓) 
>
> 💸 OpEx: Operating Expenditure
> ↳ The day-to-day costs required to keep the business running.  
>
> How It Works
> ↳ Expensed immediately through the P&L in the period incurred
> ↳ Directly reduces operating profit
> ↳ Creates no long-term asset or future balance sheet value
>
> Key Examples
> ✅ Salaries and contractors
> ✅ Rent, utilities, and admin costs
> ✅ SaaS subscriptions
>
> ⏳ CapEx: Capital Expenditure
> ↳ Investment in long-term assets designed to create value long-term.
>
> How It Works
> ↳ Recorded on the balance sheet, not expensed immediately
> ↳ Depreciated over the asset’s useful life
> ↳ Improves future capability rather than short-term profit
>
> Key Examples
> ✅ Core technology platforms
> ✅ Equipment and machinery
> ✅ Proprietary internal software
>
> 📈 RevEx: Revenue Expenditure
> ↳ Costs that scale directly with generating and delivering revenue.
>
> How It Works
> ↳ Moves in line with sales volume
> ↳ Impacts gross margin, not operating margin
> ↳ Determines how profitable growth actually is
>
> Key Examples
> ✅ Cost of goods sold
> ✅ Fulfilment and logistics
> ✅ Sales commissions
>
> 💵 FinEx: Financial Expenditure
> ↳ The cost of capital and decisions that shape your financial structure.
>
> How It Works
> ↳ Affects cash flow rather than daily operations
> ↳ Driven by leverage, risk, and timing
> ↳ Often tax deductible depending on structure
>
> Key Examples
> ✅ Loan and debt interest
> ✅ Credit facility fees
> ✅ Investor and legal transaction costs
>
> If you don't understand these four types of expenditures, 
> You simply can't build a profitable business. 
>
> Even if your revenue looks impressive, 
> It doesn't guarantee long-term profitability. 
>
> Learn these to align revenue growth with actual progress. 
>
> Are you measuring OpEx, CapEx, RevEx, and FinEx? 
> Or are they completely new to you? 
>
> Share your questions/concerns in the comments. 
>

## Post 172 — 2025-12-19

**Likes:** 2565 | **Comments:** 461 | **Shares:** 276

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_most-people-blindly-use-chatgpt-for-everything-activity-7407765973665075200-19up)

> Most people blindly use ChatGPT for everything.
>
> The top 1% switch between AI tools: 
>
> I've spent the last year testing every major AI tool.
>
> And I can confidently say that ChatGPT can't do it all. 
>
> Different tools excel at different tasks. 
>
> ChatGPT is a great starting point. 
> But Claude destroys it for coding and detailed analysis.
> And if you're in the Google sphere, Gemini is the obvious choice. 
>
> This cheat sheet will tell you when to use each one: 
>
> 🤖 ChatGPT
>
> What it is: 
> ↳ An all-round generative model for text, vision, audio, etc.
>
> When to use it: 
> - You need versatile output, including writing, coding, image, browsing.
> - You want access to plugins, memory, and browsing features.
> - Ideal for creative workflows and automation tasks.
>
> Use cases: 
> ✅ Turn a Notion doc into a polished guide.
> ✅ Summarise your competitor’s homepage.
> ✅ Auto-generate outreach emails.
>
> Pros: 
> 👍 Fast, intuitive, multimodal.
> 👍 Massive custom GPT ecosystem.
> 👍 Built-in browsing and memory features.
>
> Cons: 
> 👎 Free tier = old model (4o).
> 👎 Still prone to incorrect responses.
> 👎 Still needs human judgement.
>
> Rating:
> ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️
>
> 🤖 Gemini
>
> What it is: 
> ↳ Google’s response to GPT. Fully wired into Gmail, Docs, and Search.
>
> When to use it: 
> - You live inside Google Workspace.
> - You need true multimodal input/output.
> - You work with long documents, images, audio, and video together.
>
> Use cases: 
> ✅ Summarising email threads + attachments.
> ✅ Creating drafts with chart/image content.
> ✅ Multimodal research and design workflows.
>
> Pros: 
> 👍 Deep integration with Google apps.
> 👍 Handles multi-modal content better.
> 👍 Great for team collaboration + async prep.
>
> Cons:
> 👎 Advanced capabilities stuck behind paywall.
> 👎 Still polishing general chat UX.
> 👎 Most powerful within the Google ecosystem.
>
> Rating:
> ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️
>
> 🤖 Claude
>
> What it is: 
> ↳ Anthropic’s answer to high-context reasoning and ethics.
>
> When to use it: 
> - For legal, policy, or research output.
> - When context depth (200k+ tokens) matters.
> - When accuracy and defensibility are non-negotiable.
>
> Use cases: 
> ✅ Digest a 90-page legal agreement and highlight risks.
> ✅ Break a research-heavy article into social posts.
> ✅ Drop in a long script and get code back.
>
> Pros: 
> 👍 Superior handling of long documents.
> 👍 Strong accuracy in technical domains.
> 👍 Writes with a more conversational tone.
>
> Cons:
> 👎 Doesn’t generate images or audio.
> 👎 Can be overly conservative in style.
> 👎 Lacks “quick idea” speed compared to ChatGPT.
>
> Rating:
> ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ 
>
> TL;DR:
>
> Don't rely on ChatGPT for everything. 
> It's a great tool, but not the only one worth using.  
>

>

> Most people are doing designs wrong on LinkedIn. 
>
> These 19 laws govern viral content: 
>
> LinkedIn is more nuanced than Instagram or X. 
> There are formats that work and others that simply don't. 
>
> But it's not nearly as hard as you think to learn them. 
>
> I've spent years testing what works and what doesn't...
> So you can hit the ground running on content creation. 
>
> Here are the 19 laws that all great content design follows: 
>
> Law #1: Make It Instantly Scannable
> If someone can't understand your design in 3 seconds, they won't bother. 
>
> Law #2: Mobile First
> Preview everything on mobile before you hit publish.
>
> Law #3: Portrait Over Landscape
> Portrait formats dominate reach because they fill the screen. 
> (Landscape formats cut your reach in half.)
>
> Law #4: Centre the Core Message
> If you leave people guessing where to look, you've already lost them.
>
> Law #5: Don't Avoid Guides
> A clean grid makes your design look intentionally built.
>
> Law #6: Contrast Is Non-Negotiable
> If your text doesn't pop, your message never lands.
>
> Law #7: White Space Is a Power Tool
> Beginners cram all the info. Professionals let it breathe. 
>
> Law #8: Use Professional Visuals Only
> High-quality icons and imagery make you look credible.
>
> Law #9: Pick a Font That Matches Your Brand
> Choose fonts that match your style and return to them consistently.
>
> Law #10: Lead With a Scroll-Stopping Title
> If it doesn't stop the scroll, nothing else matters.
>
> Law #11: Make Every Section Bite-Sized
> Break your content into chunks people can digest at a glance.
>
> Law #12: Visual Hierarchy Wins Attention Battles. 
> Your design should guide them naturally from start to finish.
>
> Law #13: Design for Real Reader Flow
> Place your strongest elements where their eyes land first.
>
> Law #14: Use Colour With Purpose
> Brand colours should enhance readability, not fight with it.
>
> Law #15: Density Over Decoration
> Remove anything that doesn't help someone take action.
>
> Law #16: Make Saving Easy
> Ask yourself: "Would I save this?" If not, refine it.
>
> Law #17: Build a Clear CTA Into the Footer
> Tell them what to do next: follow, save, repost, sign up, download.
>
> Law #18: Test With Real People Before Posting
> If someone can't explain your visual back to you, it isn't ready.
>
> Law #19: Turn Every Winning Layout Into a System
> When a format works, systemise it, use it again and improve it.
>
> Even as the algorithm changes (which it will), these will remain true. 
>
> Learn them now, and they'll serve you for years to come.

## Post 179 — 2025-12-12

**Likes:** 709 | **Comments:** 370 | **Shares:** 57

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_google-still-processes-85-billion-searches-activity-7405229037448765440-fXSS)

> Google still processes 8.5 billion searches daily. 
>
> But now you're competing across AI systems too...
>
> That means it's time to update your vocabulary, 
> And make sure you have at least a basic understanding of the new SEO terms.  
>
> Traditional SEO still drives traffic. 
> But businesses with hopes to scale in 2026 need to grasp AI search as well.  
>
> Here are 20 essential concepts you need to know:
>
> 1. AEO (Answer Engine Optimisation)
> ↳ Optimising content so it gets pulled into AI-powered search answers.
>
> 2. GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation)
> ↳ Targeting platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity.
>
> 3. AIO (AI Optimisation)
> ↳ Adapting content to maximise visibility across AI search engines.
>
> 4. SXO (Search Experience Optimisation)
> ↳ Blending SEO with UX to improve the user journey and boost conversions. 
>
> 5. Keywords
> ↳ Search terms and phrases people use to find anything online.
>
> 6. Backlinks
> ↳ External links that signal credibility and relevance to search engines.
>
> 7. Site Health
> ↳ The overall technical performance of a site.
>
> 8. SERP (Search Engine Results Page)
> ↳ The page displayed after a search query, showing organic and paid listings.
>
> 9. Organic Traffic
> ↳ Visitors who arrive at your website through unpaid search engine results.
>
> 10. Bounce Rate
> ↳ The percentage of visitors who leave a website after viewing a single page.
>
> 11. Indexing
> ↳ How search engines store, organise, and prepare your content for ranking.
>
> 12. Ranking
> ↳ The position your site achieves in search engine results.
>
> 13. On-Page SEO
> ↳ Optimising website titles, content, structure, and code for relevance.
>
> 14. Off-Page SEO
> ↳ External activities such as link-building and PR that strengthen authority.
>
> 15. Schema Markup
> ↳ Structured code that helps AI systems interpret and display content details.
>
> 16. Query Fan-Out
> ↳ When AI expands a single user query into related sub-queries.
>
> 17. Chunking
> ↳ Breaking long-form content into smaller sections that AI can cite.
>
> 18. Passage Ranking
> ↳ Google’s system for ranking a single section of text.
>
> 19. Zero-Click Results
> ↳ Search results where answers appear directly on the page.
>
> 20. AI Overviews
> ↳ Google’s AI summaries that appear above organic search listings.
>
> Traditional SEO still works, but it's no longer enough. 
>
> Staying ahead now depends on learning and applying these concepts. 
>
