## Post 180 — 2025-12-11

**Likes:** 2410 | **Comments:** 494 | **Shares:** 280

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_you-can-build-an-ai-agent-in-10-minutes-activity-7404866592708395008-Ic2P)

> You can build an AI agent in 10 minutes. 
>
> But 99% of people will never attempt it: 
>
> I've built multiple AI agents for Searchable, 
> And I'm still shocked at how easy it is.  
>
> If you can write a basic checklist, you can build an agent. 
>
> One that will genuinely save you 100s of hours.
>
> Here's exactly how to build one:
>
> 1. Pick One Boring Job
>
> Choose one painful workflow you repeat weekly.
>
> Define success in one sentence:
> "Given X, the agent should output Y so that Z happens."
>
> 2. Map The Steps Like A SOP
>
> Turn that job into 4 to 7 clear steps.
> Write it as: Input → actions → decision → output.
>
> 3. Choose Your Agent Platform
>
> Decide where this thing lives so you're not reinventing infrastructure.
>
> No/low code: OpenAI Agent Builder, Zapier, Make, n8n
> Dev friendly: LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI
>
> 4. Define Inputs, Outputs, And Tools
>
> Treat the agent like an API, not a vague chatbot.
>
> Specify inputs: what fields are required (text, file, URL, ID)
> Define outputs: JSON fields or a fixed template
> Attach tools: data tools, action tools or orchestration tools
>
> 5. Give The Agent A Job Description
>
> Write the brain with a clear system prompt:
>
> - Role: "You are a [job title] focused on [task]"
> - Boundaries: what it must never do
> - Style: concise, structured
> - 1-2 example conversations
>
> 6. Add Memory And Context
>
> Stop the agent forgetting everything after each message.
>
> Three layers:
>
> - Conversation state: pass recent messages
> - Task memory: store key decisions for the current run
> - Knowledge memory: connect a vector store over your docs
>
> 7. Add Guardrails And Human Checks
>
> Mark high-risk actions that need approval. 
>
> Add simple rules:
>
> - Never invent logins or IDs
> - Ask for clarification when the brief is ambiguous
> - Log every tool call and decision
>
> 8. Wrap It In A Simple Interface
>
> Turn the agent into something people will actually use.
> Options: internal chat, button in an existing app or Slack command
>
> 9. Test On 5 Real Tasks
>
> Catch issues at the step level, not after it breaks something.
>
> For each example:
>
> - Watch which tools it called and in what order
> - Score correctness, steps taken, and time saved
> - Tighten the prompt, tools, or rules where it failed
>
> Businesses adopting AI now will be too far ahead to catch later.
>
> If you want to be one of them, you need to start automating your work. 
>
> Founders who grow fastest aren't working hardest.
> They're building systems that run without them.
>
> This is what we're doing at Searchable.
>
> We built an AI system that handles SEO and AEO automatically. 
> It analyses your site, finds opportunities and optimises content.

## Post 195 — 2025-11-26

**Likes:** 1715 | **Comments:** 410 | **Shares:** 269

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_seo-is-not-the-full-picture-for-businesses-activity-7399450902891499520-FYzl)

> SEO is not the full picture for businesses. 
>
> In 2025, it's just a piece of the search puzzle. 
>
> Ranking on Google is not the primary goal anymore.
> The search volume inside LLMs is increasing day by day.
>
> Which makes GEO/AEO/AIO/SXO an untapped goldmine for visibility.
>
> I launched Searchable fully this week and hundreds of marketers have signed up.
>
> People are already seeing incredible results, which is amazing to see.
> (Like 200% increases in AI traffic in under a month)
>
> So, if you want to dominate search in 2025 and beyond...
> There's still plenty of time to be ahead of the curve.
>
> Get going by learning these terms 👇
>
> 🧩 SEO: Search Engine Optimisation
> ↳ Ranking pages on Google through keywords and backlinks. 
>
> ✅ Pros: Proven traffic driver, builds long-term authority.
> 🚫 Cons: Competitive and slow to drive results.
> 🏆 Rank by targeting high-intent keywords clusters and refresh content.
>
> 🧩 GEO: Generative Engine Optimisation
> ↳ Optimising to be cited by AI engines like ChatGPT or Perplexity.
>
> ✅ Early-mover edge, builds trust, captures new channels.
> 🚫 Harder to measure a direct impact.
> 🏆 Rank with entity-rich content, forums, clear tables & FAQs.
>
> 🧩 AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation
> ↳ Optimising for zero-click answers (snippets, AI overviews).
>
> ✅ Instant authority, high CTR when clicks occur.
> 🚫 Fewer clicks, volatile snippet positions.
> 🏆 Rank by answering in 40–60 words, using schema & PAA topics.
>
> 🧩 AIO: AI Optimisation
> ↳ Ensuring your brand appears accurately in AI training data.
>
> ✅ Builds trust when AI tools surface your business.
> 🚫 Influence on training data can be limited.

## Post 199 — 2025-11-22

**Likes:** 853 | **Comments:** 343 | **Shares:** 88

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_whether-youre-using-gpt-claude-or-perplexity-activity-7397981053287608321-Dgwo)

> Whether you're using GPT, Claude or Perplexity,
>
> Weak prompts = Weak outputs 
>
> The quality of your prompts determines your results.  
>
> People tend to prompt each LLM the same, and that’s not always wise. 
>
> But in case you don’t want to learn EVERY tool in detail, 
> There are universal rules that can be applied to get good results.  
>
> These will ensure 10x better results from most LLMs: 
>
> (See the cheat sheet for more details 👇) 
>
> 1. Keep The Base Prompt Short
>
> Pick one role, goal, or definition of success. 
> The base prompt controls how the model thinks.
>
> 2. Add Context In Layers
>
> Your prompt is the headline.
> Your supporting files and data do the heavy lifting.
>
> 3. Multi-shot > One-shot
>
> Show the model good vs bad examples.
> These act like micro-training.
>
> 4. Give The Model A Thinking Path
>
> AI doesn’t assume priorities.
> Tell it the order: analyse → extract → prioritise → recommend → format.
>
> 5. Use Constraints Deliberately
>
> Constraints reduce hallucinations, and ambiguity.
> Word count, style, and format create clarity.
>
> Context Stacking 
>
> A modern prompt works like a modular system.
> It’s almost like you’re assembling it.
>
> Layer A: Role & Goal
> Layer B: Memory
> Layer C: Examples (Multi-Shot)
> Layer D: Documents
> Layer E: Parameters
>
> Connectors & MCP 
>
> This is where the next generation of prompting is going.
>
> Use connectors to link AI to:
>
> - Google Drive → briefs, scripts, docs
> - Notion → wiki, strategy hubs
> - Slack → decisions, updates, support
> - AirTable → CRM data, ICP profiles
>
> MCP (Model Context Protocol)
>
> A technical way to tell the model:
>
> - Which tools it can call
> - What data it can fetch
> - What the output format must be
>
> If your prompts aren’t working, check for these mistakes: 
>
> ❌ Mixing tone, goals, and tasks
> ❌ Asking for everything at once
> ❌ Giving no examples
> ❌ Giving too many examples
> ❌ Forgetting constraints
> ❌ Zero logic or sequencing
> ❌ Five different prompts doing the job of one system
>
> After months of building Searchable that uses agentic AI, 
> I've learned that prompting is not just writing good instructions. 
>
> It's about engineering a system that produces strong results, consistently. 
>
> What's your formula for a good prompt? 
> Drop it down below.

> Designing content that appears in AI-generated results.
>

> Ensuring your brand appears inside AI summaries.
>

> How often your brand is cited in AI-generated responses.
>
> 5. SERP: Search Engine Results Page
> Where SEO and AI Overviews now coexist.
>
> 6. Zero-Click Results: 
> When users get answers directly from AI without clicking through.
>
> 7. LLMO: Large Language Model Optimisation
> Optimising for models like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude.
>
> 8. Semantic Search: 
> AI's ability to understand context and intent.
>
> 9. Entity Recognition: 
> How AI connects people, brands, and concepts in your content.
>
> 10. Embeddings: 
> The way AI encodes meaning to determine content relevance and citations.
>
> 11. Chunking: 
> Breaking content into sections AI can easily index and cite.
>
> 12. Passage Ranking: 
> Google's ability to rank individual passages within a page.

> Failed change is rarely due to resistance.
>
> It's because a proper framework wasn't used.
>
> And a structured roadmap wasn't put in place.

>
> It provides the structure and framework for effective change management.
>
> Which, by the way, is critical to any business.
> Without change, you don't evolve, and you get left in the dust.
>
> This is how it works:
>
> Awareness 👋
> ↳ Create an understanding of the objective.
>
> Desire ✋
> ↳ Cultivate a personal drive to embrace change.
>
> Knowledge 🧠
> ↳ Equip your team with the necessary understanding of a new system.
>
> Ability 💪
> ↳ Empower individuals and teams with the capacity to enact change.
>
> Reinforcement 🔄
> ↳ Strengthen the innovation introduced by the change process.
>
> If you read the sheet, you'll find a breakdown of each stage.
>
> And typically, the perceived value of the model is low to begin with.
>
> But with time, people gain knowledge, ability, and they recognise the tangible value.
>

> Change doesn't start with a process.
> It starts from the leader.
>
> 2. Make progress visible 🏔️
> If people can see the impact...
> That's what keeps them invested.
>
> 3. Reward behaviour, not outcomes 🏆
> This builds a culture of genuine progressions.
> Which leads to results !

## Post 207 — 2025-11-14

**Likes:** 1810 | **Comments:** 657 | **Shares:** 138

> A concept everyone should know about...
>
> The Paradox Of Knowledge.
>
> Years ago, I thought knowledge was the barometer for success.
>
> The more I knew, the better I would become, the more I would earn.
>
> That wasn't necessarily true.
> Today, I feel like I have more to learn than ever.
>
> That's the Paradox Of Knowledge.
>
> When you start, everything feels simple.
> But the more we learn, the less we realise we know.
>
> From the outside, expertise can look like clarity.
> But inside, it's just navigating higher-quality confusion.
>
> These are the mindset shifts you need to adopt:
> (So you don't waste time rowing in the wrong direction)
>
> Firstly, learning isn't about collecting information.
>
> It's about repetition, refinement, and reflection.
> Learning something truly in-depth.
>
> Secondly, expertise looks boring up close.
>
> It's built by making the same decisions, but better each time.
> 99% of people chase variety. The top 1% chase precision.
>
> Finally, stay a student even when you're a teacher.
>
> The moment you think you've mastered something...
> You stop growing.
>
> Ultimately, mastery is a fallacy.
>
> The sooner you learn that, the better.
>
> Here's the thing:
>
> You HAVE to take action without full clarity sometimes.
> That's the way the world works, fair or not.
>
> But that doesn't mean you stop being a student. 
>
> Learning is forever !
>
> The more you learn, the less certain you feel...
> But the more capable you become.
>
> Happy learning, folks.
>
> Have you heard of this concept before?
> If not, what do you think of it?
>

> The more powerful AI becomes...

>
> The rise of AI has proven it to be a powerful tool. 
> Specifically for performing tasks that would normally take hours.  
>
> But even at its most powerful, it's still not human. 
>
> AI can handle technical tasks, but it can't replace human judgement. 
> It cannot replace the ability to connect with others.
> And it cannot replace adaptability.
>
> The future belongs to those who take action and improve these 8 skills: 
>
> 1. Analytical Thinking
> ↳ The ability to break problems down and see what drives results.
>
> Spend 15 minutes today working out why a result happened.
> Review your last three business decisions and look for patterns. 
>
> 2. Emotional Intelligence
> ↳ Understanding your emotions and how you respond to others.
>
> Before your next meeting, consider how each person might feel about the topic.
> End the day by asking yourself: Did I listen more than I spoke?
>
> 3. Adaptability
> ↳ Adjusting quickly when things don't go to plan.
>
> Do one thing this week that forces you out of your usual routine.
> When plans alter, reframe the situation with: What's still in my control?
>
> 4. Social Influence
> ↳ Moving people towards a shared goal. 
>
> Before every conversation, be clear on the outcome you want.
> Influence through conviction and consistency rather than pressure.
>
> 5. Decision-Making
> ↳ Choosing quickly and standing by the result.
>
> Give yourself a 1-minute limit for small decisions. 
> When unsure, ask: What will future me thank me for doing today?
>
> 6. Discipline
> ↳ Doing the work long after motivation wears off.
>
> Start your day with one task that moves your business forward.
> Remove one thing from your schedule that adds no real value.
>
> 7. Curiosity
> ↳ Staying open, interested, and willing to learn from anyone.
>
> Read something today outside your industry. 
> Ask "why?" more often. Especially when things are going well.

## Post 211 — 2025-11-12

**Likes:** 2082 | **Comments:** 461 | **Shares:** 244

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_if-you-give-level-1-prompts-youll-get-level-activity-7394362529436573696-PvG0)

> If you give level 1 prompts, you'll get level 1 results. 
>
> Here's how to go from beginner to pro: 
>
> Prompting AI is the same as any skill.  
> Level 1 inputs give level 1 outputs...
>
> And learning how to prompt well is a process. 
>
> Most people are stuck at level 1, maybe level 2 if they're trying.
> But the real power of LLMs is hidden in levels 3 and 4.
>
> That's where you stop getting generic outputs, and start: 
>
> - Creating higher quality outputs with fewer iterations
> - Building reusable systems that scale with your business
> - Working with a 24/7 digital assistant trained on your data
>
> Here are the 4 levels of prompting broken down: 
>
> Level 1: The Commander
>
> “Write me a post.”
>
> Goal: Get something fast.
> Mindset: Task-first, no context.
>
> This is where most people stay. 
> You get quick answers but generic results. 
>
> How to improve:
> - Add a clear role and goal to every request.
> - Ask AI to explain how it got to the answer.
>
> Level 2: The Architect
>
> “Act as a content strategist. 
> Build a LinkedIn post using this brief, audience, and tone.”
>
> Goal: Add structure and clarity.
> Mindset: Context-first, single focus.
>
> You’re starting to give direction. 
> You define who the output is for, the purpose, and the format. 
>
> How to improve:
> - Use simple structure: Role → Task → Context → Output.
> - Include examples of great work to show the standard you expect.
>
> Level 3: The Strategist
>
> “Here’s the audience, style, and examples. 
> Build three options, critique them, and improve the best one.”
>
> Goal: Create consistent, high-quality work.
> Mindset: Iteration and reasoning.
>
> This is where results compound. 
> You build systems, test ideas, and refine based on feedback. 
>
> How to improve:
> - Use feedback loops: create → review → refine → finalise.
> - Ask it to think through trade-offs or risks before giving the answer.
>
> Level 4: The Master
>
> “You are my Growth Engineer. 
> Use context from Notion, Google Drive, 
> and previous brand frameworks to draft this week’s content plan.”
>
> Goal: Automation and leverage.
> Mindset: Integration and systems thinking.
>
> AI becomes part of your workflow. 
> It understands your data, preferences, and strategy. 
>
> How to improve:
> - Layer context from your documents, briefs, and past results.
> - Build reusable prompt systems that evolve over time.
>
> My team and I use level 3 and 4 prompting every single day.
>
> It's how we produce content at scale and save countless hours each week.

## Post 214 — 2025-11-09

**Likes:** 1340 | **Comments:** 453 | **Shares:** 122

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_7-business-terms-everyone-needs-to-know-activity-7393255078050279426-_6FT)

> No founder is too good for the fundamentals.
>
> The top 1% always go back to basics: 
>
> From experience, a lot of founders tend to overlook the fundamentals. 
>
> They jump straight into execution without learning the language of business.
>
> I would know... I was one of them. 
>
> When I launched my first proper business,
> I was clueless about the importance of these business terms. 
>
> I thought I didn't need to learn them to succeed. 
> That line of thinking cost me countless hours I won't get back. 
>
> Don’t make the same mistake. 
>
> Learn these 7 terms like the back of your own hand:  
>
> 1. EBITDA
>
> Earnings Before Interest Taxes Depreciation Amortisation
>
> It allows investors to see how much your business really makes. 
>
> It’s one of the key numbers used to value a company.
>
> 2. Product-Market Fit
>
> When your idea solves a problem that customers want to pay for. 
>
> It ensures your business is actually addressing a customer need.
>
> 3. Working Capital
>
> This is a simple equation: Current Assets - Current Liabilities
>
> It’s the cash you’ve actually got available to keep things moving day to day. 
>
> No working capital means no real business. 
>
> 4. Assets
>
> Assets are everything your business owns that makes you money or holds value.
>
> Such as: Cash in the bank, Equipment, Property, Your brand + IP
>
> The stronger your assets, the stronger your foundation.
>
> 5. Leveraged Buyout (LBO)
>
> LBO is basically buying a company with borrowed money.
>
> You can use the company’s cash flow and assets to back that loan. 
>
> If it works, you get the reward without risking all your own cash.
>
> 6. Amortisation
>
> Spreading the cost of something you can't touch over the time you use it.
>
> These are invisible assets that give your business real value.
>
> Examples: Patent, Trademark, Licence 
>
> 7. Liabilities
>
> Liabilities are what your business owes rather than what it owns.
>
> This comes in a few forms: Wages, Loans, Mortgage, Tax
>
> Knowing assets and liabilities is how you stay in control of your business.
>
> If you don't know the parts of your business and how they function, 
> You will waste time and resources trying to muddle through. 
>
> Now I know these terms inside out, 
> It's making it much easier to build my AI tech company. 
>

>

> COO: Execution, Efficiency, Operations.
>
> If you're a new founder, it's critical to get these hires right.
>
> Here's what each role does, and why it's important:
> (Check the sheet for expanded info)
>
> 👤 Chief Executive Officer (CEO)
> ↳ The visionary and ultimate decision-maker.
>
> ❓ What They Do:
> ↳ Set long-term strategy and protect the company’s overall direction.
>
> ☄️ Purpose In The Company:
> ↳ Drive growth and create shareholder value.
>
> ⚙️ How They Do It: 
> - Translate vision into actionable strategy.
> - Hire leaders who are better than them.
> - Allocate resources across departments.
> - Represent the company to investors and press.
> - Make the final call when priorities conflict.
>
> 📊 Main KPIs:
> - Revenue Growth Rate (% YoY)
> - EBITDA or Net Profit Margin (%)
> - Enterprise Value / Valuation Growth (£ or %)
> - CAC to LTV Ratio
> - Strategic Goal Achievement(% of OKRs hit)
>
>
> 👤 Chief Financial Officer (CFO)
> ↳ The financial architect of the business.
>
> ❓ What They Do:
> ↳ Control the company's financial health.
>
> ☄️ Purpose In The Company:
> ↳ Protect the company's runway/maximise capital efficiency.
>
> ⚙️ How They Do It: 
> - Create financial forecasts and models.
> - Oversee accounting, audits, and compliance.
> - Manage investor relations and capital structure.
> - Monitor cash flow, costs, and margins.
> - Build frameworks for sustainable growth.
>
> 📊 Main KPIs:
> - Gross Margin (%)
> - Operating Margin (%)
> - Cash Conversion Cycle (Days)
> - Burn Multiple (Net Burn / Net New ARR)
> - Runway (months of cash on hand)
>
>
> 👤 Chief Operating Officer (COO)
> ↳ The execution engine of the company.
>
> ❓ What They Do:
> ↳ Oversee day-to-day operations and scale internal efficiency.
>
> ☄️ Purpose In The Company:
> ↳ Deliver operational excellence by turning everything into performance.
>
> ⚙️ How They Do It: 
> - Design workflows, org structure, and more.
> - Lead cross-functional execution.
> - Implement systems and automation to improve output.
> - Manage project delivery and quality control.
> - Turn board-level strategy into daily accountability.
>
> 📊 Main KPIs:
> - Operating Efficiency Ratio (Opex / Revenue %)
> - Cost per Unit (£)
> - Net Promoter Score (NPS)
> - Employee Productivity (Revenue per FTE)
> - Churn Rate (% of customers lost)

## Post 220 — 2025-11-03

**Likes:** 2121 | **Comments:** 669 | **Shares:** 296

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_people-second-guess-41-of-their-choices-activity-7391083922400636928-ap80)

> People second guess 41% of their choices every single day. 
>
> Here's how to stop this in seconds: 
>
> You have to master making smarter and faster decisions. 
> Every. Single. Day. 
>
> 99% of people don't know how to respond to problems in their life. 
> They waste precious time trying to address the symptoms... 
>
> These 7 mental models will help you find real solutions, faster: 
>
> 1. The OODA Loop (By John Boyd) 
>
> A continuous loop for rapid learning and response.
>
> Steps:
>
> Observe: Gather the facts.
> Orient: Analyse context and biases.
> Decide: Choose the best action.
> Act: Execute fast, then loop again.
>
> Use it for: Strategic pivots and crisis response. 
>
> 2. First Principles Thinking
>
> Deconstruct problems to their foundational truths.
>
> Use it for: Innovation, product design, and creative problem solving.
>
> 3. 6 Thinking Hats Model (By Edward de Bono) 
>
> Switch between different modes of thinking instead of mixing them. 
>
> How to use it:
>
> 1. Define the problem or decision.
> 2. Assign hats so everyone uses one hat at a time.
> 3. Cycle through all six then summarise under the Blue Hat.
> 4. End with a decision or action plan.
>
> Use it for: Brainstorming sessions, strategy meetings, and conflict resolution.
>
> 4. The 80/20 Principle (By Vilfredo Pareto)
>
> Identify the inputs that create the majority of your results.
>
> How to use it:
>
> 1. List all your activities.
> 2. Measure outcomes: revenue, engagement, etc.
> 3. Identify the 20% driving most of the results.
> 4. Double down on those activities.
> 5. Eliminate, automate, or delegate the rest.
>
> Use it for: Optimising systems, scaling operations, and reviewing performance.
>
> 5. Root Cause Analysis (By Sakichi Toyoda) 
>
> This helps you uncover why something happened.
>
> Use it for: Persistent issues, system failures, and complaints.
>
> 6. Occam’s Razor
>
> The simplest outcome or solution is usually correct.
>
> How to use it:
>
> 1. Define the problem.
> 2. List all possible explanations.
> 3. Apply the razor: 
> Which explanation requires fewest assumptions?
> 4. Act on the Simplest Viable Answer.
>
> Use it for: Diagnosing poor performance and evaluating data.
>
> 7. The 5x5 Rule
>
> A simple framework for perspective and emotional control.
>
> How to use it:
>
> 1. Pause before reacting.
> 2. Ask the 5x5 question.
> 3. Act, don’t overthink.
> 4. Reframe instantly.
> 5. Repeat daily.
>
> Use it for: Handling business stress and overcoming overthinking.
>
> These mental models will help you: 
>
> - Understand the problems in your life and how to solve them 
> - Get closer to your financial/business/personal goals 
> - Make faster decisions to create more time in your life 
>

## Post 221 — 2025-11-02

**Likes:** 3215 | **Comments:** 461 | **Shares:** 339

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_okrs-are-destinations-kpis-are-your-map-activity-7390718565844275200-hBqU)

> OKRs are destinations. KPIs are your map.  
>
> Ignore either and you won't scale.  
>
> No great business was ever built on guesswork and opinions. 
>
> You need systems that tell you where you need to go, 
> And whether you're actually getting there.
>
> Two of those systems are OKRs and KPIs, respectively. 
>
> The difference between a 7-figure exit and an 8-figure one is a founder who uses both correctly. 
>
> Here's everything you need to know to approach them correctly: 
>
> Objective Key Results (OKRs) 
>
> A system for setting direction. 
> OKRs define what success looks like.
>
> What They’re Great For:
>
> - Setting ambitious growth goals.
> - Aligning teams around one clear outcome.
> - Turning long-term strategy into short-term action.
>
> When to Use Them:
>
> - You’re scaling quickly and need focus.
> - You want your team rowing in the same direction.
> - You’re setting quarterly or annual priorities.
>
> Questions To Ask:
>
> Which single result would make the biggest impact today?
> Are our goals stretching, or just safe?
> Can every team member explain what success looks like?
>
> End Goal:
>
> Everyone knows the mission, the milestones, and the measurement.
>
> KPIs (Key Performance Indicators) 
>
> Metrics that indicate if your systems are healthy, efficient, and improving.
> Without them, you’re guessing where things are breaking.
>
> What They’re Great For:
>
> - Monitoring business health.
> - Keeping performance consistent.
> - Highlighting problems early.
>
> When To Use Them:
>
> - You want to measure stability, not just growth.
> - You’re tracking ongoing performance.
> - You’re managing teams or systems that run continuously.
>
> Questions To Ask:
>
> Which metrics prove we’re on track?
> What early indicators warn us when something’s off?
> Are we measuring progress or just activity?
>
> End Goal:
>
> Visibility and consistency.
> You can’t improve what you don’t measure. 
>
> TL;DR: 
>
> OKRs tell you where your business is headed.
> KPIs tell you if you're on the right path. 
>
> If you don't understand the difference, 
> You'll be trying to reach a destination without a map.  
>
> Are you setting/tracking both KPIs and OKRs?

## Post 222 — 2025-11-01

**Likes:** 2708 | **Comments:** 532 | **Shares:** 423

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_you-do-not-rise-to-the-level-of-your-goals-activity-7390355986110373889-pjbn)

> "You do not rise to the level of your goals. 
>
> You fall to the level of your systems."
>
> - James Clear, Atomic Habits
>
> Atomic Habits is a classic and one of my all-time favourite books.
>
> It's probably a bit overdone on this platform by now, 
> But that doesn't make it any less useful for founders. 
>
> It was foundational in helping me build and scale multiple 8-figure companies. 
>
> Clear's message is simple (but genuinely effective): 
>
> Success isn't about big leaps or moments of "inspiration." 
> It's about small, consistent actions that compound over time.
>
> In other words: 
>
> Success = Systems × Consistency × Time
>
> First, start with The Habit Loop (The 4 Laws Of Behaviour Change)
>
> This will help you build and break habits. 
>
> Cue: Make it obvious
> Craving: Make it attractive 
> Response: Make it easy  
> Reward: Make it satisfying  
>
> (For the full breakdown, see the sheet 👇) 
>
> Here are other key takeaways from the book: 
>
> 1. Tiny changes, big impact
> Small 1% improvements compound faster than you think.
>
> 2. Identity-based habits win
> Focus on who you want to become, not just what you want to achieve.
>
> 3. Systems beat motivation
> Success is a result of structure as opposed to willpower.
>
> 4. Environment is stronger than intention
> Shape your surroundings to make good habits the default.
>
> 5. Never miss twice
> One mistake is a blip. Two is a new pattern. Acknowledge both.
>
> But be warned...
>
> Building habits isn't always smooth sailing. 
>
> Here are 5 common traps that can occur while habit building: 
> (And how to avoid them) 
>
> ❌ Chasing goals, not systems. 
> ✅ Focus on daily process, not the outcome.
>
> ❌ Expecting perfection. 
> ✅ Aim for consistency over intensity.
>
> ❌ Relying on motivation. 
> ✅ Build habits that don’t need it.
>
> ❌ Starting too big. 
> ✅ Start small enough that you can’t fail.
>
> ❌ Forgetting identity.
> ✅ Become the type of person who does the habit naturally.
>
> Ultimately, it's your habits, not your "drive," that determine your trajectory. 
>
> The more consistent you are, the bigger the compound effect over time. 
>

>
> 📜 Law #2: Start With the Friction
> Start every problem with the thing you're stuck on. 
>
> 📜 Law #3: Prioritise Use Over Theory
> Ask for real advice you can implement right away. 
>
> 📜 Law #4: Ground It In Reality
> Use real references from your site, offer, or customers. 
>
> 📜 Law #5: Declare the Constraints
> Specify what you want AND what you don't want. 
>
> 📜 Law #6: Timebox the Lens
> Set clear deadlines for references and research. 
>
> 📜 Law #7: Make It Choose
> Present options and ask for the best one. 
>
> 📜 Law #8: Ask It to Judge, Then Justify
> Don't just get an output, get a critique. 
>
> 📜 Law #9: Simulate Real Scenarios
> Use setups that mimic reality. 
>
> 📜 Law #10: Lock in the Persona
> Tell it how it should think and analyse. 
>
> 📜 Law #11: Focus on Leverage
> Ask for the highest-leverage option. 
>
> 📜 Law #12: Make It Build With You
> Prompt to create a productive feedback loop. 
>
> 📜 Law #13: Include What You’ve Tried
> Let it learn from mistakes and reduce reprompts. 
>
> 📜 Law #14: Push It Into Action
> Give actionable steps in every prompt. 
>
> 📜 Law #15: Give It Tone 
> Tell it exactly what tone you want with examples. 
>
> 📜 Law #16: Ask It to Steal Smartly
> Upload examples that it can easily draw from. 
>
> 📜 Law #17: Use Negative Prompts
> Tell it what to ignore in terms of tone and style. 
>
> 📜 Law #18: Invite Pushback
> ChatGPT is a yes-man. Bypass that altogether. 
>
> 📜 Law #19: Refine Into a System
> Double-down on what works and reuse it. 
>
> These principles won't tell you what to create,
> But they'll guarantee you extract maximum value from every prompt.
>
> Use them to get better outputs from ChatGPT every time.

> Any founder worth their salt should establish:  
>
> - Where the company is going 
> - Why they want to go there 
> - What needs to happen today to get there
>
> And frameworks are the best way to build that roadmap. 
>
> Here are 8 that every founder should know:
>
> 1️⃣ The Flywheel Model
>
> Don't treat growth as a one-off event... it's a flywheel. 
> Every small win builds energy for the next. 
>
> Useful for: Building a company with long-term growth. 
>
> 2️⃣ Blue Ocean Strategy
>
> Most companies fight for the same customers. 
> The smart ones create new markets. 
>
> Useful for: Finding uncontested market space and avoiding price wars. 
>
> 3️⃣ OKRs (Objectives & Key Results)
>
> Forget endless task lists. 
> Set one clear objective and three measurable results. 
>
> Useful for: Creating focus and alignment across all teams.
>
> 4️⃣ Jobs To Be Done
>
> Customers don't buy products, they buy progress. 
> Understand what they really want, and you'll never lose relevance.
>
> Useful for: Achieving data-based product clarity and customer insights. 
>
> 5️⃣ McKinsey Three Horizons Model
>
> Horizon 1: Protect the core. 
> Horizon 2: Grow the emerging. 
> Horizon 3: Build the future. 
>
> If you only focus on today, you won't have a business tomorrow.
>
> Useful for: Balancing short-term performance with long-term growth.
>
> 6️⃣ The Value Proposition Canvas
>
> It's simple: what your customer wants vs what you actually deliver. 
> The gap between the two is where most founders lose.
>
> Useful for: Strengthening product-market fit and your marketing message. 
>
> 7️⃣ The Balanced Scorecard
>
> Revenue isn't the only metric that matters. 
> Track performance through customers, operations, and learning. 
>
> Useful for: Keeping growth measurable and balanced.
>
> 8️⃣ The Execution Gap Model
>
> Strategy is worthless without follow-through. 
> Bridge the gap between what's planned and what's done. 
>
> Useful for: Turning strategy into results with accountability/clarity.
>
> You won't need to implement all 8 of these. 
>
> But you need at least 1 that fits how you think, 
> And how your unique business operates.

## Post 230 — 2025-10-24

> Something everyone needs to know about...
>
> The F-E-A-R Paradox.
>
> Fear isn't going anywhere. 
>
> It's a basic defence mechanism, and it's there to keep you safe. 
>
> But if you don't understand it, it can end up controlling you...
>
> Instead of fueling you. 
>
> Most people perceive fear as a warning sign telling them to stop. 
>
> But it can also be a signal pointing towards growth. 
>
> Some people see fear and run. Others see fear and rise.
> It's the same feeling, with two vastly different outcomes.
>
> In practice, fear shows up in the moments that matter most.
>
> - The investor pitch you're avoiding.
> - The sales call you're putting off.
> - The hard conversation with your co-founder.
>
> Every high performer I've known has leaned into these moments. 
> Because they've learned to reframe what fear actually means.
>
> The F-E-A-R Paradox teaches three critical lessons.
>
> First, reframe the signal.
>
> Fear usually points directly to the thing that will grow you. 
> If you're scared to do it, that's often a sign you probably should.
>
> The question isn't "how do I eliminate fear?" 
> It's "what is this fear trying to tell me?"
>
> Second, shrink the step.
>
> Fear is louder when the task feels massive. 
> Break it down into the smallest possible move forward.
>
> Don't think about launching the business. 
> Think about sending one email today.
>
> Finally, detach the outcome.
>
> The fear of failing is heavier than failure itself. 
> Shift the goal from "succeed" to "take action."
>
> Success compounds when you stop protecting your ego,  
> And start protecting your progress.
>
> After building and scaling businesses for over a decade, 
> I've faced my fair share of fear. 
>
> I've had pitches go sideways. 
> Launches that completely flopped. 
> Times when our systems completely fell apart. 
>
> And I'm grateful for those moments. 
>
> Every single one taught me a lesson I never would have learned playing it safe. 
>
> So, I urge you to adopt the F-E-A-R Paradox: 
>
> Reframe the signal, shrink the step, and detach from outcomes.
>
> Your comfort zone is not where growth and success take place. 
> It's always in the things you fear doing.
>
> Face fear, and rise.
>
> What's one thing you've been avoiding because of fear?
> Let me know in the comments below.
>

> And build the life you want...

## Post 234 — 2025-10-21

**Likes:** 1938 | **Comments:** 516 | **Shares:** 271

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_1-better-every-day-37x-better-by-end-of-activity-7386369698034188289-wfzT)

> 1% better every day = 37x better by end of year.
>
> That's the secret power of Kaizen.
>
> In the 1950s, Japanese companies like Toyota introduced this concept.
>
> It means "continuous improvement" in Japanese, 
> And it was designed to increase efficiency across the business. 
>
> It worked. 
>
> Toyota became one of the most efficient manufacturers in the world.
>
> The idea is focusing on small changes that compound daily, 
> Rather than waiting for a massive breakthrough that never comes. 
>
> This is what the Kaizen cycle looks like in practice: 
>
> 1. Identify Problems
> Pick one (or multiple) problems that need improving.
>
> 2. Analyse Current Processes
> Question whether it could be done better.
>
> 3. Create Solutions
> Use creative and critical thinking to problem-solve.
>
> 4. Test The Solutions
> Apply your theoretical solution in practice.
>
> 5. Measure The Results
> Ask if it worked. Assign a measure to it if possible.
>
> 6. Standardise The Solution
> If it worked, create a system that solves the problem forever.
>
> It's insanely simple. But most founders still ignore it. 
>
> It can be applied professionally and personally.
>
> For your business:
>
> - Simplify onboarding: Remove one unnecessary step each month
> - Customer pulse checks: Send a survey after every project
> - Automate one manual task: Use AI to handle recurring tasks
> - Fix one meeting a week: Replace it with a written update
>
> For yourself:
>
> - Post-it Progress: Each day, jot one win and one improvement
> - Morning improvement focus: Ask "What can I improve today?"
> - Small failure review: Each week, learn from one mistake
> - Micro-learning habit: Read one short resource daily 
>
> Implement them simply in 4 steps:
>
> ✅ Pick your focus: 
> Start small with just one process to improve. 
>
> ✅ Set one clear metric: 
> Choose something measurable (e.g. "Save 2 hours a week"). 
>
> ✅ Make progress visible: 
> Use dashboards to log wins and ideas. 
>
> ✅ Review weekly: 
> Spend 10–15 minutes reviewing what improved. 
>
> No truly successful business is making massive changes overnight. 
>
> They focus on improving consistently, every single day.
>
> Because progress doesn't need to happen in leaps and bounds. 
>
> Even small steps move you forward. 
>
> What's one small thing you could improve today? Or this week?

> Despite popular belief, no one is born a great Founder. 
>
> You become one through continuous action.
>
> I've built and scaled multiple 8-figure businesses over the past decade and a half. 
>
> In that time, I've worked with 100s of founders, and invested in dozens more.
>
> The majority of them are competent enough to get the job done. 
>
> But exceptional founders have rare traits that take their businesses to 7, 8, or even 9-figures in revenue.
>
> Here are the 6 that I think are the most important:
>
> 1. Clarity
> They know exactly what they're building and why.
>
> 2. Conviction
> They don't need external validation to move forward.
>
> 3. Resilience
> They've been knocked down enough times to stop fearing failure.
>
> 4. Discipline
> They do the unglamorous work long after motivation runs out.
>
> 5. Self-Awareness
> They know their strengths and hire fast for their weaknesses.
>
> 6. Curiosity
> They know that learning doesn't stop after traditional education.
>
> This is the combination that separates average from extraordinary. 
>
> If you can develop all 6, nothing can stand in your way. 
>
> Here's where I would start: 
>
> 1. Build a one-page vision document
> ↳ Write down what you're building and why it matters.
> ↳ Revisit it monthly and observe how it evolves over time. 
>
> 2. Make decisions faster
> ↳ Set a 24-hour rule for decisions under £10k.
> ↳ Trust your instinct and keep moving forward. 
>
> 3. Document your failures
> ↳ Keep a log of what didn't work and what you learned.
> ↳ Treat mistakes as data points for faster improvement. 
>
> 4. Schedule the boring work
> ↳ Block time weekly for admin and ops tasks.
> ↳ Discipline is showing up when you don't feel like it.
>
> 5. Run a strengths audit
> ↳ List your top three strengths and your top three weaknesses.
> ↳ Hire or delegate your weaknesses within 90 days.
>
> 6. Commit to learning one new thing weekly
> ↳ Read, listen, or watch content outside your industry.
> ↳ Curiosity keeps you sharp and ahead of trends.
>
> Exceptional founders aren't born with these traits. 
>
> They build them through hard work, education, and consistency. 
>
> You don't need to master all 6 traits immediately. 
>
> But if you're serious about building something ambitious,

> And growth depends on supporting your team in a personalised manner.
>
> You meet them where they are, not where you wish they were.
>
> That's why I return to this Skill/Will Matrix.
> (Created by Max Landsberg)
>
> It's a simple way to determine: 
>
> - Level of skills/experience
> - Level of motivation
>
> Use it to maximise relationships and results at all levels: 
>
> ➡️ Low Will, Low Skill (The Wrong Fit)
>
> They don't have the skills.
> They're not interested in building them.
> Help them move on quickly and respectfully.
>
> ➡️ Low Will, High Skill (The Unmotivated Expert)
>
> They've got the ability...
> But they're disconnected from purpose.
> Reignite ambition with clear goals and ownership.
>
> ➡️ High Will, Low Skill (The Eager Learner)
>
> They make mistakes fast. 
> But they learn from them even faster.
> Give them structure and pair them with a mentor. 
>
> ➡️ High Will, High Skill (The High Performer)
>
> They raise standards for everyone.
> These people will shape your culture.
> Give them ownership rather than instructions.
>
> Unfortunately, most managers treat everyone the same or 'fairly.' 
>
> But a one-size-fits-all approach only chases your best people away. 
>
> AI can help you move and scale faster than ever before...
> But investing into your best people is still so valuable.
>
> Guiding your team in the right direction is still vital.

>
> 1️⃣ Hero's Journey
>
> A common adventure arc that mirrors every great story.
> Useful for: Pitch decks, brand messaging, and customer case studies.
>
> 2️⃣ The Golden Circle
>
> Lead with why you exist, not what you sell.
> Useful for: Investor pitches, team alignment and brand positioning. 
>
> 3️⃣ What, So What, Now What
>
> Turn boring facts into a reason to act.
>
> What = The fact.
> So What = Why it matters.
> Now What = What to do about it.
>
> Useful for: All-hands meetings, investor updates and board meetings. 
>
> 4️⃣ Freytag's Pyramid
>
> Narrative arc that shows struggle, breakthrough, and resolution.
> Useful for: Any content that needs emotional pull.
>
> 5️⃣ The Origin Story Framework
>
> Every founder has a story. 
> Structure it like this:
>
> Before = The problem you faced.
> Turning Point = The moment everything changed.
> After = The mission you're now on.
>
> Useful for: Intros, investor pitches, and rallying your team.
>
> 6️⃣ Pixar's Story Framework
>
> Mirrors classic narrative arcs used in every Pixar film.
> Useful for: Any narrative that needs structure and flow.

## Post 250 — 2025-10-04

**Likes:** 2444 | **Comments:** 409 | **Shares:** 354

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_ive-tried-100s-of-time-management-techniques-activity-7380209304559333376-0w5f)

> I've tried 100s of time management techniques.  
>
> This is by far my favourite: 
>
> I used to work 80 hrs/week and call it "productive." 
>
> When really I was: 
>
> - Attending pointless meetings
> - Fighting countless small fires
> - Being involved in every decision
>
> Now I work less than 70% the time and get 4x as much done.
>
> The Eisenhower Matrix helped me get there.  
>
> It teaches you to categorise tasks by importance and urgency.
>
> Here's how it works:
>
> 1. Do It Now (Urgent + Important)
>
> Examples:
> - Finalise pitch deck before investor meeting tomorrow.
> - Fix website crash during peak customer traffic.
> - Respond to press interview request before deadline.
>
> Best Practices:
> - Attack these tasks first each morning with full focus.
> - Set a strict deadline so urgency fuels execution.
>
> 2. Schedule It (Important + Not Urgent)
>
> Examples:
> - Plan quarterly strategy session with leadership team.
> - Map long-term hiring plan for next 18 months.
> - Build a personal brand content system for LinkedIn.
>
> Best Practices:
> - Protect time blocks in advance. Never leave them floating.
> - Tie them to measurable outcomes, not vague intentions.
>
> 3. Delegate It (Urgent + Not Important)
>
> Examples:
> - Handle inbound customer service queries this week.
> - Organise travel logistics for upcoming conference.
> - Update CRM with latest sales call notes.
>
> Best Practices:
> - Build playbooks so your team executes without confusion.
> - Delegate with deadlines to avoid wasting time.
>
> 4. Eliminate It (Not Urgent + Not Important)
>
> Examples:
> - Tweak logo colour palette again for fun.
> - Attend generic networking events with no ICP fit.
> - Review endless “best productivity tools” articles.
>
> Best Practices:
> - Audit weekly. Cut anything that doesn’t compound long-term.
> - Replace low-value busywork with rest, thinking, or selling.
>
> If you are always reacting to what feels urgent,  
> You'll never focus on what matters. 
>
> Attend to the tasks in quadrant 1 efficiently, 
> Then spend 60-70% of your time in quadrant 2. 
>  
> That's work that actually builds your business.
>
> Which quadrant are you spending too much time in right now? 
> Drop your thoughts in the comments.

> Years of hidden work suddenly materialise very quickly.

>
> It feels like nothing is happening. 
> When you're building the foundations that no one can see. 
>

>
> But it takes years of patience, consistency, and compounding.
>
> It took me 10 years of pure hustle to scale my first business to an 8-figure exit. 
>
> The success looked instant to everyone else, but the roots had been growing for nearly a decade.
>
> The bamboo mentality teaches three critical lessons. 
>
> First, that the right markets matter. If bamboo is planted in the wrong soil, it never grows. 
>
> If you choose the wrong market, no amount of effort can save you. 
>
> Second, the right timing matters. Bamboo explodes only after years of steady preparation. 
>
> Founders succeed when they prepare early, then strike when conditions shift. 
>
> Finally, resilience matters. Most people give up before the roots are even finished forming.

> The only way to ensure failure is to throw in the towel too soon.

> 4. Decision fatigue will haunt you

>
> 7. Business is full of failure

> ↳ Some months, work will eat everything. Other times, it's a juggling act.

>

> ↳ Keep a sharp eye here and invest in the right tools and people.

> ↳ Learn to quickly spot high performers.

> 17. Hire slow, fire fast

> Waiting for the "perfect time" = never starting. 
>
> Both mean you never reach your goals. 
>
> Luck isn't as big a factor for success as people think it is. 
>
> You can control and dictate the conditions in which your success is achieved. 
>
> So, if you're still: 
>
> - Blaming your circumstances
> - Waiting for the perfect conditions 
> - Or hoping things work out on their own...
>
> You're wasting precious time. 
>
> But all it takes is a new way of framing your thoughts.
>
> Here are 10 mindset shifts to adopt now:
> (To guide you toward future success)
>
> 1. Instead of "I'll wait until I feel fully ready to start"
> Think "I'll start now and get better as I go along"
>
> Every expert was once a beginner who simply began.
>
> 2. Instead of "I don't have enough time to take this on"
> Think "I'll cut what doesn't matter and focus only on what moves me forward"
>
> Time isn't the issue, priorities are.
>
> 3. Instead of "What if this goes wrong and ends up failing?"
> Think "If it fails, I'll take the lessons and adjust quickly"
>
> Failure becomes fuel when you view it as data, not defeat.
>
> 4. Instead of "I don't have the motivation I need to start"
> Think "I need systems that get it done whether I feel like it or not"
>
> Motivation is unreliable. Systems execute consistently.
>
> 5. Instead of "I should figure everything out on my own"
> Think "I'll put myself in rooms where others are already winning"
>
> Your environment shapes your outcomes.
>
> 6. Instead of "This feels too overwhelming to manage"
> Think "When it feels overwhelming, that means I'm growing"
>
> Discomfort will often lead to expansion.
>
> 7. Instead of "I can't move forward until I have certainty"
> Think "I'll move first, learn on the way, and adjust later"
>
> Seeking certainty causes paralysis.
>
> 8. Instead of "I don't want to risk looking stupid in front of others"
> Think "Embarrassment is just the price you pay to grow"
>
> Ego protection will keep you small.
>
> 9. Instead of "I really hope this ends up working out"
> Think "I'll create conditions where success becomes inevitable"
>
> Hope is passive. Successful people stack advantages.
>
> 10. Instead of "I've made it to where I want to be"
> Think, "This is only the start of what I can achieve"

> Complacency always kills momentum.

> Most people are still prompting GPT-5 like it's GPT-4.
>
> This is the structure to unlock its full potential:
>
> This is my adapted model from a popular framework.
> I just added a couple steps to squeeze the most out of it.
>
> Ultimately, prompt engineering is a vital skill in 2025.
> But a lot of people don't know where to start.
>
> The easiest way to start is by copying a framework !
>
> This one almost acts as a $500/hr consultant...
> It's saved me so much time since GPT-5 released.
>
> 💾 Save this post to use the prompt later:
>
> 1. Role 👤
> ↳ Tell the AI who it should be exactly.
> ↳ You get answers grounded in experience.
>
> 2. Task 📕
> ↳ Set the exact job you want it to complete.
> ↳ You get a more focused output as a result.
>
> 3. Format 📄
> ↳ Force structure: i.e. roadmap, KPIs, owner, etc.
> ↳ The output is like a playbook, not a brain dump.
>
> 4. Warnings ⚠️
> ↳ Call out the no-no's, ask for zero vagueness.
> ↳ Forces the AI to stay on brief with its answers.
>
> 5. Reasoning 🧠
> ↳ Make it justify every move - why, how, and what.
> ↳ Turns tasks into testable steps and expected impact.
>
> 6. Stop Conditions 🛑
> ↳ Tell it when to quit: i.e. 90 days, 5 actions, etc.
> ↳ You avoid the GPT waffling on with useless info.
>
> 7. Context Dump 🗑️
> ↳ Load it with specifics: i.e. product, target, budget, etc.
> ↳ Cuts out generic answers and forces relevance.
>
> My team and I now use this prompt framework at the start of every new project.
>
> Prompting doesn't have to be as complex as it seems.
> Just have you vision in mind and follow this structure.
>
> This works especially well for GPT-5.
> But the same thinking applies to all LLMs:
>
> The clearer you are, the better your results will be.
>

## Post 259 — 2025-09-25

**Likes:** 2476 | **Comments:** 554 | **Shares:** 306

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_ai-agents-and-agentic-ai-are-not-the-same-activity-7376947857418919936-TMtJ)

> AI Agents and Agentic AI are not the same.
>
> Your top competitors already know this:  
>
> There are 3 types of AI workflows worth knowing, 
> And each one serves a different purpose.
>
> If you don't understand them, you're falling behind...  
>
> (While your competitors are building autonomous systems that run 24/7.) 
>
> Here's how to tell them apart: 
>
> 🤖 Non-Agentic AI
> ↳ Basic prompt-response AI with no memory/reasoning. 
>
> ⚙️ How it works:
>
> - User types a single prompt, model processes 
> - Generates a direct response immediately 
> - Interaction ends with no context retention
>
> ✅ Pros:
> ↳ Fast, cheap, and universally accessible
> ↳ Requires no technical build or integration
> ↳ Great for clear, one-off tasks
>
> 🚫 Cons:
> ↳ No reasoning or context awareness
> ↳ Quality depends heavily on prompts
> ↳ Struggles with multi-step work
>
> 📈 How to build fast:
> ↳ Open ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini
> ↳ Write clear, specific prompts with context
> ↳ Copy output, edit as needed, and repeat
>
> 🧠 Agentic AI
> ↳ Self-managing AI system that can plan and execute. 
>
> ⚙️ How it works:
>
> - The system breaks your goal into sub-tasks
> - Connects to tools, APIs, data sources 
> - Evaluates results with feedback loops
>
> ✅ Pros:
> ↳ Handles complex, changing projects 
> ↳ Can integrate with tools and databases
> ↳ Produces more reliable outcomes 
>
> 🚫 Cons:
> ↳ Slower and more expensive than agents
> ↳ Requires human oversight and guardrails
> ↳ Risk of overbuilding for simple problems
>
> 📈 How to build fast:
> ↳ Use LangChain, CrewAI, or AutoGen frameworks
> ↳ Assign roles: Planner, Executor, Critic 
> ↳ Add memory and feedback layers for consistency
>
> ⚡ AI Agent
> ↳ Single-task AI worker designed to automate one task.
>
> ⚙️ How it works:
>
> - User defines one clear responsibility
> - Agent receives inputs, accesses connected tools
> - Executes and outputs without guidance
>
> ✅ Pros:
> ↳ Automates repetitive, time-consuming tasks
> ↳ Quick setup and cost-efficient
> ↳ Easy to test and refine within roles
>
> 🚫 Cons:
> ↳ It can't handle broader projects 
> ↳ Breaks if inputs are unclear or data is missing
> ↳ Needs orchestration to work alongside other agents
>
> 📈 How to build fast:
> ↳ Define one specific, repetitive task for automation
> ↳ Use Zapier, LangChain, or OpenAI Assistants API
> ↳ Connect required inputs/outputs, test before deploying
>
> TLDR; 
>
> AI Agents = Single-task automation
> Agentic AI = Multi-step problem solving
>
> Most businesses need both, but they're building neither.
>
> The dominant businesses will master all 3, and build accordingly. 
>
> How are you using AI for business? 
> Drop your answer in the comments. 
>
> I'm building an Agentic AI called Searchable. 
> It analyses and optimises your site automatically for SEO/AEO. 
>

> Most brands are missing the 4 layers of SEO.  
>
> (These are holding them back without realising.)
>
> SEO isn't just about keywords and backlinks anymore.
> Search now happens across multiple engines, AI systems, and user behaviours.
>
> Traditional SEO still matters: 
> Google processes 8.5 billion searches daily. 
>
> But if you're only optimising for traditional search, 
> You're missing out on real visibility (aka revenue) opportunity.  
>
> 🔍 Layer 1: SXO - Search Experience Optimisation
> ↳ Turn clicks into conversions with UX that actually works.
>
> Best practices:
>
> - Optimise page speed for sub-2 second loads
> - Design mobile-first experiences (60% of searches are mobile)
> - Align your content with user intent
> - Test your conversion funnels ruthlessly
> - Track dwell time and scroll depth, not just rankings
>
> 🔍 Layer 2: AIO (AI Optimisation)  
> ↳ Scale visibility with AI-powered content systems.
>
> Best practices:
>
> - Automate internal linking strategies
> - Use AI for content drafting and optimisation at scale
> - Create content templates that maintain quality across volume
> - Implement AI-powered site audits for continuous optimisation
> - Build systems for multi-format content repurposing
>
> 🔍 Layer 3: GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation) 
> ↳ Be cited by AI in summaries and retrieval-based answers.
>
> Best practices:
>
> - Publish factual, data-backed content that AI systems trust
> - Create comprehensive industry studies and original research
> - Build topical authority through consistent, expert-level content
> - Structure information in formats AI can easily extract and cite
> - Focus on being the definitive source on specific topics
>
> 🔍 Layer 4: AEO (Answer Engine Optimisation) 
> ↳ Get chosen by AI overviews and zero-click answers.
>
> Best practices:
>
> - Structure content with clear questions as headers
> - Lead every section with one-sentence answers AI can extract
> - Implement schema markup (FAQ, How-To, Q&A structured data)
> - Target question-based keywords people ask voice assistants
> - Create content that directly matches how people prompt AI systems
>
> If you've noticed your SEO stalling, 
> The answer might be in what you're lacking...
>
> Not in what you're doing wrong.

> ↳ Add sidebar modules for lead magnets

## Post 264 — 2025-09-20

**Likes:** 1146 | **Comments:** 376 | **Shares:** 133

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_the-majority-of-entrepreneurs-are-tracking-activity-7375135767976747008-vknB)

> The majority of entrepreneurs are tracking the wrong metrics.
>
> (I learned this through heavy, heavy research) 
>
> It doesn't matter how sleek your product is, 
> If you can't communicate the results. 
>
> This is where a lot of entrepreneurs go wrong.
>
> They either don't track any KPIs at all (a huge error)
> Or they measure the wrong ones entirely.
>
> For example, I see a lot of new entrepreneurs measure website traffic.
> But they completely ignore the conversion off the back of that.
>
> So if you're a new or seasoned entrepreneur,
> I highly recommend saving this sheet and coming back to it later.
>
> Make use of these 15 KPIs and how to track them (in the sheet):
>
> ✅ Net Revenue Retention (NRR)
> ↳ Measures revenue kept after churn and expansions. 
> ↳ This is your North Star.
>
> ✅ Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)
> ↳ Average revenue a customer generates over their relationship with you.
> ↳ Pair with CAC to prove ROI of growth.
>
> ✅ Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
> ↳ Average spend required to win a new customer.
> ↳ Set budgets and check efficiency of growth.
>
> ✅ LTV to CAC Ratio
> ↳ Compares lifetime value of a customer to acquisition cost.
> ↳ Validate sustainable growth. >3 is strong.
>
> ✅ Monthly Active Users (MAU)
> ↳ Number of unique active users in a month.
> ↳ Measure adoption and stickiness.
>
> ✅ Churn Rate
> ↳ Percentage of customers or revenue lost. 
> ↳ Rising churn = weak product-market fit.
>
> ✅ Burn Multiple
> ↳ Cash burned for every $1 in new ARR.
> ↳ Track during fundraising and growth phases. 
>
> ✅ EBITDA
> ↳ Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, amortisation.
> ↳ Measure profitability at scale.
>
> ✅ Operating Cash Flow
> ↳ Net cash from operating activities.
> ↳ Confirm the business can fund itself.
>
> ✅ Customer Retention Rate
> ↳ Percentage of customers who continue to buy from you over a set period.
> ↳ Measure loyalty and product-market fit.
>
> ✅ Revenue Growth Rate
> ↳ Percentage increase in revenue over a given period.
> ↳ To show business momentum and scalability.
>
> ✅ AI Search Visibility
> ↳ Share of prompts where your brand/product is surfaced in AI answers.
> ↳ Measure discoverability in AI-led search.
>
> ✅ Runway (Cash Runway)
> ↳ How many months your business can operate before running out of cash.
> ↳ When planning budgets, to balance growth vs. cash preservation.
>
> ✅ Experiment Velocity
> ↳ Number of product, content, or GTM experiments shipped.
> ↳ Track speed of iteration and learning.
>
> ✅ Gross Margin
> ↳ Profitability after direct costs. 
> ↳ Prove scalability and efficiency to investors.
>
> Use these to spot weak foundations, 
> And learn how to fix or improve them.
>
> Are you tracking any of these already? 
> Let me know in the comments. 
>
> I share more like this in my weekly newsletter, Step By Step. 
> It will help you build your business faster and smarter.

## Post 272 — 2025-09-13

**Likes:** 2534 | **Comments:** 415 | **Shares:** 249

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_90-of-chatgpt-users-are-still-using-simple-activity-7372598977692717056-l_rl)

> 90% of ChatGPT users are still using simple prompts.
> The other 10% are using the tool to make millions.
> Which are you?
>
> People always ask me where they should start with AI,  
> And my answer is always the same: master the art of prompting. 
>
> Asking basic questions will get you average responses. 
> Quite frankly, it's a misuse of insanely valuable technology. 
>
> My team and I have learned this deeply as a skill.
> The results are incredible:
>
> - Operations are streamlined and optimised. 
> - Automated tasks are freeing up hours of work.  
> - And more time spent on the truly valuable tasks.
>
> These are 8 prompt frameworks I use to power my businesses:
> (so I can focus on preparing for my new baby boy !)  
>  
> 1️⃣ R-T-F
> Role: Define the persona or expertise the AI should take on.
> Task: Outline exactly what you want it to do.
> Format: Clarify how you’d like the answer delivered.
>
> 2️⃣ S-O-L-V-E
> Situation: Lay out the scenario or problem.
> Objective: State the end goal clearly.
> Limits: Flag any boundaries or constraints.
> Vision: Share the bigger-picture aim.
> Execution: Break down the steps to get there.
>
> 3️⃣ T-A-G
> Task: What needs to be done.
> Action: The process or method to use.
> Goal: The success measure or desired result.
>
> 4️⃣ R-A-C-E
> Role: Assign the persona or angle.
> Action: Give the core instruction.
> Context: Provide key background or details.
> End Result: Describe what the final answer should look like.
>
> 5️⃣ D-R-E-A-M
> Define: State the challenge or objective.
> Research: Specify the insights or data needed.
> Execute: Show how to act on it.
> Analyse: Assess the output or results.
> Measure: Set criteria for tracking success.
>
> 6️⃣ P-A-C-T
> Problem: Highlight the issue.
> Approach: Suggest the way forward.
> Checks: Identify possible trade-offs or adjustments.
> Test: Decide how success will be verified.
>
> 7️⃣ C-A-R-E
> Context: Give the backdrop or scenario.
> Action: State the step to take.
> Result: Show the intended outcome.
> Example: Share a sample or reference for clarity.
>
> 8️⃣ R-I-S-E
> Role: Assign who the AI should be.
> Input: Provide the key information to use.
> Steps: Ask for a clear, logical sequence.
> End Goal: Define the outcome you want.
>
> AI is the biggest source of leverage across all my businesses. 
> But we couldn't have gotten there without learning to prompt.  
>
> If you have an hour to scroll Instagram, 
> I know you have time to learn these methods...

> But AI-driven rankings are shaping recommendations and buyer intent. 
>

>
> ➡️ Step 1: Be Found (SEO) 
> ↳ Search engines still matter, but they’ve changed. You need to:
>
> ✅ Nail the fundamentals: fast site, schema, structured data.
> ✅ Build clusters around full topics, not just keywords.
> ✅ Own authority with consistent on-page optimisation and backlinks.
>

>
> ➡️ Step 2: Be Chosen (AEO) 
> ↳ AI Overviews are now the front door of discovery. To win, you must:
>
> ✅ Optimise for voice queries, FAQs, and instant answers.
> ✅ Structure content so LLMs can “lift” your answers directly.
> ✅ Prioritise clarity, short snippets, and schema-rich responses.
>
> If you aren’t AI’s first choice, you will be invisible.
>
> ➡️ Step 3: Be Cited (GEO) 
> ↳ Generative engines reward those they can reference. To earn citations:
>
> ✅ Create high-trust, insight-led content.
> ✅ Publish data, original thinking, and frameworks AI can reference.
> ✅ Use prompt-led publishing to match how people query LLMs.
>
> If the machines don’t cite you, humans won’t find you.
>
> ➡️ Step 4: Be Scaled (AIO)
> ↳ AI has changed the economics of content. Scale comes from:
>
> ✅ Automating content production without losing voice.
> ✅ Repurposing into multiple formats (text, video, carousel).
> ✅ Using AI for editorial planning, clustering, and coverage.
>
> This is how you compete on volume without burning resources.
>
> ➡️ Step 5: Be Dominant (SXO)

>

> ✅ Dominate a niche with topic-layering across search, AI, and platforms.
> ✅ Push traffic off platforms into owned channels (newsletter, community).

> - Will challenge and stretch you
> - Will push way past what you thought was possible 
>

>

> And after attending every networking event under the sun. 
>
> Here's how to surround yourself with great people: 
>
> 1. Stay late at events.

>

> ↳ AI Overviews pull 67% from top rankings
> ↳ ChatGPT references 28% from high-ranking pages
>
> Nail your keyword rankings, win at AI search too.
>
> Most people are still using 2020 ranking strategies in 2025.
>
> Here's what actually works now:
>
> 1. Track Like a Pro (Not Like a Beginner)
>
> Use Google Search Console for the basics:
> → Shows average position across 1,000+ queries
> → Reveals which keywords drive actual traffic
> → Completely free (no excuses)
>
> But if you're serious, upgrade to Position Tracking:
> → Daily ranking updates
> → Competitor monitoring
> → AI visibility tracking
> → Custom alerts when rankings move
>
> 2. Create Content That Crushes Competition
>
> Study the top 10 results and ask:
> → What depth are they missing?
> → Where are the content gaps?
> → How can I add unique value?
>
> Then implement E-E-A-T like your business depends on it:
> → Experience: Share first-hand, real-world experience
> → Expertise: Interview subject matter experts
> → Authoritativeness: Conduct original research and cite trusted sources
> → Trustworthiness: Build credibility through transparency and accuracy
>
> 3. Satisfy Search Intent 
>
> Four types of intent in 2025:
> → Informational (how-to guides)
> → Navigational (brand searches)
>
> → Commercial (comparison content)
> → Transactional (ready to buy)
>
> Match your content format to the intent.
>
> A product page won't rank for "how to" queries.
>
> 4. Refresh Content Strategically
>
> Find pages that used to rank well but dropped off.
>
> Update with:
> → Fresh statistics and data
> → New screenshots/examples
> → Improved formatting
> → Additional visual elements
>
> Even small updates can resurrect dead rankings.
>
> 5. Build Links That Actually Matter
>
> Quality > quantity, always.
>
> Focus on:
> → Industry publications
> → Partner websites
> → Guest posting on authority sites
> → Creating linkable assets (studies, tools)
>
> 6. Fix Technical Issues
>
> Use Site Audit tools to catch:
> → Page speed problems
> → Mobile-unfriendly pages
> → Broken internal links
> → Missing schema markup
>
> Google can't rank what it can't properly crawl.
>

> Keyword rankings aren't dead. They're evolved.

## Post 284 — 2025-09-01

**Likes:** 1474 | **Comments:** 532 | **Shares:** 186

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_push-marketing-isnt-completely-dead-its-activity-7368250420663578627-N9-l)

> Push marketing isn't completely dead. 
>
> It's just lazy when that's all you rely on. 
>
> Great businesses take advantage of two types of marketing: 
>
> 🫸 Push to drive urgency and attention. 
> 🤜 Pull to focus on value and trust.
>
> Most founders lean too heavily to one side. 
>
> They run ads without building authority, 
> Or post endless content without making an ask.  
>
> In 2025, that won't cut it. 
>
> Here's why using both is vital 👇
>
> 🫸 Push Marketing = “Buy this now.”
>
> Actively promoting your product or service to generate immediate demand.
>
> What It's Great For: 
>
> ✅ Fast revenue wins
> ✅ Clearing inventory or seasonal offers
> ✅ Keeping a broad audience aware of you
>
> Use It When: 
>
> ➡️ You need short-term cash flow
> ➡️ You’re entering a new market fast
> ➡️ You want to push an offer to the masses
>
> Questions to Answer: 
>
> ❓ Urgency – What reason are you giving people to act today?
> ❓ Message – Is your pitch simple enough to understand in seconds?
> ❓ Targeting – Are you reaching the right people?
> ❓ Conversion – How will you track ROI?
>
> Potential Problems: 
>
> ❌ Can burn cash quickly if ads flop
> ❌ Audience fatigue from constant promotions
>
> The end goal is immediate conversions. 
>  
> Measured in direct sales, sign-ups, or booked calls.
>
>
> 🤜 Pull Marketing = “Discover with us.”
>
> Attracting consumers by creating value, so they come to you voluntarily.
>
> What It’s Great For:
>
> ✅ Building brand equity over time
> ✅ Establishing thought leadership and trust
> ✅ Driving organic traffic and inbound leads
>
> Use It When:
>
> ➡️ You want to scale sustainably
> ➡️ You’re building a premium or trusted brand
> ➡️ You’d rather nurture an audience than chase one
>
> Questions to Answer:
>
> ❓ Value – What’s pulling people towards you?
> ❓ Consistency – Can you show up regularly?
> ❓ Community – Are you creating conversations, not just broadcasts?
> ❓ Patience – Are you willing to play the long game?
>
> Potential Problems:
>
> ❌ Takes longer to see results
> ❌ Requires strong consistency and patience
>
> The end goal is long-term brand loyalty.
>
> Measured in organic traffic growth, community size, and referrals.
>
> TLDR; 
>
> You need push and pull marketing working together. 
>
> Push drives cash flow.
> Pull builds equity.
>
> I break down more lessons for business growth in Step By Step, 
> My weekly newsletter read by 200K+ founders and operators.
>

## Post 292 — 2025-08-24

**Likes:** 669 | **Comments:** 333 | **Shares:** 43

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_every-aeo-expert-is-overcomplicating-this-activity-7365351317529104384-whup)

> Every "AEO expert" is overcomplicating this.
>
> They'll sell you:
>
> "Advanced schema optimisation!"
> "AI-specific content frameworks!"
> "Proprietary citation methodologies!"
>
> Here's the truth after testing everything:
>
> The 5-Step AEO Strategy That Actually Works
>
> 1. Target Real User Questions
>
> Research natural language, conversational queries your audience asks.
>
> Pull data from:
> ↳ Google Search Console
> ↳ People Also Ask (PAA)
> ↳ Community forums
> ↳ AI prompt analysis tools
>
> Mirror the exact phrasing of these questions in your content headings and FAQs.
>
> AI assistants prioritise content that directly matches query intent,.
>
> Phrased in a way users naturally speak.
>
> 2. Optimise for Featured Snippets
>
> Lead with a 40–50 word direct answer before expanding into detail.
>
> Structure content with:
> ↳ H2/H3 headings
> ↳ Bullet points and tables
> ↳ Short paragraphs
> ↳ Schema markup
>
> Featured snippets are the crown jewels of AEO. 
>
> They feed AI assistants the answer directly and dominate SERP visibility.
>
> 3. Win People Also Ask (PAA) Boxes
>
> Monitor recurring PAA questions using SERP tracking tools.
> Always back up answers with trusted citations and credible data.
> Write fact-based, authoritative answers that are 2–4 sentences long.
>
> PAA boxes are excellent for visibility in both search engines and AI assistants. 
>
> These questions often reflect the exact prompts AI tools use for retrieval.
>
> 4. Build FAQ Pages with Schema
>
> Create dedicated FAQ pages for each core topic.
> Use JSON-LD FAQ schema to mark up each Q&A pair.
> Include verifiable statistics, real examples, and references.
>
> FAQ schema dramatically boosts machine readability.
> It ensures your content is eligible for enhanced search features.
>
> 5. Earn Topic Authority
>
> Cover your core topic and its related subtopics in-depth (topic clusters).
>
> Follow E-E-A-T principles:
> ↳ Experience - Demonstrate first-hand use
> ↳ Expertise - Show credentials and knowledge
> ↳ Authoritativeness - Get cited by reputable sites
> ↳ Trustworthiness - Provide accurate, sourced information
>
> AI platforms favour authoritative, well-cited sources. 
> By building topical depth and credibility over time.
> You become the go-to source for AI assistants.
>
> Here's what I've learned after 8 months of testing:
>
> Most businesses are chasing complex AEO tactics...
>
> While ignoring the fundamentals.

> They know the "perfect idea" or "perfect timing" is a myth. 
>
> Instead, they go for an idea that "good enough", 
> And focus everything on executing that idea with precision. 
>
> So, the next time you get hit with an idea, even an average one, 
> Here's what I want you to do:  
>
> 1️⃣ Trim The Fat
> ↳ Boil the concept down to its simplest form.
> ↳ Start with the smallest MVP (a landing page or a sign‑up form). 
>
> 2️⃣ Set a Hard Finish Date
> ↳ Apply Parkinson’s Law by giving yourself a strict completion deadline.
> ↳ The less time you allow, the faster you’ll find what really matters.
>
> (Parkinson’s Law: “Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.”)
>
> 3️⃣ Gather Early Feedback
> ↳ Share it with a handful of your target users.
> ↳ Identify what resonates and what falls flat.
>
> 4️⃣ Track Early Signals
> ↳ Watch closely for patterns in reactions and feedback.
> ↳ Decide if it’s worth committing more resources.
>
> 5️⃣ Launch, Then Improve
> ↳ Don't wait for perfection, just get it out there. 
> ↳ Keep refining based on real‑world usage and user insights.
>

> It's painful to see people use GPT-5 like it's GPT-4o.
>
> Instead, get 87% more out of it with this: 
>
> The ultimate GPT-5 Prompting guide. 
>
> I’ve been testing GPT-5 since it was released, 
> And it's undoubtedly more powerful.  
>
> It’s faster, smarter, and capable of PhD-level reasoning.
>
> But the quality of your prompts still decides your results. 
>
> And prompting for GPT-5 works a little differently...
>
> Here’s what you need to know to get the most out of it 👇
>
> The Anatomy Of The Perfect Prompt:
>
> 1️⃣ Role: Who the AI should be.
> 2️⃣ Task: Exactly what you want.
> 3️⃣ Context: Background info, constraints, and tone.
> 4️⃣ Format: How the output should be delivered.
> 5️⃣ Examples: Optional, but accelerates accuracy.
> 6️⃣ Deadline: Encourages concise, complete answers.
>
> Quality Prompt Structures to Steal:
>
> (See the sheet for full details 👇)
>
> ✅ R-T-F
> R: Role 
> T: Task
> F: Format
>
> ✅ S-O-L-V-E
> S: Situation
> O: Objective
> L: Limitations
> V: Vision
> E: Execution
>
> ✅ T-A-G
> T: Task
> A: Action
> G: Goal 
>
> ✅ R-A-C-E
> R: Role 
> A: Action
> C: Context
> E: Expectation
>
> ✅ C-A-R-E
> C: Context
> A: Action
> R: Result
> E: Example
>
> GPT-5 Prompting Do’s & Don’ts
>
> Do: 
>
> ✅ Be specific. 
> ✅ Provide examples and style references.
> ✅ Break long jobs into steps.
> ✅ Ask follow-ups. 
>
> Don't: 
>
> 🚫 Use vague prompts like “Write me a marketing plan.”
> 🚫 Expect perfect results first time.
> 🚫 Overload with unrelated instructions.
> 🚫 Forget to set the role/tone. 
>
> Cautions & Considerations
>
> ➡️ Keep style and voice consistent.
> ➡️ Frontload context and critical info.
> ➡️ Prioritise clarity for the best results.  
> ➡️ Split big tasks into smaller steps to maintain focus.
> ➡️ Examples beat adjectives. (“Write like this” > “Write professionally.”)
>
> Tips & Tricks for GPT-5 Prompting
>
> 1️⃣ Use the 6-line anatomy: Role, Task, Context, Format, Examples, Deadline.
> 2️⃣ Ask for a plan first: “Outline the steps you’ll take, then execute.”
> 3️⃣ Provide few-shot examples: One good sample and one to avoid.
> 4️⃣ Split big asks into micro prompts: Iterate and refine.
> 5️⃣ Generate options: “Give me 3 approaches, evaluate them, and recommend one.”
>
> Prompt engineering isn't nearly as complex as it seems. 
>
> Just have your vision in mind and follow these parameters. 
>
> Like all GPT models, the clearer you are, the better your results will be. 
>

## Post 299 — 2025-08-17

**Likes:** 1509 | **Comments:** 397 | **Shares:** 147

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_the-common-start-up-killer-overinflated-activity-7362814689816289280-V9p9)

> The common start-up killer: Overinflated egos
>
> Your “billion-dollar” idea is likely worth 1000s. 
>
> I've seen founders go after a $200B market...
>
> Only to realise their market size is closer to $2M.  
>
> That's why you need to know TAM vs SAM vs SOM: 
>
> TAM → Everyone in the world who could buy your product.  
> SAM → The select people who can feasibly buy your product. 
> SOM → The number of places you'll actually deliver to. 
>
> But here are the real differences to know: 
>
> 🌎 TAM → Total Addressable Market
> ↳ The full revenue opportunity if you captured 100% of the market.
>
> How It Works
> ↳ Calculate the broadest possible market
> ↳ Includes every potential customer 
>
> When To Use
> ↳ Validate if a market is big enough to pursue
> ↳ Attract investors who want to see scale potential
>
> How To Calculate
> ↳ Customer base × average annual spend
> ↳ Use industry reports or analyst research
>
> Pros
> ✅ Shows market ceiling — easy to communicate scale
> ✅ Useful in high‑level planning and fundraising
>
> Cons
> 🚫 Unrealistic — you’ll never capture it all
> 🚫 Can mislead founders into overestimating opportunity
>
> 👥 SAM → Serviceable Addressable Market
> ↳ The portion of the TAM your product can actually serve.
>
> How It Works
> ↳ Takes TAM and removes markets you cannot serve
> ↳ Factors in product features, language, or region limitations
>
> When To Use
> ↳ Planning go‑to‑market and expansion strategy
> ↳ Setting realistic growth goals
>
> How To Calculate
> ↳ Start with TAM → remove areas you can’t serve
> ↳ Focus on the audience matching your product scope
>
> Pros
> ✅ Grounds big market numbers in reality
> ✅ Useful for targeting and prioritisation
>
> Cons
> 🚫 Still assumes 100% share in reachable segment
> 🚫 Requires detailed market data (not always easy to get)
>
> 📦 SOM → Serviceable Obtainable Market
> ↳ The slice of SAM you can realistically win in 1–3 years.
>
> How It Works
> ↳ Starts with SAM and factors in execution capacity + competition
> ↳ Represents the share you could actually capture 
>
> When To Use
> ↳ Building 1–3 year revenue forecasts
> ↳ Setting sales targets and hiring plans
>
> How To Calculate
> ↳ Estimate achievable market share of SAM 
> ↳ Analyse competitor penetration and your growth rate
>
> Pros
> ✅ Forces realistic planning
> ✅ Anchors forecasts to achievable milestones
>
> Cons
> 🚫 Conservative — can underplay upside
> 🚫 Requires accurate competitive intel
>
> Most founders overestimate their market, 
> And capture a fraction of their SAM.  
>
> Keep your SOM as your baseline. 
> It will determine funding, hiring, etc. 
>
> If you want to size your real market and rank where AI sends buyers, 
> I'm launching a new AI business...
>
> It can analyse and optimise your website for SEO/AEO/GEO. 
>

> https://bit.ly/4fofoBH
>

>
> The launch could have gone better...
> (Even Sam Altman admitted it was a 'bumpy' start)
>
> But now we are over the kinks, 
> The leverage you can build is truly phenomenal. 
>
> Here’s everything you need to know packaged into one cheat sheet 👇
>
> What is GPT-5?
> ↳ The smartest, fastest, and most useful ChatGPT yet.
>
> If GPT-3 was a clever high schooler
> And GPT-4 was a solid university grad...
>
> GPT-5 is a PhD-level expert that can plan, reason, and execute, 
> With elite precision.
>
> Upgrades from GPT-4 → GPT-5
>
> 1️⃣ Smarter reasoning → Knows when to pause, think, and go deeper.
> 2️⃣ Elite coding → Cleaner, more complex code, and faster debugging.
> 3️⃣ Better writing → More expressive, structured, and less generic.
> 4️⃣ Fewer mistakes → Far fewer hallucinations.
> 5️⃣ Twice the memory → Remembers 2,000+ words of context (up from ~1,000).
> 6️⃣ Faster responses → Feels instant, even for complex tasks.
> 7️⃣ Customisable UI → More control over your workspace.
>
> Model Options
> ↳ GPT-5 (Default): Balanced speed + quality.
> ↳ GPT-5 Thinking: Slower, unmatched for complex reasoning.
> ↳ GPT-5 Pro: Paid, deep analysis + long-form projects.
> ↳ GPT-5-Mini: Lightning fast + cheapest for bulk tasks.
>
> Tips & Tricks
>
> ✅ Using follow-up prompts will improve it with iteration. 
> ✅ Switch to GPT Thinking for strategy or deep planning.
> ✅ Break your request into steps for more accuracy.
> ✅ Upload files and set a clear goal to save time. 
> ✅ GPT-5 can match tone/style examples exactly. 
>
> Limits & Considerations
>
> ⚠️ Reasoning Mode is slower.
> ⚠️ Vision accuracy depends on image quality.
> ⚠️ Internet browsing by default needs a plugin/tool.
> ⚠️ Large uploads should be split due to file size limits. 
> ⚠️ Memory is opt-in (No recall between chats unless enabled).
>
> Pricing
>
> 💸 Free → GPT-5 Mini + basic GPT-5, limited memory, slower speed.
> 💸 Plus ($20/mo) → Full GPT-5 + Thinking Mode, faster, priority access.
> 💸 Pro ($200/mo) → Longest memory, deepest reasoning, fastest for heavy workloads.
>
> The jump from GPT-3 → GPT-4 felt huge.
>
> GPT-5 might not seem as mind-blowing, but it’s a serious upgrade...
>
> One that will likely change how you work every day.
