## Post 307 — 2025-08-09

**Likes:** 1648 | **Comments:** 491 | **Shares:** 194

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_42-of-startups-fail-because-they-built-something-activity-7359915518641799168-hK2-)

> 42% of startups fail because they built something nobody wants.
>
> Here’s how to fix that:   
>
> The purpose of your minimum viable product (MVP) is in the name. 
>
> It's your product pared down to the most viable parts. 
>
> It shouldn't: 
>
> 🚫 Have an excessive amount of features
> 🚫 Solve multiple problems instead of one
> 🚫 Basically be a full product, instead of a test
>
> That just a waste of time and resources. 
>
> When in doubt, subtract, don't add. 
>
> Strip back your offer to the fundamentals and see what works. 
> Then go back and build from there. 
>
> I'm currently in the process of building an MVP myself, 
> And this is the exact process I'm using:  
>
> (It's the same roadmap I used to kickstart multiple 7 and 8-figure businesses, 
> Including The Creator Accelerator) 
>
> 1. Who is my MVP for?
>
> 👥 Who is your target audience?
> ❓ What problem are you solving?
> 💸 How does your MVP provide value?
>
> 2. The Problem Validation Phase
>
> Go through the checklist of validation steps (below) 👇
>
> 💬 Would you actually pay for this?
> 🔸 If no one is eager for a solution, rethink your MVP.
>
> 3. The Core MVP Features
>
> 🏆 The golden rule: Solve ONE specific problem in the simplest way possible.
>
> What your MVP should do:
> ✅ Focus on the absolute essential feature(s).
> ✅ Be usable without extensive training.
> ✅ Provide immediate value.
> ✅ Be built in 4–8 weeks max.
>
> Common MVP mistakes:
> ❌ Trying to build the full product vision from day one.
> ❌ Packing too many features into v1.
>
> 4. The MVP Launch Strategy
>
> Get early adopters through:
>  
> 🔗 Social Media
> 🎟️ Early Access
> 📧 Email Outreach
>
> First users = your best testers.
>
> 5. Feedback & Iteration Process
>
> Measure everything, improve constantly.
>
> 🌀 Key Feedback Loop:
> Launch → Get Feedback → Iterate → Relaunch
>
> 6. Monetisation & Scaling Strategy
>
> Ways to monetise:
> 💵 One-time purchase
> 💳 Subscription
> 🛒 Upsells
>
> Key signs your MVP is ready to scale:
> ✅ Strong retention & repeat users
> ✅ Demand for more features
> ✅ Customers willing to pay
> 	
> (See the cheat sheet below for the full guide. 👇)
> 	
> Developing a successful MVP is about repetition and consistency. 
>
> To ensure success, make sure you: 
>
> ⚙️ Build fast, validate often, and iterate quickly. 
> 👥 Launch it early and use incoming feedback to improve. 
> ❌ Remove any features that aren't working before adding more. 
>
> When it comes to an MVP, simplicity will always beat complexity. 
>
> What's been your biggest MVP roadblock? 
> Let me know in the comments. 👇
>

> 20 AI Concepts You Need To Know In 2025 
>
> (It's not enough to know what an LLM is...) 
>
> If you want to compete or protect your business in the age of AI, 
> You need to understand how this technology actually works. 
>
> If it were a game...
>
> Prompting ChatGPT is basically level 1. 
> And the top businesses are already at level 50.  
>
> But the rules of that game are changing fast, 
> And your best time investment is keeping up with them. 
>
> Here are 20 AI concepts to get your head around now 👇
> (See the sheet for full details) 
>
> 🤖 AI Ethics & Bias
> ↳ Fairness, transparency, and regulation are critical for trust.
>
> 🤖 Generative AI
> ↳ AI that creates content, powering tools like ChatGPT.
>
> 🤖 Large Language Models (LLMs)
> ↳ Massive models that can reason, write, and converse.
>
> 🤖 Multimodal AI
> ↳ Models that can process and combine text, images, audio, and video.
>
> 🤖 Prompt Engineering
> ↳ The skill of crafting instructions to get better results from AI.
>
> 🤖 AI Agents
> ↳ Autonomous AI that can take actions without constant user prompts.
>
> 🤖 Computer Vision
> ↳ AI that “sees” and interprets images or video. 
>
> 🤖 Natural Language Processing (NLP)
> ↳ How AI understands and generates human language.
>
> 🤖 Machine Learning (ML)
> ↳ The foundation of AI. Systems that learn from data. 
>
> 🤖 Deep Learning
> ↳ A more advanced form of ML using multi-layered neural networks. 
>
> 🤖 Transfer Learning
> ↳ How AI reuses knowledge to accelerate learning for tasks.  
>
> 🤖 Supervised Learning
> ↳ AI learns from labelled data where the correct answer is known. 
>
> 🤖 Unsupervised Learning
> ↳ AI finds patterns in unlabelled data on its own.
>
> 🤖 Reinforcement Learning
> ↳ AI learns by trial and error, receiving rewards or penalties. 
>
> 🤖 Transformers
> ↳ The architecture powering GPT and modern language models. 
>
> 🤖 Training Data & Datasets
> ↳ The raw material AI learns from affecting performance and bias.
>
> 🤖 Explainability / Interpretability
> ↳ The ability to understand how and why an AI model makes decisions. 
>
> 🤖 Hallucinations
> ↳ When AI confidently generates false or made-up information. 
>
> 🤖 Model Evaluation
> ↳ Judges whether an AI model is performing well or needs retraining.
>
> 🤖 AGI
> ↳ AI capable of performing any intellectual task a human can.
>
> You don’t need to master every concept.
>
> But you do need to understand the landscape you’re now operating in.

## Post 314 — 2025-08-03

**Likes:** 2283 | **Comments:** 499 | **Shares:** 288

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_top-businesses-arent-just-optimising-for-activity-7357741169851727872-Ey3X)

> Top businesses aren't just optimising for Google. 
>
> They're already adapting to AI: 
>
> Ranking for classic search engines used to be the goal. 
>
> But answer engines (ChatGPT, Claude, etc) are taking over...  
>  
> If you want your business to stay relevant, 
> You need to start investing in AI-driven rankings (AEO, GEO). 
>
> Organic traffic is still powerful...
>  
> But combining that with ranking highly for SEO/AEO/GEO is unbeatable.
>
> In 2025, I'd put my money toward these 3 types of search:
> (See the cheat sheet for more details 👇)  
>
> 💻 SEO: Search Engine Optimisation
> ↳ Ranking pages on Google. 
>
> ⚙️ How it works:
>
> - Identify high-intent keywords
> - Build backlinks and internal linking
> - Optimise content, speed and mobile experience
>
> ✅ Pros:
> ↳ Consistent traffic driver
> ↳ Builds long-term authority
> ↳ Underpins AEO and GEO efforts
>
> 🚫 Cons:
> ↳ Competitive and slow to show results
> ↳ Vulnerable to algorithm updates
> ↳ Requires ongoing upkeep
>
> 📈 How to rank higher:
> ↳ Focus on fewer, high-intent keyword clusters
> ↳ Refresh content quarterly
> ↳ Run technical audits
>
> 🤖 AEO: Answer Engine Optimisation
> ↳ Optimising for zero-click answers (like voice search) 
>
> ⚙️ How it works:
>
> - Provide concise, direct answers
> - Use schema mark-up (FAQ, How-to) 
> - Format content bullets and headings
>
> ✅ Pros:
> ↳ Instant authority and visibility
> ↳ Strong for mobile and voice queries
> ↳ High CTR when clicks happen
>
> 🚫 Cons:
> ↳ Some users get the answer without clicking
> ↳ Snippet positions change frequently
> ↳ Requires constant content monitoring
>
> 📈 How to rank higher:
> ↳ Answer questions in 40–60 words
> ↳ Optimise for “People Also Ask” queries
> ↳ Add schema markup to FAQ and How-To pages
>
> 🎯 GEO: Generative Engine Optimisation
> ↳ Optimising content pulled by AI-driven search engines (like ChatGPT)
>
> ⚙️ How it works:
>
> - Publish clear, well-structured content 
> - Build presence on credible sources (Reddit, Quora)
> - Use AI-readable formatting
>
> ✅ Pros:
> ↳ Early mover advantage in AI search
> ↳ Positions brand as a trusted source
> ↳ Captures future-facing traffic streams
>
> 🚫 Cons:
> ↳ Hard to attribute direct traffic
> ↳ AI citation rules are still evolving
> ↳ Requires off-site presence, not just on your domain
>
> 📈 How to rank higher:
> ↳ Use entity-rich, fact-checked content 
> ↳ Get cited on known AI training sources
> ↳ Prioritise clarity with FAQs, tables, lists
>
> Don’t get buried by brands already adapting.
>
> It's not about just ranking on Google anymore. 
>
> You're content is training machines that people trust for knowledge. 
>

## Post 318 — 2025-07-31

**Likes:** 2120 | **Comments:** 514 | **Shares:** 300

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_analytical-thinking-critical-thinking-activity-7356654235851071488-6Ani)

> Analytical thinking ≠ critical thinking.
>
> Mixing them up is costing you time and money.  
>
> They are 2 of the most in-demand skills for the next 5 years, 
> According to the WEF Future of Jobs Report. 
>
> Not just for knowledge workers or creatives, 
> But for founders, operators and leaders. 
>
> If you want to build faster, smarter and more confidently, 
> You need to understand the difference between the two.
>
> If you don't know the difference,
> You will most likely hit roadblocks. A lot.
>
> That will stall your growth significantly !
>
> Here's the difference laid out in as much detail as I can provide:
>
> 🧠 Critical Thinking
>
> What is it?
> Pressure-testing assumptions before you waste time building the wrong thing.
>
> Key framework:
> 🔴 The RED Model
> R = Recognise Assumptions → What are you accepting as true, and should you?
> E = Evaluate Arguments → Is the reasoning legitimate?
> D = Draw Conclusions → What’s the most logical, bias-free outcome?
>
> What it’s great for:
> 📄 Strategic planning
> 🧑‍💼 Hiring, messaging, positioning
> 🧑‍💻 High-stakes meetings
>
> Use it when:
> - Something feels off, but no one’s saying it
> - The team’s rushing to solutions
> - You’re deciding what’s even worth analysing
>
> Questions to answer:
> ❓Biases: What’s really driving this decision?
> ❓Risk: What’s the downside no one’s admitting?
> ❓Assumptions: What do we believe that might not be true?
> ❓Intent: Are we solving the real problem, or the obvious one?
>
> Watch out for:
> 🚩 Playing devil’s advocate endlessly
> 🚩 Getting stuck in “think mode” with no action
>
> End goal:
> Make sure you’re building the right thing before you start.
>
> 📊 Analytical Thinking
>
> What is it?
> Breaking problems down into parts to test, measure, and scale what works.
>
> Key framework:
> 🔁 OODA Loop
> Observe → Orient → Decide → Act
> (Military-grade thinking, business-grade execution.)
>
> What it’s great for:
> 📈 Scaling challenges and GTM strategy
> 🧪 Testing ideas with fast feedback
> 📊 Monthly reviews and metrics
>
> Use it when:
> - You’ve got traction and want to scale
> - You’re testing real ideas with real risk
> - You’re drowning in data, but not sure what it means
>
> Questions to answer:
> ❓ Deconstruct: What are the inputs and outputs?
> ❓ Detect: Where’s the pattern hiding?
> ❓ Measure: What signals matter?
> ❓ Iterate: What’s worth doubling down on?
>
> Watch out for:
> 🚩 Optimising for the wrong metric
> 🚩 Drowning in spreadsheets instead of deciding
>
> End goal:
> Faster, evidence-based decisions that compound over time.
>
> Learn the distinction now, and you'll be ahead of 99% of people.  
>
> Which one do you rely on more: critical or analytical thinking?
> Drop your thoughts in the comments. 
>

## Post 320 — 2025-07-30

**Likes:** 1984 | **Comments:** 635 | **Shares:** 309

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_great-teams-dont-react-to-problems-they-activity-7356292187443085312-pdl0)

> Great teams don't react to problems.  
>
> They anticipate them before they arise. 
>
> Problems are an inevitable part of life and business,  
> And they will appear on a constant, daily basis. 
>
> Some problems are tiny, while others feel existential. 
>
> But all of them have one thing in common: 
> You have to rise to meet them. 
>
> By definition, problem solving is how you:
>
> - Break down challenges into clear, actionable steps
> - Identify root causes instead of surface-level symptoms
> - Find solutions that work long-term, instead of quick fixes 
>
> Vague problems will only lead to misdirection and confusion. 
> If you want to find a solution, you need to clarify the problem. 
>
> This cycle is the one system I've used for 15+ years, 
> To diagnose and solve any problem I'm faced with: 
>
> 1️⃣ Define The Problem
> ↳ What are you trying to solve?
> ↳ Establish a goal of what you want to achieve.
>
> ⚡️ Trigger: You’ve hit a wall, or you know something could be better.
> ✅ Outcome: A one-sentence problem statement + a measurable goal.
>
> 2️⃣ Brainstorm Ideas
> ↳ What are some ways to solve the problem?
> ↳ Create a list of possible solutions to choose from.
>
> ⚡️ Trigger: You’ve got a goal and enough context to think creatively.
> ✅ Outcome: A shortlist of real options worth testing or pressure-testing.
>
> 3️⃣ Select A Solution
> ↳ What are you going to do?
> ↳ The ideal solution is effective, efficient, and has the fewest side effects.
>
> ⚡️ Trigger: You’ve got options on the table and a clear end goal.
> ✅ Outcome: One solution locked in and a reason why it’s the one.
>
> 4️⃣ Implement The Solution
> ↳ What are you doing?
> ↳ Implement the solution in cycles of testing and feedback.
>
> ⚡️ Trigger: You’ve picked your play and mapped the first few steps.
> ✅ Outcome: Solution launched, tested, and starting to show signals.
>
> 5️⃣ Review The Results
> ↳ What did you do?
> ↳ Review what worked, what didn’t and what impact the solution had.
>
> ⚡️ Trigger: You’ve shipped the fix and seen some outcomes.
> ✅ Outcome: Clear learnings, real insight, and a better playbook.
>
> 6️⃣ Systemise The Solution
> ↳ Can you make it work without you?
> ↳ Turn the outcome into a repeatable asset, i.e. a checklist, SOP, or automation.
>
> ⚡️ Trigger: The solution worked, and you don’t want to solve it twice.
> ✅ Outcome: A system your team can run without thinking (or you).
>
> Problems are inevitable if you want to build anything of significance.  
>
> Most people will spend their time solving them one by one... 
>
> But the top 1% will focus on building systems that preempt them, 
> And create solutions that solve them in the background. 
>
> How do you approach problem-solving? 
> Let me know in the comments. ⬇️
>

> I’ve obsessed over time management for the last 15 years.
>
> These 9 frameworks are the best of the best:
>
> When you're a founder, your time is your business.
>
> If you don’t control it, something else will.
>
> I’ve scaled service businesses, tech platforms, and media products.
>
> I’ve worked 80-hour weeks, burned out, recovered, 
> And restructured my life completely.
>
> Today, I run an 8-figure company and work fewer hours than ever...
>
> Because I know how to choose what matters most. 
>
> These are the frameworks that helped me get there. 
> (Save this, revisit it, or even build your own version 👇) 
>
> 🟩 1. Time Blocking
> ↳ Ditch the endless to-do lists.
>
> Plan your day by blocks:
>
> → Deep work
> → Admin
> → Rest
>
> (Colour-coded calendars help massively here.)
>
> 🔁 2. The Pomodoro Technique
> ↳ 25 minutes focused work → 5-minute break (no screens)
> ↳ Repeat 4 times → Then take a longer break.
>
> ⏳ 3. Parkinson’s Law
> ↳ Work expands to fill the time you give it.
> ↳ Set tighter deadlines.
>
> (e.g. Block out specific times each day to work on a goal.) 
>
> 📦 4. Task Batching
> ↳ Group similar tasks into one session.
> ↳ Saves switching costs and increases flow.
>
> (e.g. Admin batching (invoices, approvals, payroll = one focused window weekly.))
>
> 🔟 5. The 10/10/10 Rule
> ↳ Ask: How will I feel about this in...
>
> → 10 minutes
> → 10 months
> → 10 years
>
> Build long-term clarity into short-term choices.
>
> 📅 6. The Seinfeld Strategy
> ↳ Make your habit visible.
> ↳ Cross off each day you follow through. 
>
> (Try not to break the chain!)
>
> ⏱ 7. The 2-Minute Rule
> ↳ If it takes less than 2 minutes, do it immediately.
> ↳ This stops small tasks from becoming overwhelming.
>
> ⚡ 8. Biological Scheduling
> ↳ Work with your energy, not against it.
> ↳ Track your peak hours (e.g. 10am–12pm) and schedule accordingly. 
>
> 📴 9. Digital Detox
> ↳ Schedule regular periods of time away from digital devices.
> ↳ Return to your work with superior mental clarity and productivity. 
>
> Mastering your time isn't about hacks or hustle. 
> It's about building systems that scale with you. 
>
> Which of these frameworks will you try next? 
> Let me know in the comments.

## Post 326 — 2025-07-24

**Likes:** 1021 | **Comments:** 529 | **Shares:** 103

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_creativity-is-not-a-tool-limited-to-creative-activity-7354117329107992577-y4I5)

> Creativity is not a tool limited to creative industries.
>
> It's a skill absolutely everyone needs to develop:
>
> Why is that?
> Creativity is something you can use in order to:
>
> ✅ Think of innovative solutions in business.
> ✅ Approach challenges from new angles.
> ✅ Adapt to brand-new change.
>
> If you're still waiting for that "lightning bolt" to strike, 
> Eventually, you'll wait so long you miss your shot. 
>
> Meanwhile your peers might have a system that allows them to get ahead. 
>
> That's why I put together this Wheel of Creativity. 
>
> It has 4 frameworks & 20 Qs you can ask yourself... 
> That help you get out of any creative rut. 
>
> 🧠 First Principles Thinking
> ↳ Strip everything back and build from zero.
>
> 1. What do I know to be 100% true here?
> 2. What if I had to invent this from scratch?
> 3. What’s just a habit, not a fact?
> 4. What would this look like if no one had done it before?
> 5. What’s the simplest version that still works?
>
> ⚙️ SCAMPER Method
> ↳ Systematically rework what already exists.
>
> 1. What could I substitute to make this better?
> 2. What ideas could I combine to create something new?
> 3. How might I adapt this to a different use or user?
> 4. What can I eliminate without losing value?
> 5. What happens if I reverse the flow, format, or structure?
>
> 🎨 Five A’s Framework
> ↳ Break down the anatomy of a creative act.
>
> 1. Who’s creating this, and what’s their voice or edge? (Actor)
> 2. What are they actually doing — educating, provoking, entertaining? (Action)
> 3. What’s the final creative product or outcome? (Artifact)
> 4. Who’s it for and what do they care about? (Audience)
> 5. What does the platform or medium make possible? (Affordances)
>
> 💭 Four-Stage Model of Creativity
> ↳ The classic flow of how real ideas happen.
>
> 1. What inputs do I need before anything starts? (Preparation)
> 2. What if I stepped away and let it breathe? (Incubation)
> 3. What’s the actual insight I want to bring? (Illumination)
> 4. How do I make this usable, testable, or shippable? (Verification)
> 5. What feedback or reaction will shape the next version of this? (Bonus!)
>
> The top 1% don't expect creativity to come to them...
> They create the conditions that allow it to thrive. 
>
> That's the difference between high-achievers and average ones.
>
> What's your go-to method to inspire creativity? 
> I'd love to read your approach in the comments.

## Post 327 — 2025-07-23

**Likes:** 2702 | **Comments:** 571 | **Shares:** 253

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_if-youre-only-using-one-ai-chatbot-youre-activity-7353754977162432512-08Qb)

> If you're only using one AI chatbot...
>
> You're missing out on some incredible value.
>
> I've spent the last year learning as much as I can about AI. 
>
> Here's the popular belief I see:
> "ChatGPT is the best LLM for all-round tasks."
>
> While true, this ignores the potential of other LLMs.
>
> For example, if you're in the education industry...
> Claude should absolutely be your go-to.
>
> If you're in the tech space...
> Gemini has some serious advantages as well !
>
> I tested 3 of the most popular gen AI tools,  
> And built this cheat sheet to help you navigate all three. 
>
> (Check out the full sheet below !) 
>
> 🤖 ChatGPT
>
> What it is: 
> ↳ An all-round generative model for text, vision, audio, and browsing.
>
> When to use it: 
> - You need versatile output, including writing, coding, image, browsing.
> - You want access to plugins, memory, and browsing features.
> - Ideal for creative workflows and automation tasks.
>
> Use cases: 
> ✅ Turn a Notion doc into a polished guide.
> ✅ Summarise your competitor’s homepage.
> ✅ Auto-generate outreach emails.
>
> Pros: 
> 👍 Fast, intuitive, multimodal.
> 👍 Massive custom GPT ecosystem.
> 👍 Built-in browsing and memory features.
>
> Cons: 
> 👎 Free tier = old model (3.5).
> 👎 Still prone to incorrect responses.
> 👎 Still needs human judgement.
>
> Rating:
> ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️
>
> 🤖 Claude
>
> What it is: 
> ↳ Anthropic’s answer to high-context reasoning and ethics.
>
> When to use it: 
> - For legal, policy, or research output.
> - When context depth (200k+ tokens) matters.
> - When accuracy and defensibility are non-negotiable.
>
> Use cases: 
> ✅ Digest a 90-page legal agreement and highlight risks.
> ✅ Break a research-heavy article into social posts.
> ✅ Drop in a long script and get code back.
>
> Pros: 
> 👍 Superior handling of long documents.
> 👍 Strong accuracy in technical domains.
> 👍 Writes with a more conversational tone.
>
> Cons:
> 👎 Doesn’t generate images or audio.
> 👎 Can be overly conservative in style.
> 👎 Lacks “quick idea” speed compared to ChatGPT.
>
> Rating:
> ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️1/2
>
> 🤖 Gemini
>
> What it is: 
> ↳ Google’s response to GPT. Fully wired into Gmail, Docs, and Search.
>
> When to use it: 
> - You live inside Google Workspace.
> - You need true multimodal input/output.
> - You work with long documents, images, audio, and video together.
>
> Use cases: 
> ✅ Summarising email threads + attachments.
> ✅ Creating drafts with chart/image content.
> ✅ Multimodal research and design workflows.
>
> Pros: 
> 👍 Deep integration with Google apps.
> 👍 Handles multi-modal content better.
> 👍 Great for team collaboration + async prep.
>
> Cons:
> 👎 1M token mode = still in preview.
> 👎 Still polishing general chat UX.
> 👎 Most powerful within Google ecosystem.
>
> Rating:
> ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️
>
> TL;DR:
>
> Don't just use ChatGPT. 
> It's fantastic, but it's not the only one worth using.
>
> Have you used any of these tools before? 
> Would love to hear what you think of them. ⬇️

> Statistically, we'd rather die than do public speaking.
>
> Overcome that fear with these 9 strategies:
>
> It's like Jerry Seinfeld said, 
> "At a funeral, most people would rather be in the casket than doing the eulogy."
>
> But ultimately, public speaking is a more important skill than you realise.
>
> It shows up in:
> 🗣️ The Monday team meeting
> 🗣️ The investor update
> 🗣️ The client pitch
>
> It’s one of the most important skills in business, genuinely. 
>
> If you can’t explain your ideas clearly when it matters, 
> You’ll miss out on opportunities others are getting.
>
> And yet, no one really teaches us how to do it well.
>
> So here are 9 strategies that will change the way you communicate forever 👇 
>
> 1️⃣ The Power Pause
> ↳ Say something important, then stop talking.
>
> ✅ 2-3 seconds of silence makes people listen closer.
> ✅ If you can hold a pause, you’re in control.
>
> 2️⃣ The Rule of Three
> ↳ The human brain loves patterns.
>
> ✅ Three ideas, beats, or bullet points. 
> ✅ Go beyond that, and they forget everything.
>
> 3️⃣ The 2-Minute Story Rule
> ↳ Stories sell, until they start dragging on for too long.
>
> ✅ You’ve got 120 seconds max.
> ✅ Then, onto the next point.
>
> 4️⃣ Punchline First
> ↳ Don’t warm up and definitely don’t waffle.
>
> ✅ Lead with your conclusion, then explain how you got there.
> ✅ Audiences generally aren’t patient, so hit them early.
>
> 5️⃣ The Chair Test
> ↳ Ask yourself this: Would your talk work sitting down?
>
> ✅ If not, you’re hiding behind your energy, not clarity.
> ✅ Great speakers don’t rely on theatrics.
>
> 6️⃣ The Echo Effect
> ↳ Repeat the one line you want them to remember.
>
> ✅ Repetition = retention. Repetition = retention. Repetition = retention. 
> ✅ Say it twice, pause, let it land.
>
> 7️⃣ The Suspense Setup
> ↳ Don’t lead with the answer when making a point.
>
> ✅ Start with tension → Delay the reveal
> ✅ If you want attention, make them wait for resolution.
>
> 8️⃣ The Contrast Trick
> ↳ ”This is what most people do.” ”Here’s what I do instead.”
>
> ✅ Use contrast to highlight your edge.
> ✅ It turns a boring point into a memorable one.
>
> 9️⃣ The 10-Second Hook
> ↳ You’ve got 10 seconds to prove you’re worth their time.
>
> ✅ Use a stat, a story, or even something uncomfortable. 
> ✅ If you don’t win them early, you don’t win them at all.
>
> Public speaking is a fundamental skill. 
>
> The better you explain ideas, the faster they can spread... 
> Inside your team, on stage, or on LinkedIn. 
>
> That's a bit of hack in your career.
>
> What's your biggest struggle with public speaking? 
> Let me know your thoughts in the comments 👇 
>

## Post 340 — 2025-07-15

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_a-multi-million-one-person-business-is-activity-7350857794574581761-oB-4)

> A multi-million $ one-person business is possible. 
>
> These 6 steps will get you there: 
>
> If you're feeling stuck, want real financial security, 
> Or simply want more time to focus on what matters...
>
> A one-person business is the answer. 
>
> It is the key to financial and time freedom. 
> But you have to be willing to put in the work. 
>
> These 6 steps are your roadmap: 
>
> 1️⃣ Ask yourself these ❓
>
> 1. What tasks are eating up my time that could be delegated/automated?
>
> 2. Can you find signs of growth, spending, and pain in your market?
>  
> 3. How can I build once and sell over and over with minimal intervention?
>  
> 4. How can I simplify my services/products for maximum impact?
>  
> 5. What can I automate that would save me hours each week?
>  
> 6. What problem do I solve better than anyone else?
>  
> 2️⃣ Create digital products 📈
>
> These are high-margin and scalable: 
>
> ↳ Digital courses
> ↳ Ebooks and guides
> ↳ Subscription services
> ↳ SaaS tools
> ↳ Templates, frameworks, or checklists
>
> Here's how to know if it's a high-leverage business:
> Time in × Systems × Scale = Equity
>
> 3️⃣ Finding a rising tide market with AI: 
>
> Step 1: Go to ChatGPT and ask it to give you the most recent consumer trend reports from the big four consulting firms. 
>
> Step 2: Upload those reports into a custom GPT and ask for the most significant consumer trend changes over the last 24 months. 
>
> Step 3: Type the trend into Reddit or niche communities. If there are real genuine problems, it means that there could be a real opportunity.
>
> Step 4: Cross-check content demand: if creators are blowing up on TikTok or YouTube around your topic, it’s probably a real trend.
>
> 4️⃣ Audience funnel 🪹
>
> Think about it like this:
>
> TOFU: People who are curious but not ready.
> MOFU: People exploring options.
> BOFU: People ready to buy.
>
> 💡 Pro tip: 
> ↳ Niche audience = easier targeting and marketing.
> ↳ Broader audience = larger brand potential. 
>
> 5️⃣ Choose your platform ⌨️
>
> 🔗 LinkedIn: 
> Best for: B2B, consultants, coaches, service providers.
>
> 📸 Instagram: 
> Best for: Creatives, eCommerce, lifestyle brands.
>
> 📹 YouTube: 
> Best for: Educators, entertainers, fitness, tutorials.
>
> 📲 TikTok: 
> Best for: Quick tips, personal brands, viral content.
>
> 6️⃣ Keep optimising 📊
>
> 1. Track what works using analytics from Google or social media platforms. 
> 2. Refine your funnel based on real data. 
> 3. Double down on what drives results. 
>
> In just 1 year, I've built a $10M business with just 5 team members. 
> And now I teach others the exact playbook to do the same. 
>

> "Likes don't pay the bills" they say...
>
> That's right and wrong. Let me explain:
>
> People think getting leads means hard selling in every post.
> They then find they get no engagement and zero traction for their business.
>
> Allow me to debunk something.
> Growing quickly and making a lot of money quickly are not antithetical. 
>
> You can do both. I've done it. 
> 100s of Creator Accelerator students have too.
>
> You can go all in, grow your personal brand quickly, 
> And see even BETTER results than people who grow slowly and 'authentically'. 
>
> To go into more detail on which types of posts grow and which sell...
> Check out the carousel below.
>
> Here's a quick summary:
>
> Content That Grows
> ↳ Top-of-funnel content that gets eyes on your business. 
>
> ✅ Punchy hooks create intrigue.
> ✅ Lighter subjects and highly shareable. 
> ✅ Gets reach, builds an audience, and creates trust.
>
> Content That Sells
> ↳ Middle/bottom-of-funnel that generates sales.
>
> ✅ The CTA can be subtle or more obvious.
> ✅ Talks directly to the audience that is ready to buy.
> ✅ Highlights a pain point → offers the solution → shows proof. 
>
> One is there to provide value, build trust, and position your brand.
> The other is there to leverage that trust and generate demand.
>
> The biggest mistake you can make is leaning too much either way.  
>
> If you want real results, you need a system that uses both, strategically. 
>
> TLDR: 
>
> ✅ Reach the right people first. 
> ✅ Provide them with value. 
> ✅ Give them a next step.
>
> Do you struggle to sell on LinkedIn?

> ChatGPT is ruining your critical thinking. 
>
> The new MIT brain scans study proves it:
>
> But only if you let it...
>
> MIT released a study on the impact of ChatGPT on the brain. 
>
> It found that ChatGPT users had: 
>
> ➡️ Lower brain activity across 32 regions
> ➡️ Weaker recall of ideas and information
> ➡️ Less originality in responses
>
> However, that's only half the story. 
>
> The study also found that partial use of ChatGPT, 
> Heightened brain activity across all EEG frequency bands. 
>
> That's why it's important to look at these negative headlines 
> about AI with a pinch of salt...
>
> They don't give the full picture. 
>
> I fundamentally think ChatGPT is one of the best 
> Competitive advantages that creators and founders have today. 
>
> And it would be dangerous to ignore it, 
> The same way it was to ignore the internet in 2001.
>
> However, there are right ways and wrong ways to use it, 
> And this study has created an opportunity to touch on those. 
>
> So, here are my thoughts and takeaways from this study: 
>
> ✅ Think before you prompt.
> ↳ Jot down your thoughts first for more clarity.
> ↳ It’s better for your brain and your growth. 
>
> ✅ Outline with AI, write without it.
> ↳ Let ChatGPT help shape the plan, not the final product.
> ↳ You stay in control of the thinking.
>
> ✅ Check sources before summarising.
> ↳ Make sure the info is actually worth using.
> ↳ Then use AI to speed up the synthesis.
>
> ✅ Never publish raw output.
> ↳ Rewrite, restructure, and test the logic. 
> ↳ Your voice should still sound like you.
>
> I hope creators today know better than to post pure ChatGPT content.
> Not without refining it first. 
>
> Copy and pasting from any generative AI is simply lazy, 
> And won't truly capture your unique brand or voice. 
>
> AI can, however, be an incredibly helpful assistant. 
> (One that can 10x your outputs and never gets tired!)  
>
> The difference is your involvement. 
> The more you engage, the better the outputs. 
>

>
> Many creators make the mistake of posting infographics that are: 
>
> 🚫 Too wide
> 🚫 Too cluttered
> 🚫 Not optimised for mobile 
>
> These small errors will cause your content to be overlooked. 
>
> To get the additional 2.9x reach on your posts, 
> Follow these essential design principles: 
>
> 🚫 Don’t: Post landscape images (portrait performs 62% better).
> ✅ Do: Post portrait images (1200 x 1500 pixels).
>
> 🚫 Don’t: Design with desktop in mind.
> ✅ Do: Design for mobile first.
>
> 🚫 Don’t: Ignore the reading flow.
> ✅ Do: Put key info in the centre.
>
> 🚫 Don’t: Not implement any guide for your posts.
> ✅ Do: Set margins on the outsides of your visuals.
>
> 🚫 Don’t: Make your text unreadable.
> ✅ Do: Use colour contrast for high readability.
>
> 🚫 Don’t: Use icons that look unprofessional.
> ✅ Do: Find high-quality icons using IconScout.com
>
> 🚫 Don’t: Use a font that doesn’t fit your brand.
> ✅ Do: Use a unique font that matches your brand.
>
> 🚫 Don’t: Ignore the power of white space in design.
> ✅ Do: Utilise the power of white space in your visuals.
>

>

> 5. Video (1.7x) - hook in 3 seconds, always caption

## Post 370 — 2025-06-18

**Likes:** 3097 | **Comments:** 558 | **Shares:** 272

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_most-people-are-using-chatgpt-wrong-these-activity-7341071570104180736-dtw4)

> Most people are using ChatGPT wrong. 
>
> These are the 19 prompt laws to live by:
>
> ChatGPT isn't a brain, so much as a mirror:  
> How well you use it determines how productive you can be. 
>
> If you give it vague, one-line prompts, 
> You are going to get generic outputs in return.  
>
> That's why I developed these 19 laws to improve my prompts, 
> And get clear, structured outputs. 
>
> Use them to elevate your AI game 👇
>
> 📜 Law #1: Clarity > Cleverness
> Avoid fancy phrasing. Say what you want in plain language.
>
> 📜 Law #2: Start With the Friction
> Begin your prompt with the thing you're stuck on.
>
> 📜 Law #3: Prioritise Use Over Theory
> Ask for advice like you’re about to implement it.
>
> 📜 Law #4: Ground It In Reality
> Reference something real: your site, your customer, or your offer. 
>
> 📜 Law #5: Declare the Constraints
> Don’t just say what you want. Say what you don’t want.
>
> 📜 Law #6: Timebox the Lens
> Set a specific time boundary for references and research. 
>
> 📜 Law #7: Make It Choose
> Present trade-offs and ask it to select the best one. 
>
> 📜 Law #8: Ask It to Judge, Then Justify
> Don’t just get output. Get a critique.
>
> 📜 Law #9: Simulate Real Scenarios
> Use setups that imitate reality. 
>
> 📜 Law #10: Lock in the Persona
> Tell it how to think, not just who to be.
>
> 📜 Law #11: Focus on Leverage
> Ask it to give you the highest-leverage option. 
>
> 📜 Law #12: Make It Build With You
> Prompt like you’re in a feedback loop:
>
> 📜 Law #13: Include What You’ve Tried
> Skip reinventing the wheel and reduce reprompts.
>
> 📜 Law #14: Push It Into Action
> Wrap your prompt with actionable steps. 
>
> 📜 Law #15: Give It Tone 
> Tell it how it should feel. Tone drives output. 
>
> 📜 Law #16: Ask It to Steal Smartly
> Offer it examples that it can use to repurpose. 
>
> 📜 Law #17: Use Negative Prompts
> Tell it what to ignore to help you shape tone/style.
>
> 📜 Law #18: Invite Pushback
> Avoid the yes-man tendencies of ChatGPT. 
>
> 📜 Law #19: Refine Into a System
> If it works once, make it reusable. 
>
> These laws won't give you direction for your content,  
> But they will make sure you get the most out of your prompts.  
>

> 99% of jobs can be taught. 
>
> This is a message I've shared before, 
> And I'll keep sharing until I'm convinced otherwise. 
>  
> (Which I don't predict happening any time soon...)
>
> Most founders are STILL obsessed with hiring whoever looks best on paper.  
>
> This is a huge mistake that could cost you more than just money. 
>
> The truth is, a candidate might be the perfect fit on paper, 
> But without the right attitude, none of that matters.  
>
> Some of my best hires had absolutely no background in the role. 
> But they were fast, adaptable, and fully committed to their work. 
>
> They came in and elevated our performance further. 
>
> So, after decades of hiring, 
> Here's what I look for in new hires now: 
>
> 1️⃣ Resourcefulness 
> ↳ Can they come up with solutions without guidance? 
> ↳ Do they approach situations proactively or wait for instructions? 
>
> 2️⃣ Curiosity
> ↳ Do they ask questions that show they really care? 
> ↳ Do they genuinely want to understand how the business works?
>
> 3️⃣ Bias to action
> ↳ Are they able to complete and ship tasks quickly? 
> ↳ Or do they sit on ideas waiting for sign-off?
>
> 4️⃣ Self-awareness
> ↳ Can they articulate their strengths and gaps?
> ↳ Or do they just tell you what they think you want to hear?
>
> 5️⃣ Ownership
> ↳ Do they treat the outcome like it’s theirs?
> ↳ Are they able to own their successes and setbacks? 
>
> Don't get me wrong, experience does matter. 
> But it's not the first thing I consider when hiring. 
>
> I look for candidates with the skills and attitude to
> Grow with the business and contribute to our long-term goals. 
>
> Because when someone has the traits you can’t teach,
> Teaching the job is the easy bit.

> In 2025, there's one skill you can't afford to ignore: 
>
> Mastering the art of prompting. 
>
> Most people are still using AI incorrectly. 
>
> They are asking the wrong questions, 
> And getting average answers. 
>
> Meanwhile, the top 1% are turning it into the invisible engine, 
> Running their operations while saving them time and energy. 
>
> If you want AI to 10x your productivity, 
> Start by elevating your prompts. 
>
> Here are 8 that I use every week: 
> (Check the sheet for examples of each)
>  
> 1️⃣ R-T-F
>
> Role: Specify the role you want the AI to assume.
> Task: Define the task you want the AI to perform.
> Format: Indicate the format in which you want the output.
>
> 2️⃣ S-O-L-V-E
>
> Situation: Define the context or situation.
> Objective: Specify the goals.
> Limitations: Define any limitations or constraints.
> Vision: Outline the vision or goal.
> Execution: Plan the steps for execution.
>
> 3️⃣ T-A-G
>
> Task: Define the task at hand.
> Action: State the action needed.
> Goal: Clarify the goal to be achieved.
>
> 4️⃣ R-A-C-E
>
> Role: Specify the character you want the AI to play.
> Action: State the basic instruction or the job you need to be done.
> Context: Provide the background information the AI will need.
> Expectation: Describe the outcome you need.
>
> 5️⃣ D-R-E-A-M
>
> Define: Define the problem or context.
> Research: State the research needed.
> Execute: How to execute the plan.
> Analyse: How to analyse the results.
> Measure: Define how to measure the outcomes.
>
> 6️⃣ P-A-C-T
>
> Problem: Define the problem.
> Approach: Describe the approach.
> Compromise: Write about potential compromises.
> Test: Define the test or measurement.
>
> 7️⃣ C-A-R-E
>
> Context: Give the context.
> Action: Describe the action needed.
> Result: Clarify the expected result.
> Example: Provide an example for clarity.
>
> 8️⃣ R-I-S-E
>
> Role: Specify the role.
> Input: Describe the input needed.
> Steps: Could you ask for steps to follow?
> Expectation: Describe the expectation.
>
> Once you learn how to prompt, 
> The potential for what you can do with AI is limitless. 
>
> My team and I leverage AI every single day in content creation.

> Your business is only as strong as its people. 
>
> Try these 12 tips to keep your top talent:
>
> Keeping your best people is critical for building a business. 
>
> Because a business without its people is no business at all. 
>
> When the workplace becomes a negative environment: 
>
> 📉 Morale plummets.  
> 🫠 Productivity declines. 
> 👋 Your best people leave (to join your competitors).  
>
> Alternatively, successful businesses have a vision that includes everyone. 
> And this compels people to work hard for 8+ hrs per day. 
>
> In these businesses, people:  
>
> ✅ Are motivated to stay together. 
> ✅ Aligned in their vision for the company. 
> ✅ Work collectively to get better, faster.  
>
> If you want a thriving business, start with your people. 
>
> Here are 12 tips for better retention:  
>
> 1. Ask for input, then act on it. 
> ↳ Listen closely and make real changes based on their suggestions. 
>
> 2. Let them outgrow their job. 
> ↳ Ambitious people need room to experiment and level up. 
>
> 3. Make purpose part of the job. 
> ↳ Connect their work to the bigger picture that they're building. 
>
> 4. Say “thank you” in public and in detail. 
> ↳ Offer specific praise and let them know they are genuinely valued.  
>
> 5. Implement The 70/20/10 Development Rule. 
> ↳ Learning should be 70% action, 20% collaboration, and 10% formal.
>
> 6. Create visible wins within 90 days. 
> ↳ Make sure they can point to meaningful accomplishments. 
>
> 7. Tackle conflict head-on. 
> ↳ Build a safe environment by addressing problems early and fairly.  
>
> 8. Acknowledge The Three Rs of Retention. 
> ↳ Respect, Recognition, and Responsibility. 
> (If one of these goes missing, people start looking elsewhere.)
>
> 9. Use the “Career GPS” framework. 
> ↳ Help them map where they are and how you can help them grow. 
>
> 10. Expose them to the why, not just the what. 
> ↳ Don't just hammer in instructions; explain your intentions. 
>
> 11. Avoid death by process. 
> ↳ Smart people hate jumping through hoops. Symplify your systems.  
>
> 12. Use “stay signals” often. 
> ↳ People don’t always know they’re valued until you say it.  
>
> In short, if you want to retain your top people: 
>
> ✅ Make your common goal clear and actionable. 
> ✅ Offer opportunities for growth and learning. 
> ✅ Explicitly acknowledge their contributions. 
>
> Employee retention will elevate your operations and culture.

## Post 390 — 2025-05-29

**Likes:** 1652 | **Comments:** 489 | **Shares:** 210

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/donnellychris_clinging-on-to-everything-is-holding-you-activity-7333823926269042688-PmUS)

> Clinging on to everything is holding you back.  
>
> Reclaim your time by learning to delegate: 
>
> If you're feeling overwhelmed, 
> It's not because you've run out of time. 
>
> It's most likely because you're trying to do everything, 
> And refusing to let go.  
>
> This is a common mistake I see founders make. 
>
> They hold on to every detail and end up: 
>
> 🚫 Losing all their energy.  
> 🚫 Slowing the business down.  
> 🚫 Limiting their potential.
>
> If that sounds familiar, these 4 frameworks will help you: 
>
> ⛓️‍💥 Break free of the need for control. 
> ⏱️ Identify what’s worth your time.
> 📈 Operate at a higher level.  
>
> Each one is guided by series of questions. 
> Answer all 20 and I guarantee your delegation skills will improve: 
>
> 🤲 The Delegation Matrix 
> ↳ Start passing on tasks that aren't high value for you. 
>
> 1. What tasks am I doing that someone else could do 80% as well?
> 2. Which tasks drain my energy but don’t move the business forward?
> 3. What am I still doing just because “it’s easier if I do it”?
> 4. Which tasks are tied to my ego or identity?
> 5. What tasks do I fear delegating — and why?
>
> ⚖️ The 80/20 Rule
> ↳ Understand which tasks are truly moving the needle. 
>
> 1. Which 20% of my tasks are driving 80% of the results?
> 2. What 80% of my to-do list could be delegated or deleted?
> 3. What’s a small task that takes up a disproportionate amount of my time?
> 4. Am I overinvesting in tasks with minimal upside?
> 5. What would happen if I ignored this task for a week?
>
> 💸 The $1,000 Work Model
> ↳ Categorise tasks by how valuable they are for your time. 
>
> 1. Is this a $10, $100, or $1,000/hour task?
> 2. Am I choosing familiarity over high-value work?
> 3. What would happen if I only did $1,000/hour tasks for a week?
> 4. What’s the opportunity cost of doing this task myself?
> 5. Who could take this on and unlock more upside from it?
>
> 🏆 The 70% Rule
> ↳ Take action faster and avoid the trap of perfectionism. 
>
> 1. Is 70% of my standard good enough for this task to be offloaded?
> 2. Am I holding on because I want it perfect — or because I need control?
> 3. What systems or SOPs could help them close the remaining 30% gap?
> 4. What’s the worst-case scenario if this isn’t done “my way”?
> 5. Have I allowed enough space for others to grow through doing?
>
> If your growth has stalled, 
> Working harder probably isn't the solution. 
>
> I go deeper into these types of frameworks,  
> In this week's edition of Step By Step. 
>
> I break down:  
>
> - The military framework I use to break stagnation instantly. 
> - The delegation test that exposes gaps in productivity. 
> - A brutal question that will change how you spend your time.  
>
> These have helped me move past plateaus countless times.

> Your life isn't naturally chaotic.

> You just never learned these 5 work-life rules. 
>
> Most people have convinced themselves that life is inherently messy. 
>
> They move through their days without questioning their purpose, 
> Or wondering how they can improve things.   
>
> It doesn't have to be this way. 
>
> Use these 5 laws to bring some order to the chaos:  
>
> 1️⃣ Murphy’s Law
> ↳ Anything that can go wrong, will go wrong. 
> ↳ Start building systems that expect problems. 
>
> 2️⃣ Kidlin’s Law
> ↳ If you write a problem down, you have solved half of it. 
> ↳ Externalise confusion, create distance, and clarify.
>
> 3️⃣ Gilbert’s Law
> ↳ When you take on a task, it is your responsibility to complete it.
> ↳ Take ownership over your work and leave the excuses behind. 
>
> 4️⃣ Wilson’s Law
> ↳ If you prioritise knowledge, the money will continue to come. 
> ↳ Invest in learning before you need the result.
>
> 5️⃣ Falkland’s Law
> ↳ If you don’t have to make a decision, then don’t. 
> ↳ Avoid overthinking and forcing decisions. 
>
> These 5 laws won’t solve every aspect of your life. 
>
> But they will help you: 
>
> ✅ Stay calm in chaos, 
> ✅ Move fast with clarity, 
> ✅ And build better over time.

> It's tough to succeed if you can't communicate.
>
> Here's how to do it well (in any situation):
>
> 1. Be specific. 
>
> "You always do this" means absolutely nothing. 
>
> "You interrupted me three times in the meeting" means something.
>
> 2. Describe the behavior, not the person. 
>
> "You talk over people" is a fact. 
>
> "You're disrespectful" is a cruel judgment. 
>
> 3. Name the impact. 
>
> "When you go off-script on sales calls, we lose deals" is something a person can work on.
>
> "You're hurting our team" is something a person feels badly about.
>
> 4. Use I, not You.
>
> "I felt cut off in that conversation" shows the impact of their behavior.
>
> "You never let me finish," shames someone with no lesson learned.
>
> Direct communication will always feel uncomfortable at first.
>
> You need to do it anyway.
>
> The people who master it build better teams, better relationships, and better lives.
>

>
> I say it because I've spent a lot of time studying my own decisions, trying to figure out the ones that mattered, and the answer is surprising.
>
> The choices that moved my life forward? 
>
> Almost never the ones that made sense to other people.
>
> They were the ones that made them nervous. 
>
> And I think that's because the reasonable choice and the unreasonable choice are measuring different things entirely. 
>
> The reasonable choice asks: 
>
> Is this move safe?
> Will other people approve?
> Does the money make sense?
>
> And those are fine questions. Go ahead and ask them. 
>
> They keep you employed and housed and respectable. 
>
> The unreasonable choice asks something simpler and much harder to defend:
>
> Does this life feel like mine?
>
> Not, "Is this smart?" 
> Not, "Will this impress people?" 
>
> Simply: "Is this life actually mine?"
>
> But, of course, reasonable choices are what most folks are likely to make.
>
> They're easy. 
> They're obvious. 
> They're approved by everyone.
>
> But maybe…just maybe…very wrong.

> There's one question that's saved me from making really expensive mistakes.
>
> It's not, "Do I want this?"
>
> I've found that question to be pretty useless.
>
> It's too easy to answer "yes" when you're caught up in a moment.
>
> The better question is: "WHY do I actually want this?"
>
> Because the why is the secret behind everything.
>
> "I'm lonely" is different than "I need a partner."
>
> "I miss feeling important" is different from "I miss the actual work."
>
> "I want the money back" is different from "I want to do that work again."
>
> Most of us never stop and ask ourselves, "Why?"
>
> We feel the pull, think it's real, and start chasing.
>
> Going back to the job we outgrew.
> Restarting the project we were glad to finish.
> Saying yes to things that look right but feel wrong.
>
> And then we wonder why "getting what we wanted" didn't make us happy.
>
> Yeah - the pull is almost always real.
>
> But what it means is usually something different than what it feels like.
>
> Tomorrow's newsletter is about a time I ignored this question (and what it cost me).
>
> It's one of the more personal essays I've written in a while.
>

> Ok, so you got laid off. That's not good.
>
> And most people start panicking.
>
> They update the resume.
> They blast off 100+ applications.
> They wait to hear if someone is interested.
>
> These aren't bad moves, per se.
>
> But I'd encourage you to think about a different question while you're doing all of that:
>
> "What do I know right now that people would pay me for?"
>
> If you have skills, knowledge, and experience, you have something people want.
>
> So, do these three things if you're in a pinch:
>
> 1. Write down every problem you've solved in the last 10 years.
>
> Not the different roles you had.
> The actual problems you solved at the business.
>
> "I helped improve sales team close rates by 15%." 
> "I taught people how to use Notion effectively."
> "I generated 10,000+ leads for a fintech company."
>
> The thing people paid your employer for...that's the thing you can sell directly to other people who need it.
>
> 2. Find one person who has that problem right now and offer to help.
>
> Not 100 people.
> Not 10 people.
> Just one person.
>
> A former colleague, or someone in your network, or a stranger on LinkedIn who just posted about struggling with the exact thing you know how to fix.
>
> Go search! DM them. Offer a quick call. Solve it cheaply.
>
> That's your first proof-of-concept.
>
> 3. Package what you did into something repeatable.
>
> Once you've helped one person, write down exactly what you did. 
>
> That's your first offer. 
>
> A 1-hour consultation. 
> A 4-week coaching sprint. 
> A simple PDF guide.
>
> It doesn't need to be fancy or have a damn logo. 
>
> It just needs to be clear: 
>
> "I help [specific person] do [specific thing] in [specific timeframe]." 
>
> That's it.
>
> These are the 3 steps to future-proofing yourself next time this happens.
>

> The richest people I know aren't multi-millionaires.
>
> They're people with empty calendars.
>
> They hardly have any meetings. 
> They don't have Slack on their computer. 
> Sunday night is just like Thursday night...
>
> No dread.
>
> They designed their businesses primarily for peace of mind.
>
> Everyone else is on autopilot, doing the exact opposite.
>
> More clients.
> More projects.
> More revenue.
> More complexity.
>
> And every time they add more, they get less of what actually matters in life.
>
> I know because I did this for a long time. I took a startup from $0 to $70M and nearly destroyed myself in the process.
>
> Not sleeping. 
> Coping with alcohol. 
> Paramedics at my house after a panic attack.
>
> Nobody told me to live like that. I just kept saying yes to the next logical thing until I looked up and didn't recognize my own life.
>
> So when I built my own business, I designed it around one question: What do I want my average weekday to look like?
>
> Here's how I approached it (and how you can too):
>
> 1. Set your "enough" number. 
>
> Not your dream number. 
> The one where money stops being a daily worry. 
> Build to that and don't go beyond it.
>
> 2. Work backwards from your ideal day. 
>
> What time do you stop working? 
> How many meetings do you have? 
> When do you exercise, eat, read, hang with fam? 
> If the model doesn't fit the life, change the model.
>
> 3. Subtract before you add. 
>
> Every new project costs you your time. 
> Before adding, ask "what does this take away from?" 
> If it takes away something important, don't add it.
>
> 4. Automate earning money. 
>
> Your sales page, your emails, your delivery. 
> Everything should be automated. 
> If you have to be "on" 24/7, it's not a business.
>
> 5. Protect empty time like it's revenue.
>
> The white space on your calendar is yours.
> It's where your best decisions happen. 
> Fill it, and everything gets worse.
>
> Save this post and revisit it often. 
>
> It's the difference between building something that makes you money and building something that makes you absolutely miserable.
>
> I write about this stuff every week in my newsletter for 180K+ entrepreneurs. 
>
> What's working, what I stopped doing, and what I'm still figuring out.
>

>

>
> Here's a simple 8-question framework for understanding problems:
>
> - What's the problem?
> - What exactly do you mean by that?
> - Can you give me an example?
> - What have you tried to fix it? 
> - How did it work?
> - What is that costing you?
> - How big a priority is that to fix?
> - When are you hoping to have it fixed by?
>
> Then?
>
> 1. Send a recap about what you learned
> 2. Describe how you'd fix the problem
> 3. Why your solution is unique/better
> 4. How much it will cost
> 5. How long it will take.
>
> Then ask them if they'd like to move forward on fixing it.
>
> If they say "no", try again tomorrow.
> If "yes", send them a payment link. 
>
> Congrats.
> You're running a business that will make money.

## Post 387 — 2025-09-19

**Likes:** 3814 | **Comments:** 1219 | **Shares:** 185

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/justinwelsh_i-cracked-linkedins-code-in-8-moves-783895-activity-7374771336491008000-W2Fy)

> I cracked LinkedIn's code in 8 moves.
>
> 783,895 followers later, here's the playbook: 
>
> 1. Write about your journey, not your expertise
>
> People follow stories, not resumes. I shared my burnout, my failures, my $70M walk-away. Vulnerability beats authority every time.
>
> 2. Repurpose your best content regularly
>
> My top 21 posts have generated 6.384M impressions, and 90% of them were posted before. Think like a band: play your hits often.
>
> 3. Create a signature framework people talk about
>
> "The LinkedIn Operating System" became bigger than me. When 45,000+ people use your framework, you've built a movement.
>
> 4. Solve one expensive problem repeatedly
>
> With every post, I try to answer: "How do I build attention or revenue on my own?" That's a $100K+ problem. Pick one expensive pain point and become the best solution.
>
> 5. Turn your weaknesses into your brand
>
> I got fired 3 times and made it my origin story. Your biggest embarrassments are your best content. People connect with flaws, not perfection.
>
> 6. Build in public with real numbers
>
> "$10.8M business." "783,895 followers." "2,119 straight days." Specificity creates trust. Vague claims create doubt.
>
> 7. Focus on one platform until it hurts
>
> I ignored Instagram, Twitter, and everything else. Just LinkedIn for 2.5 years straight. Depth beats width until you hit critical mass.
>
> 8. Document the system, not the success
>
> Nobody cares that you made $1M. They care HOW you made $1M. Share the process, not the prize. Systems scale. Success stories don't.
>
> Building a following AND a business here is not easy. A lot of people have the first without the second. You can't be focused on hacks and tricks. 
>
> "Will using ↳ make my posts good?" No. That's silly stuff. Learn to write and educate.
>
> "What's up with the algorithm?!" It changes. That's why fundamentals win over time. Complaining about it doesn't help you.
>
> If you want to understand why 45,000+ people and over 100 of LinkedIn's Top Voices are students of mine, come see the system. 
>
> It's deep education building a brand, not "how many letters should be in the first line of my post?" type stuff.
>
> 90 minutes, willingness to practice, and some patience.
>
> Watch it here: https://buff.ly/JeL1YAt

## Post 20 — 2026-05-06

**Likes:** 261 | **Comments:** 169 | **Shares:** 1

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mattjbarker1_in-april-i-wrote-a-linkedin-post-with-an-activity-7457760651579387904-sXMH)

> In April, I wrote a LinkedIn post with an 18 word hook. The first line was boring. But the second line broke all the "rules" and the post went nuts. Full breakdown below (you'll wanna save this):
>
> The hook:
>
> "My hottest LinkedIn writing tip of 2026: 
>
> Go to ChatGPT and ask it to write you a post."
>
> This post got 69,993 impressions (my average is 14.4k).
>
> But it wasn't the "contrarian opinion" or the "mobile optimisation" or the hook being "8 words or less" that made this work.
>
> It was the SETUP.
>
> Line one looks exactly like every other LinkedIn tip post you've read 1,000 times: 
>
> "My hottest writing tip of 2026:"
>
> Boringly familiar and the reader's brain is already deciding to scroll on. But then line two creeps in: 
>
> "Go to ChatGPT and ask it to write you a post."
>
> For 0.5 seconds, the reader is confused as hell. "Wait, is Matt seriously telling me to do this?" That confusion is what gets the click. 
>
> Here's how to confuse your reader into engaging:
>
> 1. Set up an expectation in line one
> 2. Break it in line two
>
> 99% of people obsess over making line one clever but the best move might actually be the opposite:
>
> Make line one boringly familiar, then break it and let the second line do all the work.
>
> That's how you earn the "see more" click.
>
> P.S. if you're struggling with writing on LinkedIn, I teach 14,500+ people how so they get more visibility and grow their reputation for free at mattbarker.xyz.

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mattjbarker1_ive-grown-my-linkedin-profile-to-190k-followers-activity-7457035910082277376-nUZC)

> I've grown my LinkedIn profile to 190k followers in 4 years. If I had to start from 0 again, here's one piece of advice I'd like to hear:
>
> When you're starting out on LinkedIn and nothing's working, it's tempting to rewrite your whole post.
>
> Don't.
>
> Your actual problem is in line 1 (the hook). Almost always.
>
> The hook is the most important line you write. Not just on LinkedIn but across every medium. 
>
> > linkedIn post
> > email newsletter
> > landing page
>
> The first line is where you're doing the majority of your damage.
>
> Compare:
>
> "I sold some things and made some money."
>
> vs.
>
> "In the last 17 months, I've sold the same product every day to the same audience and made $50 million. Here's how."
>
> Stop rewriting the whole post.
>
> Rewrite line 1, 10 times.
>
> P.S. if you want to grow your LinkedIn, writing fast, easy & fun posts, i teach 14,500+ people how for free at mattbarker.xyz.

> This is Richard Branson. He's one of the most famous entrepreneurs in the world. 18M LinkedIn followers. But even if me and Richard had 0 followers:
>
> We could write the exact same LinkedIn post, his would smash mine every time.
>
> Same words. 100x the reach.
>
> The reason is obvious:
>
> Because he has more credibility than me. duhhhhhh.
>
> He has conquered the business world and is a household name. Anyone that sees his name pop up in their feed, instantly stops.
>
> I am a nobody. You have to REALLY know who I am to stop. Or REALLY be intrigued by my hook. Or I need to REALLY show you that i've done a thing to trust listening to my words / advice.
>
> If you're an experienced operator like ol Dick here (Dick is a nickname for Richard in England), listen up:
>
> The credibility you've already built is your BIGGEST asset. 
>
> But most people who start writing on LinkedIn waste it entirely by letting it sit on their profile page in their experience section.
>
> So unless you are Richard Branson: 
>
> Put your credibility in the first 3 lines of ALL your posts.
>
> A stranger scrolls past a random take from someone with no context → keeps scrolling.
>

>
> Might seem like a normal kinda opening. But that tiny 3 letter word is doing WAYYY more work than you think.
>
> Here's why:
>
> Using "but" to cut across your first line instigates some sort of twist. It creates a turn of direction that retains the reader's engagement.
>
> A flat first line alone won't earn a second line.
>
> A flat first line followed by "but" does.
>
> Try it on your next hook:
>
> 1. Say a thing
> 2. Add "But"
> 3. Say a new thing
>
> Watch the whole post come alive.
>
> One word. 3 letters. Mad how much impact it has, right?

> I've learned this about writing after 1,214 LinkedIn posts:
>
> Writing isn't about word choice. 
>
> It's about word ORDER.
>
> There's a copywriting framework called PAS.
>
> (PAS = Problem Agitate Solution)
>
> The reason it works in that order is simple:
>
> When the reader sees a problem first - one they currently experience themselves - they resonate with that emotionally a lot quicker and easier than if they read a solution first, then worked backwards.
>
> Once the writer resonates with the reader's emotions, the reader is putty in their hands.
>
> I've learned this after writing 1,214 LinkedIn posts:
>
> It's not about the word choice. It can be.
>
> But 9 times out of 10, it's about word order.
>

> Short lines.
>
> Like this.
>
> Full stop after each one.
>
> It's "mobile optimised" and "easy to read".
>
> It's also annoying to read if your audience is smart and perfectly capable of processing a full paragraph.
>
> That formatting style exists for a reason:
>
> It works for broad audiences who typically read at a lower level. But if you're writing for founders, executives, people with higher reading abilities and the desire to actually read things, you're optimising for the wrong reader. And you might be actively putting off the right one.
>
> Same goes for walls of text, long hooks, emojis. 
>
> None of it is universally good or bad. The question is never "does this trick work?", it's "does this trick work for my audience?"
>
> Think about what a formatting rule is actually designed to do before you blindly apply it.
>
> Different playbooks for different people.
>
> mattbarker.xyz

>

>
> Wanna know what actually kills your posts?
>
> Not giving your best readers anywhere to go or anything to do.
>
> If someone reads every word you write and you've got no CTA, no PS, no link, nothing. My friend, you've just let your most engaged reader scroll away. 
>
> A PS at the bottom is the easiest fix in the world. 
>
> Your casual readers won't even see it. Your best readers will. And they'll click.
>
> I've since moved to dropping links mid post like mattbarker.xyz here, because people don't have to finish reading to find it.

> I wrote 610 hooks for my LinkedIn posts in 2025. Save yourself months of hook writing pain and copy my process instead:
>
> Step 1: Pick a recent Lived Experience
>
> - look back at the last 7 days
> - use your brain to recall 'things' that happened
> - calls, arguments, outcomes, wins, fails
> - anything that you can say 'this happened'
>
> Step 2: Write it out like a text message
>
> - don't try and over hookify it
> - explain the thing that happened naturally
> - just like you would text a mate 
> - or explain to a friend over coffee
> - 'last night this weird thing happened when i was...'
>
> Step 3: Refine it
>
> - check for elements like timelines, locations, actions, stakes
> - these are consistent with natural storytelling
> - make sure the hook creates some curiosity
> - make the reader need to click to find out the answer
> - ask yourself "can anyone else write this?"
>
> Here are my top 5 hooks from 2025 for you to steal:
>
> 1. This month, my little business did $27,034 with:
>
> 2. On Monday I saw a post by Spencer Matthews. It was SO obviously written by AI, it was laughable.
>
> 3. I'm 32. No kids. I run a one person writing business. Yesterday's morning routine was perfect:
>
> 4. I'm a simple guy. I don't need to:
>
> 5. Yesterday I posted about how my wife supports me and how I think that’s important for men today.
>
> Pick one. Insert your own Lived Experience. 
>
> First draft in under 10 mins. Boom.
>
> 🤘

## Post 71 — 2026-03-26

**Likes:** 308 | **Comments:** 167 | **Shares:** 3

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mattjbarker1_i-got-claude-to-analyze-the-last-15-months-activity-7442917828703477761-p5Lv)

> i got Claude to analyze the last 15 months of my own LinkedIn posts so you don't have to. 
>
> here's the data-backed guide to posting (+ growing) on LinkedIn:
>
> 1. carousels are the most underused format in my dataset by a mile.
>
> they averaged 44,896 impressions. image posts averaged 21,528. that's a 2.1x gap — and I've only posted 54 carousels out of 718 posts. I've been leaving reach on the table for years.
>
> if you're only posting text and images, you're playing the game on hard mode. carousels outperform everything. post more carousels.
>
> 2. opening with a revenue number gets 45% more impressions than not.
>
> posts where I put a dollar figure in line 1 averaged 31,533 impressions. posts without averaged 21,766. my top 5 all-time posts? every single one opens with a $ figure.
>
> "this month my business did $27k" will always beat "this month was a big one." the number isn't bragging. it's a hook. use it.
>
> 3. Monday posts reach 71% more people than Saturday posts.
>
> Monday averaged 31,124 impressions. Saturday averaged 18,231. across 95 Monday posts and 104 Saturday posts. that's not a fluke. that's a pattern.
>
> your content isn't the only variable. timing is. if you're posting your best stuff on a Friday afternoon, you're losing out. save the best posts for Monday afternoon.
>
> 4. the 12–1pm window averages 40% above my daily mean. nothing else gets close.
>
> posts published at 12–13:00 averaged 31,422 impressions. my overall average is 22,500. that's the only hour window with more than 10 posts averaging above 30k.
>
> consistency of timing matters. my audience knows when to expect me. show up at the same time every day and your average impression count will quietly rise without you changing a word.
>
> 5. a specific number in the hook consistently outperforms no number.
>
> posts with a number in line 1 averaged 24,392 impressions. posts without averaged 20,891. across 330 posts with a number and 388 without. not massive. but consistent.
>
> "7 things i learned" beats "things i learned." "i posted 10 weeks in a row" beats "i posted for a while." specificity = truth. vagueness = guesswork.
>
> what are your thoughts on this?
>
> mattbarker.xyz

> In the last 12 months, I've reviewed 473 LinkedIn posts.
>
> The difference between an 8 impression post and an 80k post?
>
> It's all decided in that first line. 
>
> Not the body or the structure. Not even the topic.
>
> The hook.
>
> Here's one lesson I've learned from writing + editing 1,000s of hooks:
>
> Most beginners write hooks that describe the post.
>
> But the hooks that work create a need to read it.
>
> Example:
>
> Describes the post → "5 tips for LinkedIn writing:".
>
> Creates a need → "I spent 3 hours rewriting the same hook last Tuesday. Here's what I finally realised:".
>
> The former is descriptive. The latter is enticing.
>
> Your hook has one job:
>
> Make reading the next line feel utterly unavoidable.
>
> That's the skill. 
>
> Master it and everything else on LinkedIn gets easier.
>
> P.S. everyone teaches the short one-liner hook. that's one approach. but here's a different one I've found works better: https://lnkd.in/dE-_BMT7

## Post 90 — 2026-03-08

**Likes:** 229 | **Comments:** 112 | **Shares:** 4

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mattjbarker1_how-to-write-linkedin-posts-that-attract-activity-7436394838385692673-3HKC)

> How to write LinkedIn posts that attract total strangers to follow you
>
> 1. ask yourself: "can anyone else write this?" before you post anything. if the answer is yes, rewrite the hook. a stranger scrolling your feed needs a reason to stop. generic advice gives them nothing. only you writing from only your experience gives them something.
>
> 2. write your hook like you're telling a friend what happened. not "here are 5 tips for LinkedIn growth." more like "last week my client went from zero engagement to their best post ever. here's exactly why." one is preaching. the other is a story you want to hear.
>
> (free training on hook writing here btw: https://lnkd.in/dE-_BMT7)
>
> 3. introduce yourself inside the post. don't assume strangers know who you are. drop one line early that signals what you do and who you do it for. "I've spent 4 years helping founders write on LinkedIn" tells me everything I need to trust what comes next.
>
> 4. educate with step-by-step actions, examples, or a framework. these are the posts that get saved. saves correlate with follower spikes. people save things they're scared of losing because they'll want to use them later.
>
> 5. when you find a post that attracts new followers, post it again the following week. and the week after. the impressions will vary. but the follower-to-impression ratio stays almost identical. winners compound.
>
> 6. mix posts for strangers with posts for your existing audience. strangers need context. existing followers need depth. you need both. roughly 2 stranger-facing posts per week is a good place to start.
>
> 7. stop writing to your followers. write to the person who has never heard of you. they're the ones you're trying to attract.
>
> TL;DR:
>
> - document your life
> - write to strangers
> - repeat and repurpose winners

> I gave him one trick. Three letters.
>
> "But".
>
> Before → But → After.
>
> Example: 
>
> "Last month I had no idea how to grow my business. But last week I signed five new clients."
>
> That's it. Two sentences. One word connecting them.
>
> What the word "but" does is simple:
>
> It forces a story. 
>
> You can't write "before → but → after" without a real moment sitting behind it. It instigates tension. It creates a reason to keep reading.
>
> He tried it. First attempt. It worked.
>
> Hooks don't feel hard when you stop trying to be clever and start recalling what actually happened.

> Before → But → After.

> 3. Use one structure until writing feels easier / faster.
> 4. Stop trying to write a perfect hook. It doesn't exist.
> 5. Treat every post like a rep, not a performance
> 6. Batch writing removes the fear. Helped me a lot.
> 7. Make writing easier, not better. Process first.
> 8. Accept your brain will try to talk you out of posting.
> 9. Momentum > knowledge. Resilience beats smarts.
>
> This alone (hopefully) gives you that 'nudge' you need.
>
> But if you're still looking for a system to make writing feel fast, easy and fun?
>
> Here's a 15 minute training I made for you: https://lnkd.in/dhyCVj2w
>
> It's free and perfect for beginners.
>
> Hope it helps you go from 0 → 1...just a little bit faster.

> 🤘

> My first LinkedIn post = total flop. Why? One reason:
>
> I 'announced' myself.
>
> - I'd just started a new freelance business
> - I wanted to let people know I was 'available'
> - I thought people would just come flooding to me
>
> I got a BIG slice of humble pie that day 😂
>
> (watch this to avoid the same mistakes i made: https://lnkd.in/dhyCVj2w)
>
> If I was starting over again, here's what I'd write for my first LinkedIn post:
>
> Not an 'announcement' post. 
>
> An 'introduction' post.
>
> 5 steps to writing the perfect 'introduction' post (your first LinkedIn post):
>
> 1. Start with the hook
>
> First line: "Hello LinkedIn, I'm {name} 👋".
> Second line: "Here's a bit about me (and why I'm here):". 
>
> Simple and easy first + second line to your post. It's clear. Perfect.
>
> 2. Explain the 'what' (in this order)
>
> - What you've been doing up to now. e.g. 10 years in marketing
> - What moment / event recently changed that e.g. retired
> - What you're doing now / next e.g. golf, holidays
>
> 3. State your 'why'
>
> The reader is asking themselves 'why is this person posting on LinkedIn?'. So answer that and tell them why. Helps the reader understand your values / purpose.
>
> 4. Show what they'll see / learn from you
>
> You need to give the reader a reason to follow you. Hard one because most don't know what they'll post about. But you could say something like this:
>
> "I'll be posting about all sorts:
>
> - How I kept my business alive for 30 years
> - Mistakes, lessons, experiences along the way
> - Being happily married for 30+ years
> - Raising two children as a business owner
> - How I juggled growing a business, marriage and kids"
>
> Anything like this is perfect.
>
> 5. Final 'Call to Action'
>
> Tell them to connect with you / follow you, like this:
>
> "If any of this interests you:
>
> Connect with me and follow along here 👉 {tag yourself}.
>
> See you soon.
>
> 👋"
>
> ---
>
> Done. You're ready to write your first LinkedIn post.
>
> Good luck!
>
> P.S. have you ever written an 'introduction' post on LinkedIn?

> I have one strict rule for writing LinkedIn hooks.
>
> (been ruthless with my clients on this in 2025 & '26)
>
> My strict rule:
>
> If your hook could be written by 10,000 other people, you are instantly a commodity.
>
> So before you post, ask:
>
> “Can anyone else write this?”
>
> If yes, your hook is generic → rewrite it.
>
> If no, your hook is specific → it stands out → it earns attention → it’s more likely to pull in new followers.
>
> How to fix a “yes” hook (quick and easy):
>
> Add one specific detail from Lived Experience.
>
> - a moment (“Last week I…”)
> - a result (“In January my client…”)
> - a confession (“I used to…”)
> - a quote (“A client asked me…”)
> - a number (“I’ve coached 38…”)
>
> That’s it. 
>
> Literally the same idea but now it feels real and it stops blending in with AI-tinted advice posts.
>
> e.g. 
>
> In this post, I mention "I have this strict rule" and "ruthless with my clients". words like "I" and "my" force Lived Experience and that = more unique.
>
> I can't see myself slowing down on this rule.
>
> What do you think?

> You don't have a content problem:
>
> You have a consistency problem.
>
> You sit down to write. Nothing comes out. Or worse you post once, then disappear for weeks.
>
> You know consistency is key.
>
> But you can't make it stick.
>
> Here's 3 steps to fix it (+ never miss a post again):
>
> 1. Schedule your writing like a meeting
>
> Don't "find time" to write. Block it out. If it's not in your calendar, it won't happen. If you skip today, you'll skip tomorrow.
>
> Action:
>
> - Open calendar
> - Pick weekly 1-2 hour slot
> - Set recurring event: "Write LinkedIn post."
>
> (here's one way i write my linkedin posts: https://lnkd.in/d29V4rih)
>
> 2. Use a simple formula to write faster.
>
> Blank pages kill. Start with a structure. An easy format is:
>
> Outcome → Explanation → Action. 
>
> If you know your format, you'll never feel stuck.
>
> Action:
>
> - Open magicpost.in​
> - Go to calendar
> - Write a hook for post: "The biggest mistake I made was…"
> - Now, fill in the rest: What happened? → What did you learn?
>
> 3. Never sit down without an idea.
>
> Thinking of an idea while writing is a surefire reason for why you struggle. Collect ideas, never start from scratch. If you do this, you'll never miss a post.
>
> Action:
>
> - Right now, go to magicpost.in
> - Go to the calendar
> - Monday to Friday, write down a thing that happened last week
> - Then, turn each 'thing' into a post
>
> You cannot fail if you don’t quit. Fact.
>
> So, don’t quit:
>
> Be relentlessly consistent.

>

> 3. Hit search
> 4. Filter by “People” (to remove company pages)
> 5. Filter by “Industry” (to niche down)
>
> By now, you have filtered a search down to 10,000s from 10,000,000s.
>
> After that it’s a case of:
>
> - Scroll down your list
> - Click on profiles 
> - Check them over quickly
> - Send a connection request with this note:
>
> “Hey name,
>
> I do {service} for {type of clients}.
>
> I post every {frequency} at roughly {time}. 
>
> Hope it’s useful for you!
>

> If they reject - no bother.

> 10 of these 5 x a week (do 20 if you can).

> 2,400 a year.

> Even if 20% connect, that’s 480 new connections.
>
> More than the 0 most people are doing.

>
> But here's the approach behind the hook:
>
> 1. Imagine your reader knows NOTHING about you
> 2. "Introduce" things about you in your hook
> 3. Make the second line something you've done / are doing
>
> e.g. 
>
> "I'm English. Soon to be first time dad. Play padel. Love coffee.
>
> But I spend 7 hours every week writing on LinkedIn because:"

> Talk to strangers more.

> I'm not sober. I love a beer. But over the last 4 years, I've drunk WAY less alcohol. I never noticed this until last week, though:
>
> My relationship with drinking is WAY better than it was.
>
> Before, I would struggle to socialise with new people or people I didn't know well without a drink.
>
> I'd have to sink a couple of pints before I can get a bit loose and feel confident chatting to people.
>
> When I was single living in London, before going on a date I would neck a couple of shots of whisky just to loosen me up before hand.
>
> Otherwise, I'd be completely in my own head.
>
> Mad stuff.
>
> Now though, after leaving London for Cyprus and living a life where I drive more on a daily basis and the local people drink less, I've been slowly adapting to that.
>
> And I've become way better at socialising without booze.
>
> There's been weeks where I've not had a drop of it. 
>
> Just isn't a big part of my life anymore.
>
> But this Christmas I gave myself permission to drink more.
>
> I had a couple beers at home. I drank some whisky watching TV. Made some margaritas with the family (pictured).
>
> I know because I don't NEED it to have fun, its just enjoyable.
>
> And I have control over it.
>
> Takeaway:
>
> When you don't NEED something, and you choose to have / do it, it's always way more fun.
>
> If you're posting on LinkedIn and not enjoying it, ask:
>
> Do I NEED to do this?
>
> If the answer is yes, may be worth revisiting why and how you can create an environment where you don't NEED to.
>
> But instead, you CHOOSE to.
>
> Way more fun.
>
> ✌️

> I ran a little experiment in the last 2 weeks of December. Every day for 15 days, I repurposed (word for word) my 15 most viewed posts from 2025. It went REALLY well.
>
> Why did I do this?
>
> Tbh, I couldnt be arsed to write new stuff because it was christmas and I wanted to take some time off creatively.
>
> But I had a little brain wave and turned it into a content series where I counted down my best posts by repurposing them to my audience.
>
> It ended up pretty great.
>
> - 465,467 impressions
> - 7,132 engagements
> - 1,823 new followers
> - 3,167 saves and sends
>
> All from posts I spent zero time writing.
>
> If this isn't a 'for' case for repurposing your best posts, I don't know what is.
>
> I'm all about writing from your Lived Experience.
>
> Writing relevant, energetic, new, fresh posts.
>
> But man, this is pretty freaking cool.
>
> Here's one thing you can do (that I'll be doing this year):
>
> Give yourself "Repurposing Weeks".
>
> 1. Once a month, create a Repurposing Week
> 2. In that week, repurpose your best posts
> 3. Enjoy continued growth of your LinkedIn profile
> 4. Spend zero time writing and chill for a week
>
> Great way to reduce content burnout.
>
> ✌️
