> Well, I did it guys. I hit $300k revenue in 2025 for my one person writing business. Smashed past it!
>
> I didn't create this goal for myself at the start of 2025.
>
> It just became a thing as I went through the year.
>
> I'm a very heavy goal orientated person. Give me a target, something to compete with and I'll go to the ends of this flat earth to hit it.
>
> (the earth is flat right?)
>
> For context, I actually did more revenue in 2024 ($369k). And 2023 was even better ($400k+ I think?? can't see the numbers on my Stripe at a glance).
>
> So even though 2025 was a worse year revenue wise, it was probably my most fun, easy and enjoyable year in business.
>
> 2023 was brilliant, launching The Digital Copywriter course and all the excitement and revenue that came from that.
>
> But 2025 felt more mature, more measured and more calm.
>
> Despite this post LITERALLY being about me showing off my revenue numbers (celebrating myself on a rare occasion), 2025 was the year I made two very important shifts.
>
> 1. I stopped tying my self worth to my revenue numbers
> 2. I focussed primarily on helping more people, better
>
> Turns out when you do number 2, you make money anyway.
>
> Who'd have thought it, eh?
>
> If I could give you one lesson from this:
>
> Set yourself a goal. Do everything you can to hit that goal.
>
> But, I guarantee:
>
> You'll never be fully satisfied with a revenue number.
>
> You'll always ALWAYS want more.
>
> And unless you have a reason for needing more, it's basically pointless numbers on a screen.
>
> Focus more on your own enjoyment.
>
> Make sure you are having fun first.
>
> THAT is WAY more satisfying than any revenue number.
>
> ✌️

## Post 175 — 2025-12-19

**Likes:** 299 | **Comments:** 163 | **Shares:** 7

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mattjbarker1_you-have-a-full-time-job-you-want-to-quit-activity-7407766224685699072-5-cX)

> You have a full time job. You want to quit ASAP. So you started posting on LinkedIn. You created a digital product because you saw multi-millionaire creators (the 0.001% of creators who made it big) saying it’s what you should do (sorry, they lied). You’re not making as much money as you hoped. 
>
> Don’t panic.
>
> Everyone started from zero. I quit my job and went freelance 3 years ago and now run a multi 6 figure one person business. I’ve been through the tough start and made it out. I only made $1,123 in my first 3 months freelancing. Sucked.
>
> But by the end of the first year, I was doing $10k/month. 
>
> The real truth: I didn’t make $10k/month from digital products.
>
> Here’s the best way to start making money (and basically my exact step by step journey from $0 → $30k/month):
>
> 1. Ditch the digital product
> 2. Offer a DFY (Done For You) service (charge more, get recurring revenue)
> 3. Work with any clients that come your way
> 4. Decide which ones you hated working with
> 5. Decide which ones you loved working with
> 6. Position yourself on LinkedIn to work with the ones you loved
> 7. Work with 5+ of those clients you love
> 8. Prove you can get results → get testimonials
> 9. Use those testimonials to get more clients
> 10. Keep getting results DFY until confident of two things:
> 11. One: who needs your solution the most
> 12. Two: how they achieve it (aka your system)
> 13. Transition from DFY → DWY (Done With You)
> 14. Because you’re not doing it for clients, you can take on more clients
> 15. Less time per client → more scale
> 16. Keep getting results for DWY clients
> 17. Create a course that shows how you get results for clients
> 18. Now you can sell three things:
> 19. One: DFY as your premium offer (most expensive)
> 20. Two: DWY as your core offer (most popular core offer)
> 21. Three: Course (cheapest way to learn from you)
> 22. Create an automated email sequence that sells your course
> 23. Send all social traffic to email sequence
> 24. Upsell course buyers into your DWY service
> 25. Upsell DWY buyers into DFY (if you want to)
>
> This is the best way, in my humble opinion.
>
> You learn everything you need to as a one person business owner on the way. The hard way. And it puts you in a better position long term to run a consistent business.
>
> Don’t panic. Don’t give up. Adapt and put the hard work in.
>
> Hope this helps anyone just getting started or is soon to be a freelancer!
>
> You got this :)
>
> P.S. day 3 of posting my top 15 posts of 2025 so you model them for YOUR LinkedIn, starting Jan 1st 26. 
>
> Follow along for the rest here → Matt Barker

> 3. Give actionable advice for the reader
> 4. Finish the post with a RELEVANT CTA
>
> (pic attached)
>
> The key is the relevant CTA.
>
> This post pictured was about how I spent the first 30 minutes of my 90 minute writing session doing nothing, because that nothing unlocks writing goodness.
>
> Takeaway:
>
> Write simple, valuable posts.
>
> Then supplement the post with a natural next step.
>
> e.g. free book / course / thing
>
> Try it out! 
>
> ✌️
>
> If you're reading this, you're active on LinkedIn in December.
>
> December's a weird month on LinkedIn.
>

> Here’s 3 LinkedIn writing lessons from showing up in December 4 years in a row:
>
> 1. It's a good time for Recap Mode
>
> Recap Mode = recapping your year. What went well? What went bad? What did you hate / love? What will you do differently next year? Everyone's looking back at the year in December, so join them!
>
> 2. Writing feels easier when you follow the mood
>
> Duno about you but nothing in me feels "strategic" in December. I've got presents on my mind. I've got family, friends, events, things on my mind. I'm winding down not winding up. My advice: follow that. If people are winding down, wind down with them. Don't push square pegs into round holes.
>
> 3. Posting less in December does not hurt growth
>
> January is THE #1 month on LinkedIn to post. 50% of people are annoyed about being back at work, doomscrolling when they should be working. The other 50% are buzzing to be back at it, motivated. You'll make up for any lost ground in January.
>
> Takeaway:
>
> Take it easy in December.
>
> I get you want to keep momentum. 
>
> But ENJOY your writing. Make that the priority.
>
> If you enjoy it you're gonna want to do it. And it won't feel like a chore / pain over the holiday szn.
>
> It'll feel easy :)

>
> Do more of what worked. Save time writing.
>
> Here's my exact 15 step process to repurpose my best LinkedIn posts (in under 10 minutes):
>
> 1. Go to magicpost.in
> 2. Go to Metrics
> 3. Select last 30 days
> 4. Sort by likes
> 5. Click on a post
> 6. Click Save as template
> 7. Go to New post
> 8. Select Template mode
> 9. Find the template you saved
> 10. Click Use this template
> 11. Select Close similarity
> 12. Write an opinionated subject, 5-10 sentences
> 13. Click Generate a post
> 14. Tweak and edit to make it ‘you’
> 15. Schedule to post

> This saves me hours every week writing LinkedIn posts.

> How quick plans are made.

>
> London has 9,000,000 people.

>
> In London, if you want to make plans with someone, it often requires texting them 4 weeks in advance just to get an afternoon / evening with them.
>
> Maybe 2 weeks if you're lucky.
>
> Everyone's so busy going to new places, seeing new people.
>
> And to meet up with a friend, it's normally a 45+ minute tube journey there and another 45+ minutes back.
>
> But it makes me laugh when, in Cyprus, this little island, it's the TOTAL opposite.
>
> If you want to go for lunch with a friend, all it takes is a text 2 days before, if that, and you're locked in ready to go.
>
> 10/15 minutes in your car. Easy.
>
> Weirdly, when I moved to Cyprus, I hated this spontaneity.
>
> But now I've come full circle. I love it.
>
> And now I resent London for making it hard to see friends!

> But I'm normal and honest enough to admit it.

>
> I advise my clients (and myself) to do this in as many posts as possible.
>
> Because writing from YOUR Lived Experience is the best way to stand out in the feed and put your hooks + posts in a category of one.
>
> You never have to compete, that way.
>
> But here's where I proved myself wrong:
>
> My 3rd most 'liked' post from last week, said 'you' in the hook.
>
> Not 'I'.
>
> In theory, anyone could've wrote this hook.
>
> Meaning my post was immediately a commodity.
>
> But it still performed well.
>
> Lesson:
>
> You HAVE to experiment. You HAVE to try different things.
>
> Because you just do not know what will work, and what won't.
>
> Sometimes, you'll surprise yourself.
>
> p.s. i still advise clients, myself (and you) to use 'I' in hooks. this will, long term, grow your reputation faster / better than using 'you' all the time. the goal here in 2025 and beyond is to be unique.

## Post 234 — 2025-11-13

**Likes:** 381 | **Comments:** 167 | **Shares:** 7

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mattjbarker1_hold-my-beer-save-yourself-10-months-learning-activity-7394720012135006209-mk5M)

> Hold my beer. Save yourself 10 months learning LinkedIn. 
>
> And copy my 3 step writing process:
>
> (i’ve written over 5,000 posts using this)
>
> 1. Write the hook FIRST
>
> - Hook first drives direction of the post
> - Stops me swerving off writing nonsense
> - Gives my writing purpose from the off
> - Helps me stay on topic throughout
> - Directs focus on the problem I’m solving
>
> 6 hook templates for you to try:
>
> - How to {dream outcome} without {main obstacle}
> - The best way to {dream outcome}
> - How I {dream outcome} in {specific timeframe}
> - My biggest struggles as a {type of person} were:
> - It’s weird {type of person} still use {tool} to {outcome}.
> - I’ve been {action} for {timeframe}.
>
> 2. Share stupidly, weirdly transparent details
>
> - I educate with 75% of my posts
> - It keeps people coming back to my posts
> - Share every detail of your process
> - If you think it’s boring, it’s not - i PROMISE you
> - People are obsessed with behind the scenes stuff
> - Help the reader solve a problem on the spot
> - Add context to the detail you give
> - Relate to own experiences, stories, learnings
> - Actionable, actionable, actionable.
>
> 4 ways to structure educational posts:
>
> - Problem → list why it’s bad → quick solution
> - Hook → step by step guide → TL;DR
> - Hook → numbered list of insights → summary
> - Problem → agitate → solution
>
> 3. Sign off the post
>
> - Simple takeaway the reader can remember
> - Last line read → last thing they remember
> - People forget the point of the post by the end
> - Need to remind them or the message gets lost
> - Emotional endings create action
> - Think about it: beginning → middle → end
> - Catch the reader off guard right at the end
> - Make them think, laugh, sob, something
>
> 6 simple methods to sign off a post:
>
> - A ‘yes or no’ question
> - A motivational line
> - An abrupt, sudden ending
> - A funny comment
> - A single emoji (i like ✌️)
> - A Callback → re-iterating the hook
>
> Then, schedule each post in magicpost.in and finito!
>
> I’ve used this silly, simple writing process for 3+ years.
>
> Over 5,000 posts.
>
> And now magicpost.in is the engine I run it through.
>
> Never fails me.
>
> ✌️

## Post 256 — 2025-11-02

**Likes:** 292 | **Comments:** 170 | **Shares:** 3

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mattjbarker1_rule-for-well-anyone-respect-your-boundaries-activity-7390658232714727424-vbMS)

> Rule for well, anyone: respect your boundaries. 
>
> But if you're running a business (like me) or side hustle or even if you're employed, here's 3 boundary rules I tend to live by:
>  
> 1. Say no to "hopping on quick calls" 
>  
> I've had 100s of enquiries and messages from "leads" asking to "hop on a quick call to discuss" pricing, details, how my offer works. I remember doing a couple of these when I first started out. But they never bought anything. They were often the busy type who like to talk more than they listen. 
>  
> The only people you should hop on a quick call with is your family and friends. 
>  
> 2. Don't take work that isn't your speciality 
>  
> Just this week a friend messaged and asked if I could take on a gig writing copy for their brand's adverts. I love that they messaged me and I'd have loved to take on a gig that isn't my normal LinkedIn writing consulting. But it's not my speciality - I'd have to figure it out. And the outcome would likely not be as good. 
>  
> If you get asked to take something on that isn't what you normally offer, respectfully decline and pass it on to someone else. 
>  
> 3. Work when YOU want to work 
>  
> The main reason I love not working in an office or being employed is because I can LITERALLY work whenever I want. I decide. I set the expectations with clients and customers and they respect that because that's how my business works. I like to think that my clients work with me because they like the sound of how I work and how I can help them. 
>  
> The minute you start working out of the hours you want to work, you've lost control. 
>  
> Don't get me wrong, it's not easy. 
>  
> You want to please people and make more cash and have happy clients. 
>  
> But nothing makes me happier than a calendar I have designed for myself. 
>  
> Respect your boundaries and design your life.
>
> P.S. I wrote a 30 page book with more strategies I used to grow my LinkedIn audience and turn it into money.
>

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mattjbarker1_this-list-of-linkedin-writing-rules-isnt-activity-7389646656138399744-7cIG)

> This list of LinkedIn writing rules isn't for YOU.
>
> It's for ME 4 years ago who:
>
> - had no clue what i was doing
> - had no clue how to write
> - had no clue what to write about
>
> Winging it like a champ.
>
> Well, these are 10 LinkedIn writing rules for any beginners who are JUST starting in 2025:
>
> 1. Start with timelines. e.g. "Last week, I".
> 2. Only write about YOUR experiences.
> 3. Take specific problems. Give solutions.
> 4. Use full stops, colons and bulleted lists.
> 5. Avoid overly "selly" language. Be helpful.
> 6. Add credibility sentences to gain reader trust.
> 7. Always end posts with actionable takeaways.
> 8. Recycle posts. Tweak hooks + formatting.
> 9. Don't be scared of failing. Test. Try things.
> 10. Add people, pain and payoff to hooks.
>
> (tip: i schedule all my posts in magicpost.in to save time and stay on schedule with my posting. makes a big big difference to my sanity in the week)
>
> Reminder:
>
> If you're a beginner, you're gonna be bad.
>
> Every beginner is. But it's how you improve that matters.
>
> Take these rules. Put them to work. Learn.
>
> Save this list → grow your LinkedIn writing chops!
>
> What rule would you add, for any beginners reading?

> You don't get 100+ likes for spending hours on 1 LinkedIn post.

> I'd never have hit 183,011 followers, if it was true.

> Here's a simple 6 step writing system I wish everyone would use to write LInkedIn posts 2x faster:
>
> 1. Go to your LinkedIn analytics
> 2. Find a post that popped off
> 3. Create a template of it
> 4. Save it in your magicpost.in template library
> 5. Next time you write, pick a template
> 6. Change the topic / experience / info
>
> Best thing about this?
>
> NOT the time saved on writing. But how it forces you to do more of what works. 
>
> You increase the % chance that it “wins” again.
>
> Extra tip: time yourself writing. Sit down. Set a timer for 15 minutes. Finish one post. Reset the timer. Repeat. 
>
> Every great LinkedIn creator does this:

> Find the winner → do more of the winner.
>
> Fast and easy way to write LinkedIn posts.

> ✌️

## Post 266 — 2025-10-28

**Likes:** 219 | **Comments:** 137 | **Shares:** 1

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mattjbarker1_i-took-a-60-minute-call-with-a-ghostwriting-activity-7388846315805503488-MsM3)

> I took a 60 minute call with a ghostwriting agency last week. Their client's LinkedIn posts impressions were struggling in October. I gave them 3 pieces of advice:
>
> 1. Mix up your content
>
> Their predictable story-post format was alienating audiences who engage with different emotional triggers (e.g. humour, education). They needed to diversify their formats (carousels, polls, images) and sentiments to start reaching more of their target audience.
>  
> 2. Align profile with content
>
> LinkedIn has made it clear the last 18 months they want experts in defined niches posting about their expert topic. That means profile and content has to match what LinkedIn thinks you're an expert in. Their client's profiles need to explicitly say what their niche is, signal credibility and show that in their content.
>  
> 3. Prioritise saveable content
>
> LinkedIn's new analytics means we can track saves and sends. Awesome. We couldn't see this before. But we knew it was important anyway. Doesn't take a genius to figure out if you create content that's really interesting, people will share it with their friends / peers, which means you multiply your reach very fast (aka going viral). Goal: make highly actionable content that people HAVE to save or they feel like they're losing out on something they'd otherwise have to pay for.
>
> TL;DR:
>
> 1. Mix up your content
> 2. Align profile with content
> 3. Prioritise saveable content
>
> If your posts aren't getting it done for you?
>
> Try new things.
>
> I'll show you what and how here: https://lnkd.in/eXrf8mV3
>
> Something stops working → fix it.
>
> ✌️

> Yesterday, I noticed someone I used to see EVERYWHERE on LinkedIn had vanished. No posts for 2 months. No mention of their business anywhere.
>
> Gone.
>
> They were the type to post revenue screenshots.
>
> Hype up their growth. Hype up their lifestyle.
>
> But now it's like it literally never happened.
>
> Mad.
>
> Made me think about what's kept me going for (nearly) 4 years.
>
> - without burning out
> - without any wild pivots
> - without any disappearing acts
>
> Here's 4 reasons I think have made the difference, why I'm still posting 4 years later (and why so many others disappear):
>
> 1. I never relied on hype to build my brand
>
> If your posts are entirely win / dopamine focused it's hard to sustain that. Not for your audience. But for YOU. Can't stay in the game for 20+ years if YOU aren't able to show up consistently and steadily, not sensationally and overly focussed on hype.
>
> (tip: use magicpost.in to schedule and manage posts. thank me later 🫡)
>
> 2. I built a system I could maintain
>
> A lot of business coaches talk about "seasons". I love that idea. One season you go hard. The next, you take it slower. I've flirted with that this year. Summer I went hard. Now I've slowed down a touch. But I've always designed my workflow around what I can keep doing long term, at a sustainable level. I personally am not an up and down person. I'm steady. So it makes consistency easy.
>
> 3. I never tied my identity to short-term success
>
> I've built my identity online as someone who shows up regardless. Whether the likes are down, whether the impressions are down, whether business is down. Doesn't matter. I'm showing up. And I believe my audience feels that. They know they can rely on me for that. And I know I can rely on myself for that instead of valuing myself on short term / vanity things.
>
> 4. I’m okay being boring
>
> I've said before - I'm not the "sexiest" creator to follow on LinkedIn. I'm also not the most groundbreaking, hyper growth and scaling businessman to follow. Because people don't really find "doing the work" that sexy. It doesn't make a very interesting, hype worthy marketing campaign. Unfortunately for you - but fortunately for me - I'm okay with that. And it's exactly what has kept me sustainable and getting results.
>
> TL;DR:
>
> 1. I never relied on hype to build my brand
> 2. I built a system I could maintain
> 3. I never tied my identity to short-term success
> 4. I’m okay being boring
>
> Consistency beats hype. Every time.
>
> If you wanna stay in this game long enough to properly win:
>
> BUILD. FOR. ENDURANCE.
>
> Not high fives from strangers on the internet.
>
> 🫠

> Client's post wasn't performing well in the first 60 minutes. 
>
> They messaged me freaking out, wondering why.
>
> My response is always the same:
>
> Let's see where it's at tomorrow.
>
> Why?
>
> Because LinkedIn isn't what it used to be.
>
> In 2023, if you post and your engagement and impressions were shit in the first 60 minutes, your post would end up performing shit.
>
> In 2025, if you post and your engagement and impressions are shit in the first 60 minutes, your post can still perform well.
>
> Why?
>
> Because LinkedIn prioritises relevance > recency now.
>
> Your post can look like a shocker after 60 minutes.
>
> But 24 hours later, suddenly catch fire and start getting engagement and getting pushed out.
>
> So I always recommend to my clients:
>
> Don't judge your post performance on the first hour.
>
> Judge it tomorrow.
>
> Or even next week.
>
> My final piece of advice on this:
>
> This is a GOOD thing.
>
> We used to create content and it was gone within a day.
>
> You spend time writing, creating all for 24 hours of opportunity, tops.
>
> Now, you can spend time writing and creating and it can last days, weeks, even months in the feed.
>
> Your content now gets more ROI for longer.
>
> This is a GOOD thing.
>
> 👍
>
> p.s. this client's post ended up getting 150+ likes and 100+ comments despite getting just 33 likes in the first 60 minutes. it'll probably hit 200 likes after a week.

> Weird observation about my linkedin posts last week:
>
> The top 3 engaged posts were all self deprecating.
>
> (self deprecating = basically, take the piss out yerself)
>
> Check out the hooks I wrote:
>
> 1. "My life is incredibly boring on paper:"
>
> 2. "Yesterday I was feeling super tired, demotivated to work and not at my "peak". I realised why:"
>
> 3. "On Monday I got this comment from a stranger. Really cool. But people say I'm an idiot."
>
> I don't speak highly of myself.
>
> Boring. Tired. Demotivated. Idiot.
>
> But this isn't by accident or because I hate myself:
>
> It's on purpose.
>
> And I do this because:
>
> - people resonate with failure
> - people resonate with vulnerability
> - people resonate with honesty
>
> Yes, people are drawn to results / wins / numbers.
>
> But this kinda stuff stands out.
>
> While everyone else is high-fiving themselves, I'm calling myself an idiot :) 
>
> There's an art to it, of course.
>
> Here's how you can write self deprecating hooks:
>
> 1. Think about a recent win or recent milestone
> 2. Flip it and think about your life before that
> 3. Start with the struggle in the life before
> 4. Think about the negative points
> 5. Talk to the "you" before you "won"
>
> Resonate with the pain → get more engagement.

> And you don't ALWAYS want to be posting for your existing audience. You gotta find new people too.
>
> Repurposing isn't cheating.
>
> It's a fast and easy posting strategy.
>
> Try my simple repurposing framework:
>
> 1. Go to magicpost.in metrics and analytics
> 2. Find posts from 3+ months ago
> 3. Pick your top 5-10 performers
> 4. Update the hook if needed
> 5. Repost without guilt
>
> Your best posts are your best posts for a reason.
>
> Don't just let it fizzle away into the internet.
>
> Resurface old posts → stay consistent + don't crash out.

> You'll slaughter me for this. But I reckon my first 96 LinkedIn posts taught me more than any university degree would've.
>
> Not because those 96 posts smashed.
>
> But because they were TERRIBLE.
>
> 3 lessons I learned about writing online and linkedin growth, by failing in public 96 times:
>
> 1. Your early posts aren't practice. They're data.
>
> Most people delete their "failed" posts and pretend they never happened. This kills your ability to learn what resonates. I kept every post live and studied the patterns instead.
>
> 2. Consistency beats perfection every single time
>
> Most people wait for the "perfect" post before they start showing up. This keeps them stuck in endless editing cycles. I published imperfect posts daily and improved through repetition.
>
> 3. Your breakthrough is always one post away
>
> Most people give up right before their content finds its audience. This means they never discover what works for them. I treated every "flop" as one step closer to my first viral post.
>
> TL;DR:
>
> Your early posts aren't failures.
>
> They're free tuition for your LinkedIn education.
>
> The data you collect from "failing" is more valuable than the likes you get from playing it safe.
>
> Stop deleting your learning → Start studying your patterns.

## Post 328 — 2025-09-26

[View on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mattjbarker1_in-the-last-6-months-ive-audited-107-linkedin-activity-7377234883351572480-hy4g)

> In the last 6 months, I’ve audited 107 LinkedIn posts for clients.
>
> The most common problem isn’t lack of experience. It’s this:
>
> They’re unsure how to write FROM their Lived Experience.
>
> Writing generic advice → easy to share.
> Writing from Lived Experience → easy to trust.
>
> More trust = more $$$ opportunities.
>
> Here’s 5 steps to turn your Lived Experience into LinkedIn posts that actually make your reader think “YES, I trust this person”:
>
> 1. Start with something you’ve actually done
>
> Don’t write “10 tips for growing on LinkedIn” if you haven’t grown on LinkedIn. Instead write: “When I started posting on LinkedIn, I thought I had to be a great writer. Turns out, I didn’t.” Use your story as the entry point. That’s what makes it feel real.
>
> 2. Use first-person language
>
> Write using “I”, “me” and “my”. Not “you should” because that’s generic advice that anyone could write. When you say “I struggled with…” or “I realised that…” you are pulling people into your actual experience.
>
> 3. Use real context
>
> When did this happen? What were you trying to do? What was the challenge? The more specific the context, the more relatable your post becomes.
>
> 4. Talk about what changed
>
> What was the realisation? What did you figure out? What decision did you make People don’t just want to know what you did, they want to know how you got there so they can also get there.
>
> 5. Show small wins, not just big numbers
>
> You don’t need to pull out crazy, multi million dollar revenue screenshots to build credibility. In fact, I’d argue that makes you less credible and less believable. Even simple lines like: "I used to average 200 impressions but now I’m seeing 2,000 regularly"…are enough to show realistic, attainable progress without feeling like you’re bragging.
>
> TL;DR:
>
> This is how you write from Lived Experience.
>
> It’s simple, relatable and human.
>
> You’ve already got the content because you’ve lived it.
>
> You just need to start documenting it ✌️
>
> This is just ONE strategy I teach my clients to grow their LinkedIn audience.
>
> Here’s a 30 page book I wrote with more strategies for you (for free): https://lnkd.in/eJvYp7wa

> I've spent the last 4 years writing on LinkedIn.
>
> Most people who try fail at this:
>
> Writing concisely.
>
> Because the majority of people use 100 words to say something they could easily say in 10.
>
> Less words = more impact, clearer message.
>
> Here's 3 tried and tested lessons to write concisely on LinkedIn (without spending years studying copywriting or spending $100s on courses): 
>  
> 1. Play "dumb" 
>  
> No, I don't mean act like a dumb person.
>
> I mean, the simpler your language the better. 
>  
> The simpler your language, the more people will understand it. The less brain power it takes to read it. The more broadly engaging your posts will be.
>  
> Write like you're writing for a 7 year old. 
>
> 2. Cut pointless words 
>  
> If the word doesn't add anything, cut it. 
>  
> I mean words like this: 
>  
> 'So therefore my hypothesis and conclusion that derived from the absolute centre of the epitomy of where I was aiming to land' 
>  
> Nah, just write: 
>  
> 'The result:' 
>  
> Quicker and easier. 
>  
> 3. Write (mostly) short sentences 
>  
> The pure breed writers will slaughter me. 
>  
> The new age digital writers will love me. 
>  
> Keep sentences short. In 1s or 3s ideally. And make use of bullet points and full stops, not commas. 
>  
> If you're using 2 commas in a sentence, start again. 
>  
> TL;DR:
>
> People get bored easy. 
>  
> I do. I barely read or watch anything unless I know it's gonna be useful to me or make me laugh.
>  
> So if you're new to this LinkedIn writing, keep it concise, clear, hit post and get the f**k outta there)
>  
> Don't waste anyone's time. 
>
> Are you a concise writer or a waffler?

> Searching one location for ideas → focussed.
>
> Focussed ideas = easy, quick, fun writing.
>
> Here's 3 rules I stick to when writing LinkedIn posts that help me write unlimited content (without just pressing a button in ChatGPT):
>
> 1. Write about stuff I've actually done
>
> Most people look at writing online completely wrong. 
>
> They write about trending topics, ideas and news, because they want to catch on to what's popular and ride the wave.
>
> This is no good.
>
> Because when you write about random stuff, it means your posts are rarely relevant to what you actually do.
>
> Instead I write about stuff I've actually done. In the last week, month, year. Outcomes, results, failures, mistakes, problems.
>
> When you write about the stuff you're doing you don't need to actually create content.
>
> You just need to document it which is really easy.
>
> 2. Ask "can anyone else write this?"
>
> 99% of the content on LinkedIn could be copy and pasted on someone else's feed and you wouldn't bat an eyelid.
>
> The leadership space is wild for this. Basic generic advice / lists of tips that literally anyone could post. 
>
> This is a brilliant way to NOT stand out.
>
> So I try to ask myself "can anyone else write this?".
>
> If the answer is yes, I'll add more uniquely relevant experiences to my post.
>
> (e.g. this post, I write from my perspective. my own rules i set. I'm not shouting generic stuff at you)
>
> 3. Enjoy the process and have fun
>
> In 2023 and 2024 I had a pretty rough time on LinkedIn.
>
> You probably never even noticed if you were following along. My posts were flying engagement was great. But I got so stuck in the routine, frameworks, strategy that I literally started resenting writing my posts. Not a good place to be because writing is something I enjoy and sell for a living.
>
> So this year I loosened up and doubled down on just enjoying the process. 
>
> I wake up every Monday looking forward to write and schedule my posts for the week in magicpost.in.
>
> And I look forward to helping my CEO, Founder and Leader clients, showing them new ways I'm making my writing process fun, so they can too.
>
> TL;DR:
>
> Do stuff. Write about it. Make it your own.
>
> Anything you'd add?

> 2025 bilan: What I got wrong (and what actually worked):
>
> 1. Influencer marketing would drive major revenue
>
> ↳ Spoiler: it didn't.
>
> Performance fell short compared to 2024. We adjusted projections mid-year and invested in SEO and Affiliate. Best decision we made.
>
>
> 2. Hiring fast = scaling fast
>
> ↳ Learned this one the hard way. Our first sales hire didn't work out. Wrong fit, wrong timing. Now? We prioritize alignment over urgency.
>
> Human fit > hard skills.
>
>
> 3. B2C would be our main growth driver
>
> ↳ Plot twist:
>
> B2B accelerated faster than expected. Focused on agencies, landed significant deals (shoutout to Matt Barker for the assist 🙌).
>
> 4. Black Friday wouldn't move the needle
>
> ↳ Wrong again. These 2 weeks crushed it. Combined with our B2B push, we hit 3x MRR growth.
>
> 5. Product features alone would sell themselves
>
> ↳ Nope. Enhanced the product, yes. But realized we need B2B-specific improvements and a robust sales strategy for 2026.
>
> 6. Doubling prices would tank growth
>
> ↳ Expected a major dip. Didn't happen. Instead, it repositioned us upmarket and reflected our actual product evolution. The right customers stayed. Better customers arrived.
>
> 7. Every challenge means you're failing
>
> ↳ This year was tough. Really tough.
>
> But also?
>
> Incredibly successful. Sometimes both things are true at the same time.
>
> Here's what I know for sure:
>
> Strategy shifts aren't failures. They're survival.
>
> And I'm grateful for everyone who supported us through the mistakes, and the wins.
>
> 2026, let's go. 💜
>
> P.S. What's the biggest strategy shift YOU made in 2025? Did it work?
> ___

>
> I still can't believe that Richard invited me in.
> And that Matt took time to answer my questions about content and posting.
>
> Sales isn’t about convincing.
> It’s about connecting.
>
> Every part of business is sales.
>
> Hiring.
> Leadership.
> Culture.
>
> We’re all selling ideas.
> And most of the time, people stop buying in
> because the message isn’t clear.
>
> If your people systems don’t sell clarity,
> you’re selling confusion.
>
> And the same principle applies to writing.
>
> Matt reminded us that the most effective writing,
> the kind that actually makes people feel something,
> comes from being human.
>
> Here are the 5 takeaways I got from yesterday:
>
> 1. Don't be stiff
> If you sound too "corporate", people scroll past/tune out.
>
> 2. Stop performing.
> Most people aren’t watching you as closely as you think.
> Say what you actually mean.
>
> 3. Write from lived experiences.
> That’s the part people trust.
> And the part they remember.
>
> 4. Don’t outsource your honesty.
> AI can help, but it can’t tell your story.
> Only you can do that.
>
> 5. Use tools to accelerate clarity, not replace it.
> Creativity is human. Tools are leverage.

>
> Leadership, HR, and entrepreneurship

>
> Clear communication that creates belief.
>

> and the reminder that strong systems
> (and strong writing)
> are built on connection, not persuasion.

> I've had four clients land job offers in the past four weeks! 
>
> Something they all had in common? 
>
> Patient persistence amidst rejection. 
>
> All of them had been searching for some time and weren't naive to the challenges of today's market.
>
> They have each faced significant resistance in their searches. 
>
> All four had multiple instances of getting to late round or final round interviews only to be rejected. 
>
> They gave themselves grace in those most painful moments, recognized when they were worn out, and weren't ashamed to pause or step away for a moment or a season before recommitting to the search.
>
> Some took on contracts or stopgap roles, viewing these as part of the journey. Others remained patient in their current role.
>
> They prioritized relationships and played the long game, with connections cultivated over months or even years (across both existing contacts and strangers). 
>
> They were bold in asking others for advice and sharing what they learned, building up advocates who believed in them and went out of their way to help. 
>
> Even when some connections ghosted them or didn't follow through, they did their best not to take it personally and kept moving. 
>
> All four invested deeply in interview prep, not just in telling good stories about themselves but also in connecting these to their target company's challenges and goals (and all of them created presentations to demonstrate how they'd approach the role).
>
> After interview processes that ended in rejection, they took time to debrief what worked and what could be improved, viewing each as an opportunity to practice and get better. 
>
> They maintained positive connections with their interviewers (in fact, two of the four landed offers at companies who had previously rejected them).
>
> And they leveraged their coach (me!) for tactical support, accountability, and encouragement throughout the highs and lows of their journeys.
>
> In the end, all four landed incredible offers at companies they're hyped about. 
>
> As a coach, I'm SO PROUD of the immense work and effort they each put in to reach this achievement. 
>
> I'm honored to get to walk with them in both those times of celebration and those especially tough moments. There's so much more to these stories than a single "I'm excited to announce" post. 
>
> Rejection is sadly a common part of today's job search, and I do not want to downplay how painful it is. All four of my clients experienced the deep frustration of repeatedly getting ghosted and passed over.
>
> But they continued to show up, took breaks when needed, and didn't let any one "failed attempt" stop them from patiently pushing forward to the next opportunity.
>
> Congrats to these four job seekers! You know who you are :) 
>
> And to all the other folks out there on this same journey, keep going. 
>
> It's only a matter of time before your persistence pays off.

>
> It’s not about spilling every secret.
> It’s about showing you’re human.
> It’s about giving people a reason to care.
>
> So I’m slowly bringing stories back into my writing.

> Not every detail of my life needs to be online.
